Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool and slice into rounds.
For the herring version, arrange the pickled fillets on the butter, scatter with red onion and dill.
For the shrimp version, bind them with mayonnaise and mound on top of the egg slices.
Garnish each open sandwich with sliced radish and a sprig of fresh dill, serve at once, chilled.

karjalanpiirakka.d: Thin rye crusts shaped into little boats, filled with a milk-and-rice porridge and baked in a very hot oven until the edges blister. Served with munavoi, a butter mashed with hard-boiled egg, a breakfast staple.
s: Cook the rice in the milk over very low heat for 40 minutes, stirring often, into a thick porridge.
Knead rye flour, flour, water and salt into a firm dough, rest 20 minutes.
Roll the dough paper-thin, cut ovals and thin the edges further.
Fill the centre with rice porridge, fold the edges in, pinching to form an open little boat.
Bake 15 minutes at 250°C, brush with melted butter on coming out and serve warm with munavoi.

plokkfiskur.d: A dish born to waste nothing: leftover poached cod or haddock, roughly flaked into a light béchamel with potatoes, served with dark rye bread traditionally steamed by volcanic ground heat.
s: Poach the cod for 8 minutes in barely simmering, lightly salted water, drain and roughly flake.
Boil the potatoes, drain and dice.
Sweat the sliced onion in butter, dust with flour and whisk in the milk for a light béchamel.
Add the curry powder, flaked fish and potatoes, fold gently without crushing.
Warm through gently for 5 minutes without boiling, serve with dark rye bread and a little butter.

irish-stew.d: A mutton or lamb stew so simple it traditionally holds only meat, potatoes, onions and water — not even a carrot originally, its thickness coming purely from the potatoes breaking down as they cook.
s: Cut the lamb into large chunks, peel the potatoes, onions and carrots.
Layer meat, onions, carrots and half the potatoes in a pot.
Cover with the water, add the bay leaves, cover and let it barely simmer for 1h30 over very low heat.
Add the remaining potatoes cut into large chunks and cook a further 30 minutes, until they break down slightly and thicken the broth.
Adjust the seasoning, scatter with chopped parsley and serve piping hot in deep bowls.

svickova.d: A beef sirloin marinated then braised on a bed of root vegetables — carrot, celery, parsnip — blended into a creamy, tangy sauce, served with knedlíky bread dumplings and a spoonful of cranberry preserve.
s: Marinate the beef overnight with the sliced roots, vinegar, bay and spices.
Brown the meat larded with bacon, then add the marinade vegetables and braise 2 hours covered.
Remove the meat, blend the vegetable sauce with the cream until smooth and velvety.
Make the knedlíky dough with flour, yeast, egg and milk, shape into logs and poach 20 minutes in boiling water.
Slice the beef, coat with sauce, serve with sliced knedlíky and a spoonful of cranberry preserve.

sarmale.d: Whole fermented cabbage leaves, rolled around minced pork, rice and dill, simmered for hours in an earthenware pot until the cabbage turns meltingly soft. A Christmas staple, even better reheated the next day.
s: Gently peel the leaves off the fermented cabbage, trim any overly thick ribs.
Mix minced pork, raw rice, chopped onion and chopped dill, season with salt and pepper.
Place a spoonful of filling at the edge of each leaf and roll tightly, folding in the sides.
Line the bottom of a pot with bacon lardons and shredded cabbage, pack in the rolls tightly, cover with tomato and water to the top.
Simmer covered for 2 hours over very low heat, adding water if needed, until the cabbage is meltingly soft.

banitsa.d: Filo sheets crumpled by hand, never stacked flat, layered with a mix of sirene white cheese and beaten eggs. On New Year's Eve, a small folded paper predicting the year's fortune is hidden inside.
s: Crumble the sirene cheese and mash it with a fork with three beaten eggs.
Butter each filo sheet generously, crumple it carelessly into a loose heap.
Arrange the crumpled sheets in circles in a buttered round tin, filling in with cheese as you go.
Whisk the remaining two eggs with the yoghurt and baking soda, pour over the top.
Bake 35 minutes at 180°C until puffed and well browned on top, let cool slightly before cutting.

pasticada.d: A beef roast larded with bacon and carrot, marinated two days in vinegar and wine before braising with prunes and cloves into an almost sweet sauce. A Dalmatian wedding dish, never cooked for an ordinary day.
s: Lard the roast with sticks of bacon and carrot using a sharp knife.
Marinate it 2 days in the fridge in the wine, vinegar, onion and cloves.
Drain and brown the meat all over, then moisten with the strained marinade and tomato.
Braise covered for 3 hours over very low heat, adding the prunes halfway through.
Remove the meat, reduce the sauce and blend it with the prunes, slice the roast and coat generously.

karadjordjeva-snicla.d: A pork escalope pounded flat then rolled around kajmak, a fermented cream cheese, before being breaded and fried. Created in the 1950s to honour a national hero, shaped like a roll to echo the medal he wore.
s: Pound thin pork escalopes with a mallet to 3 mm thickness.
Place a spoonful of kajmak at the centre of each escalope and roll tightly, closing the ends with a toothpick.
Coat each roll in flour, beaten egg then breadcrumbs, pressing well to adhere.
Repeat the breading a second time for a thicker, crunchier crust.
Fry at 170°C until the roll is golden, let it rest a minute before slicing.

fenkata.d: Rabbit, the king of Maltese tables, first fried with garlic then simmered in red wine until the meat falls off the bone. Traditionally served in two courses: the sauce over pasta first, the meat afterwards.
s: Cut the rabbit into pieces, marinate it 1 hour in the wine with crushed garlic and bay.
Drain the meat and brown it in olive oil in a large pot.
Add the sliced onion, sweat, then moisten with the marinade and tomato.
Cover and simmer 1h30 over low heat until the meat falls off the bone.
Cook the spaghetti, serve it first coated with the sauce, then the rabbit as a second course, scattered with parsley.

judd-mat-gaardebounen.d: Luxembourg's national dish: smoked pork collar, desalted then simmered until tender, served in thick slices with broad beans and a roux sauce bound with the cooking broth.
s: Desalt the smoked collar for 12 hours in cold water, changing the water once.
Poach it 2 hours in fresh water with onion, carrot and bay, at a gentle simmer.
Shell the broad beans and cook them separately with a sprig of savory until tender.
Make a roux with butter and flour, moisten with a little of the cooking broth, whisking to a coating consistency.
Slice the meat, serve with the beans and coat with the hot sauce.

souvla.d: Large chunks of pork or lamb threaded onto a long spit and hand-turned over the coals for hours, in a Sunday ritual that gathers the whole family around the charcoal.
s: Cut the pork into large 5 cm cubes, marinate 2 hours with oil, lemon juice, oregano and bay.
Thread the cubes onto a long spit, interspersing bay leaves.
Turn the spit over moderate coals for 3 to 4 hours, basting regularly with marinade.
Twenty minutes before the end, add slices of halloumi on a grill alongside to char.
Serve the meat pulled from the spit with the grilled halloumi, fresh lemon and warm pita bread.

potica.d: A very thin risen dough, stretched on a clean cloth then rolled tightly around a filling of ground walnuts, honey and cinnamon. Dozens of regional variants exist, each Slovenian family keeping its own.
s: Knead flour, yeast, eggs, milk and melted butter into a supple dough, let rise 1h30.
Stretch the dough as thin as possible on a large floured cloth, almost transparent.
Blend the walnuts with honey, sugar, cinnamon and raisins for the filling.
Spread the filling over the whole dough, roll tightly using the cloth into a long log.
Place in a ring in a tin, let rise 30 minutes then bake 45 minutes at 170°C.

bryndzove-halusky.d: Slovakia's national dish: small dumplings of raw grated potato, poached then smothered in bryndza, a creamy fermented sheep cheese, crowned with crisp fried bacon bits.
s: Finely grate the raw potatoes, drain lightly without pressing too hard.
Mix with the flour, egg and salt into a thick, sticky dough.
Drop small dumplings from a spoon or a holed strainer straight into salted boiling water.
Drain the dumplings as soon as they float to the surface, about 3 minutes.
Mash the bryndza with a little milk, mix it hot with the dumplings, crown with crisp bacon bits.

ghormeh-sabzi.d: Widely considered Iran's national dish: a mountain of fresh herbs — parsley, coriander, fenugreek, chives — slowly fried then simmered with meat and red beans, soured with sun-dried black limes.
s: Finely chop all the fresh herbs and fry them in oil for 20 minutes until they darken and lose their water.
Brown the sliced onion and cubed beef with the turmeric in a pot.
Add the fried herbs, the drained kidney beans and cover with water.
Pierce the dried black limes and add them whole, simmer 2 hours over low heat.
Lightly crush the limes in the sauce to release their tang, adjust salt and serve with rice.

masgouf.d: A Tigris carp split down the back, splayed open on wooden stakes and grilled standing upright, leaning toward the wood fire for hours. A dish over two thousand years old, mentioned on Sumerian tablets.
s: Butterfly the fish by splitting along the back without detaching the belly, and flatten it.
Brush the inside with olive oil mixed with turmeric, tamarind and salt.
Fix the opened fish onto two wooden stakes planted in the ground, flesh facing the fire.
Grill it standing at a distance from the embers for 45 minutes to 1 hour, basting regularly with oil.
Top with chopped tomato, onion and parsley, serve with lemon wedges.

kabsa.d: Basmati rice cooked in the chicken's own juices, scented with a spice blend unique to each family — cardamom, cinnamon, clove, dried lomi — served on one huge communal platter at the centre of the table, shared straight from the rice.
s: Brown the chicken, whole or in pieces, in oil with the sliced onion.
Add crushed tomato, carrot, whole spices and pierced dried limes, cover with water and simmer 40 minutes.
Remove the chicken, strain and reserve the fragrant broth.
Fry the rinsed basmati rice for 2 minutes, moisten with the strained broth and cook covered for 18 minutes without lifting the lid.
Grill or fry the chicken briefly to crisp the skin, serve over the rice scattered with raisins and toasted almonds.

khorovats.d: Armenian barbecue, marinated for hours in wine or onion juice before grilling over fruit-wood embers. Its success is judged by how much juice runs when the meat is sliced — never dry.
s: Cut the meat into large cubes, blend two onions into juice and mix with the wine and bay.
Marinate the meat at least 3 hours, ideally overnight in the fridge.
Thread the cubes onto wide flat skewers, alternating with the remaining onion wedges.
Grill over moderate embers 25 to 30 minutes, turning regularly, until the juices run clear.
Grill whole tomatoes, peppers and aubergines alongside, peel and mash them into a rough sauce to accompany.

piti.d: A lamb and chickpea stew simmered and served in its own individual clay pot, with saffron and prunes. The broth is drunk first, then the meat is mashed with a fork inside the pot for the second course.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight, drain.
Divide lamb, chickpeas, onion and tomato among small individual clay pots.
Cover with water, cover each pot and simmer 2 hours in a low oven.
Add potatoes, prunes and saffron dissolved in water for the last 30 minutes.
Pour off the broth into a bowl to drink first, then mash the rest with a fork in the pot and dust with sumac.

mansaf.d: Jordan's national dish, served on one huge communal tray of flatbread and rice, whole lamb drowned in jameed, a fermented sheep yoghurt dried into hard balls and reconstituted into sauce. Traditionally eaten standing, right hand only.
s: Soak the dried jameed balls for several hours in warm water until fully softened.
Poach the lamb with onion and cardamom for 1h30 until tender, reserve the broth.
Blend the softened jameed with a little broth until smooth, heat gently without boiling, stirring constantly.
Cook the rice in the rest of the fragrant broth until tender.
Spread the flatbread on a large tray, cover with rice then lamb, coat with the jameed sauce and scatter with almonds and pine nuts toasted in butter.

saltah.d: Widely seen as Yemen's national dish: a spiced meat stew topped with houlba, a whipped fenugreek foam beaten until firm, served bubbling hot in a scorching volcanic stone pot.
s: Soak the fenugreek seeds 6 hours in water, drain then blend with a little fresh water into a paste, whisk until it foams and triples in volume.
Fry onion, garlic and diced meat until browned.
Add crushed tomato, cumin, chilli and diced potato, moisten and simmer 30 minutes into a thick stew.
Blend some fresh coriander and chilli with a little water for a spicy green relish, on the side.
Pour the scalding stew into preheated stone bowls, crown with fenugreek foam and a drizzle of the green relish, serve with flatbread.

nihari.d: A beef shank stew simmered all night over very low heat, born in Mughal court kitchens to be served at breakfast after dawn prayer. The golden fat that rises to the surface, the nihari itself, is stirred back into the sauce with one spoonful.
s: Fry the sliced onion in ghee until deep golden, set aside half for garnish.
Add the ginger-garlic paste, beef shin and nihari spices, brown the meat all over.
Cover generously with water, bring to the boil then simmer covered over very low heat for 5 to 6 hours, until the meat shreds easily.
Mix the flour with a little cold water, stir it into the stew whisking to thicken the sauce slightly.
Serve piping hot, topped with fried onions, julienned ginger, fresh chilli, coriander and lemon wedges.

beshbarmak.d: "Five fingers": the dish of the steppes traditionally eaten without cutlery, wide flat noodles topped with boiled, shredded horse or mutton meat, with the broth sipped separately from a bowl called sorpa.
s: Poach the mutton with one onion, the bay and pepper for 2 hours at a gentle simmer, until tender.
Knead flour, egg, water and salt into a firm dough, rest 30 minutes.
Roll the dough thin and cut large irregular diamonds.
Poach the diamonds of dough for a few minutes in the strained meat broth, drain.
Slice the remaining onions and soften them in a little broth, plate the noodles topped with onions and shredded meat, serve the broth on the side scattered with dill.

ilish-bhapa.d: Hilsa, the most prized fish of the Ganges delta, marinated in a raw mustard and green chilli paste then steamed wrapped in a banana leaf, never touching direct heat that would dry it out.
s: Soak the mustard seeds 30 minutes in warm water, blend with half the green chillies into a fine paste.
Mix the mustard paste with turmeric, yoghurt, mustard oil and salt.
Coat the pieces of hilsa with this paste, marinate 20 minutes.
Wrap the marinated fish and the remaining whole chillies in a banana leaf passed briefly over a flame to soften it.
Steam 15 to 20 minutes in the closed parcel, serve straight from the opened leaf.

momo.d: Small dumplings pleated by hand into a crown, filled with pork or vegetables and ginger, steamed in stacked bamboo baskets. Always served with a tomato-sesame dipping sauce called achar, as important as the filling itself.
s: Knead flour, water and salt into a firm, smooth dough, rest 30 minutes under a cloth.
Mix minced pork, finely shredded cabbage, chopped onion, ginger, garlic and coriander, bind with soy sauce.
Roll the dough paper-thin, cut discs and fill each with a spoonful of filling.
Pleat the edges, pinching all around to close into a crown, leaving a small hole at the top.
Steam 12 minutes in stacked bamboo baskets, serve with a spicy tomato-sesame sauce blended separately.

mohinga.d: Widely regarded as Myanmar's national dish: a catfish broth thickened with chickpea flour and banana stem, poured over rice vermicelli, eaten in the street at dawn, even before the rice breakfast.
s: Poach the catfish with lemongrass and ginger for 20 minutes, drain reserving the broth, flake the flesh.
Fry the sliced onion and garlic in oil until browned, add to the reserved broth.
Mix the chickpea flour with a little cold water, whisk into the broth to thicken slightly, simmer 20 minutes with the fish sauce.
Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, shell and halve them.
Divide the cooked rice vermicelli among bowls, pour over the hot broth, top with flaked fish, hard-boiled egg, coriander, lime and crushed chilli.

fish-amok.d: A coconut-milk fish mousse with kroeung curry paste, steamed in a small folded banana-leaf cup until it sets into the texture of a light, fragrant custard.
s: Blend lemongrass, galangal, garlic, shallot and chilli into a fine curry paste.
Fry the paste dry for a few minutes until fragrant.
Blend the raw fish with the curry paste, coconut milk, egg and fish sauce until a smooth mousse forms.
Shape cups from the banana leaves, pour in the mixture, garnish with shredded kaffir lime leaves.
Steam 20 minutes until the mousse is set and slightly puffed.

larb.d: Laos's national dish: minced meat quickly seared then dressed raw with lime, chilli and mint, bound with ground toasted sticky rice that gives the warm salad its unique crunch.
s: Toast the raw sticky rice dry in a pan until deep golden, then grind it coarsely in a mortar.
Fry the minced meat dry in a very hot pan until fully cooked, breaking it up with a spoon.
Off the heat, season immediately with lime juice, fish sauce and crushed chilli.
Add sliced shallot, chopped mint and coriander, toss gently.
Fold in the toasted sticky rice just before serving, present on fresh lettuce leaves.

hainanese-chicken-rice.d: A whole chicken poached at low temperature then plunged into ice water to firm the skin, served sliced over rice cooked in the chicken's own fat and broth, with three mandatory sauces: ginger, chilli and sweet soy.
s: Rub the chicken with salt, stuff with crushed ginger and garlic, poach 40 minutes in barely simmering water, never boiling.
Plunge it immediately into ice water for 10 minutes to firm and make the skin translucent.
Fry rinsed rice with a little chicken fat, ginger and garlic, moisten with the cooking broth and cook like plain rice.
Blend chilli, remaining ginger and garlic for a hot sauce, mix soy with a little broth for a sweet-salty sauce.
Slice the chicken, serve over the rice with cucumber, coriander and the three sauces on the side.

taiwanese-beef-noodle-soup.d: A broth simmered for hours with fermented black bean paste, star anise and doubanjiang chilli bean, in which beef shank braises until meltingly tender. Every district of Taipei claims its own recipe as a family secret.
s: Blanch the beef and tendon 5 minutes in boiling water, rinse to remove the scum.
Fry ginger, garlic and doubanjiang in a little oil until the oil turns red.
Add the beef, black bean paste, star anise, tomato, soy and rice wine, cover generously with water.
Simmer covered for 2h30 over low heat until the meat is meltingly tender.
Cook the noodles and bok choy separately, plate in bowls, ladle over the scalding broth and garnish with chopped scallion.

buuz.d: Steamed dumplings of mutton coarsely chopped by knife, never minced, pleated with about twenty folds around a small hole left deliberately to vent steam — the emblematic dish of Mongolian lunar new year, Tsagaan Sar.
s: Chop the mutton coarsely by knife with the onion, more coarsely than for an ordinary filling.
Mix with crushed garlic, cumin and salt, without overworking the filling.
Knead flour, water and salt into a firm dough, rest 20 minutes, roll out and cut discs.
Fill each disc and pleat the edges into about twenty tight folds, leaving a tiny hole at the top.
Steam 12 to 15 minutes in stacked baskets, serve piping hot, eaten by hand.

ema-datshi.d: Bhutan's national dish, where chilli is not a condiment but the main ingredient: whole large green chillies simmered in melted local datshi cheese until forming a thick, fiery sauce.
s: Slit the green chillies lengthwise without seeding them, cut into large chunks.
Fry onion and garlic in butter until translucent.
Add the chillies and crushed tomato, cook 5 minutes over high heat.
Crumble the datshi cheese over the top, moisten with a little milk and let it melt over low heat, stirring.
Simmer 10 minutes until the sauce is thick and creamy, serve with red rice.

rendang.d: A Minangkabau beef stew simmered four hours in coconut milk and a spice paste, until all the liquid evaporates and caramelises into dry, near-black meat that then keeps for weeks without refrigeration.
s: Blend rehydrated dried chillies, shallot, garlic, ginger and galangal into a fine paste.
Dry-toast the grated coconut until brown and fragrant, set aside.
Fry the spice paste in a little oil until fragrant, add the cubed beef and brown it.
Pour in the coconut milk, add lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves and tamarind, simmer uncovered 3 to 4 hours, stirring regularly.
Continue cooking until the liquid has almost fully evaporated and the sauce caramelises around the meat, fold in the toasted coconut at the end.

xiaolongbao.d: Steamed dumplings that hide an entire soup inside: a pork broth set into jelly in the cold, sealed inside the filling, which turns liquid again on cooking. A minimum of twenty pleats at the top is required for a fold judged well made.
s: Boil the pork skin 3 hours in water until a gelatinous broth forms, strain and chill until it sets into firm jelly.
Cut the jelly into small dice, mix with the minced pork, ginger, scallion, soy, rice wine and sesame oil.
Knead flour and water into a smooth dough, rest 30 minutes, roll paper-thin and cut discs.
Fill each disc with filling and jelly cubes, pleat the edges into at least twenty tight folds at the top.
Steam 8 minutes in lined bamboo baskets, serve immediately with rice vinegar and shredded ginger.

chongqing-hotpot.d: A pot of scarlet broth made with beef tallow, dried chillies and Sichuan pepper, kept bubbling at the centre of the table where everyone takes turns dipping meat, vegetables and tofu with their own chopsticks.
s: Melt the beef tallow in a large pot, add the doubanjiang and fry until the oil turns red.
Add dried chillies, Sichuan pepper, ginger and garlic, let infuse 10 minutes over low heat.
Moisten with water or broth, bring to the boil and keep the pot simmering at the centre of the table on a burner.
Prepare individual dipping bowls of sesame oil and crushed garlic to cool each bite.
Everyone takes turns dipping thin beef slices, tofu, napa cabbage and enoki mushrooms for a few seconds in the bubbling broth before dipping into their sauce.

naengmyeon.d: Chewy buckwheat noodles served ice-cold in a clarified beef and kimchi broth, chilled for hours. Born in Pyongyang to endure harsh winters, the soup is traditionally eaten cold even in the depths of winter outside.
s: Poach the beef brisket 2 hours in water until tender, strain and chill the broth overnight.
Skim the fat off the cold broth from the surface.
Mix the skimmed broth with kimchi juice, rice vinegar and mustard, adjust seasoning.
Cook the buckwheat noodles al dente, rinse immediately in ice water to stop cooking and firm the texture.
Plate the noodles in chilled bowls, cover with the very cold broth, top with sliced beef, hard-boiled egg, cucumber, pear and thinly sliced radish.

brik.d: A malsouka pastry sheet so thin it shatters like glass, folded into a triangle around a whole raw egg, tuna and capers, deep-fried just long enough for the yolk to stay runny at the first bite.
s: Lay a sheet of malsouka pastry on the worktop, place flaked tuna, sliced onion, capers and parsley in the centre.
Crack a whole egg into the middle of the filling without beating it.
Fold the pastry into a triangle enclosing the egg, working fast so it does not run before cooking.
Slide gently into hot oil and fry 2 minutes per side, never flipping more than once to keep the yolk runny.
Drain on paper towel and serve immediately piping hot, with a lemon wedge.

bazin.d: A compact ball of barley flour beaten for a long time with a wooden paddle until smooth and firm, set as a dome at the centre of a meat and hard-boiled egg stew, from which pieces are torn off by hand.
s: Pour the barley flour into salted boiling water in a stream, beating constantly with a wooden paddle.
Keep beating 20 minutes over low heat until you get a smooth, firm, lump-free ball.
Brown the lamb pieces with onion, garlic and turmeric, add the tomato and cover with water.
Simmer 45 minutes until the meat is tender, add the shelled hard-boiled eggs at the end.
Shape the bazin into a smooth dome at the centre of a plate, surround with the stew and eggs, serve tearing off pieces by hand.

ful-medames.d: Brown fava beans simmered all night over very low heat in a conical copper pot itself called "ful", roughly mashed with a fork with olive oil, lemon and cumin. Sudan's quintessential breakfast, scooped up with flatbread.
s: Soak the brown fava beans overnight in cold water.
Cook them covered for 1h30 over very low heat in fresh water, until very tender.
Roughly mash them with a fork in their cooking water, without reducing to a smooth purée.
Season with crushed garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and cumin, mix.
Serve warm in a deep dish, topped with diced tomato and onion, with flatbread for scooping.

moambe-chicken.d: Chicken simmered in palm nut pulp, moambe, whose orange colour and rich flavour make it the national dish on both banks of the Congo River. Served with cassava fufu and pounded cassava leaves, pondu.
s: Brown the chicken pieces in a pot, set aside.
Fry sliced onion, garlic and ginger, add crushed tomato and chilli.
Return the chicken, stir in the palm nut cream and cover with water.
Simmer covered 45 minutes until the sauce thickens and the palm oil rises to the surface.
Make the fufu by pouring cassava flour into boiling water in a stream, beating vigorously into a smooth ball, serve with the chicken.

ndole.d: Cameroon's national dish: ndolé leaves, a slightly bitter amaranth variety, boiled then simmered with pounded peanuts, meat and dried shrimp, into a thick, almost brown sauce.
s: Boil the ndolé leaves twice, changing the water to remove bitterness, drain and chop them.
Dry-roast the peanuts then blend with a little water into a thick paste.
Brown the beef cubes with onion, garlic, ginger and chilli.
Add the peanut paste, dried shrimp and crushed crayfish, moisten and simmer 30 minutes, stirring often to prevent sticking.
Stir in the chopped ndolé leaves, cook a further 15 minutes into a thick sauce, serve with plantain or rice.

attieke.d: Fermented cassava semolina steamed into light grains, almost a plant-based couscous, served with a whole fish grilled over charcoal and a tomato-onion sauce spiked with kpakpo shito chilli.
s: Moisten the cassava semolina with a little water, fluff it with a fork.
Steam it 15 minutes in a couscoussier, fluffing halfway through to avoid lumps.
Rub the whole fish with salt and lemon, grill it over charcoal 8 minutes per side.
Blend tomato, onion, chilli and garlic into a fresh sauce, season with olive oil and salt.
Serve the warm attiéké with the whole grilled fish and the tomato sauce on the side.

maafe.d: A beef stew simmered in a peanut paste sauce, thickened until nearly creamy, with cabbage, carrot and sweet potato. Born among the Bambara and Malinké peoples, now found across West Africa in countless variations.
s: Brown the cubed beef with sliced onion and garlic in oil.
Add crushed tomato, cover with water and simmer 30 minutes.
Loosen the peanut butter with a little hot broth, stir it into the stew.
Add cabbage, carrot, sweet potato and a whole chilli, cook a further 30 minutes over low heat, stirring regularly to prevent sticking.
Adjust seasoning once the sauce is thick and creamy, serve with white rice.

sadza.d: A cornmeal porridge beaten until it forms a firm, smooth ball, the country's staple food, served with stewed meat and bitter leafy greens called muriwo. Eaten with the fingers, pinching a small spoon shape out of the hot ball.
s: Mix a third of the cornmeal with a little cold water, pour into boiling water whisking.
Cook 5 minutes into a thick porridge, then stir in the rest of the flour, beating vigorously with a wooden paddle.
Keep beating and cooking over low heat for 15 minutes until the ball is smooth, firm and pulls away from the sides.
Simmer the beef pieces with onion and tomato until tender, sauté the leafy greens with a little peanut butter.
Serve the sadza as a ball with the meat and greens on the side, eat with the fingers.

piri-piri-chicken.d: A butterflied chicken marinated in a sauce of African bird's-eye chilli, garlic and lemon, born from the crossing of Portuguese settlers and local spices. Grilled over charcoal then basted one last time with fiery sauce before serving.
s: Butterfly the whole chicken by partially removing the backbone, so it cooks flat.
Blend chillies, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil, paprika and bay into a hot sauce.
Rub the chicken with sauce, working it under the skin, marinate at least 2 hours in the fridge.
Grill over charcoal 35 minutes over moderate heat, skin down first, turning regularly.
Baste one last time with hot piri-piri sauce off the grill, rest 5 minutes before carving.

zanzibar-pilau.d: Rice scented with pilau masala — cinnamon, cardamom, cumin, clove — dry-toasted before the meat is added, inherited from the Omani trade routes that made Zanzibar a spice crossroads.
s: Dry-toast cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and cloves for 2 minutes until fragrant, grind coarsely.
Fry the sliced onion in oil until deeply golden and caramelised, set half aside.
Brown the beef with garlic, ginger and the toasted spices, add crushed tomato.
Add the rinsed rice, moisten with hot broth and cook covered 18 minutes without lifting the lid.
Scatter the reserved caramelised onion over just before serving.

isombe.d: Cassava leaves pounded at length in a mortar into a fine paste, simmered with palm oil, local eggplant and sometimes small dried fish, served with sweet potato or fufu.
s: Pound the cassava leaves at length in a mortar into a fine, smooth paste.
Boil them 20 minutes in water, drain.
Fry onion and garlic in palm oil, add the diced eggplant and crumbled dried fish.
Stir in the cassava paste and peanut butter, simmer 15 minutes, stirring.
Boil or steam the sweet potatoes, serve alongside the isombe.

seswaa.d: Botswana's festive dish: beef boiled in salted water for hours with no other seasoning, until so tender it falls apart on its own when pounded in a mortar, served over sorghum bogobe porridge.
s: Cut the beef into large chunks, place in a large pot with the onion and salted water.
Bring to the boil then simmer covered 2h30 to 3 hours, until the meat is extremely tender.
Drain the meat, reserving a little broth, let it cool slightly.
Pound it in a mortar or shred with a fork into fine fibres, moisten with a little of the reserved broth.
Make the bogobe by cooking sorghum flour in boiling water, stirring into a thick porridge, serve with the shredded beef.

calulu.d: Angola's national dish, simmering dried and fresh fish together with sweet potato or cassava leaves in palm oil, inherited from enslaved cooks who had to use every available part of the fish.
s: Soak the dried fish 30 minutes in warm water to desalt, drain.
Fry onion and garlic in palm oil, add crushed tomato and chilli.
Add both fish, moisten and simmer 20 minutes over low heat.
Stir in sweet potato leaves, diced eggplant and okra, cook a further 15 minutes.
Add the sweet potato in chunks, simmer another 15 minutes until tender, serve with rice or fufu.

rolex.d: A vegetable omelette rolled inside a warm chapati, born at Kampala's university food stalls where vendors called out "roll eggs" to rushing customers — a pun that became the name of Uganda's most popular street food.
s: Knead flour, water and salt into a supple dough, rest 20 minutes, roll into thin discs.
Cook each chapati dry in a hot pan until it puffs in places and browns lightly.
Beat the eggs with finely chopped tomato, onion and cabbage.
Pour the mixture into the oiled pan and cook into a thin omelette, without flipping.
Lay the hot chapati onto the omelette still in the pan, press lightly then roll everything together tightly before slicing.

pepian.d: A Maya-Quiché national dish declared cultural heritage of Guatemala, whose thick sauce owes its character to toasted pumpkin and sesame seeds ground fine, blended with dried chillies charred until slightly blackened.
s: Poach the chicken in salted water for 30 minutes, reserve the broth.
Dry-toast pumpkin seeds, sesame and dried chillies until fragrant.
Char-grill tomato, tomatillo, onion and garlic dry in a pan until spotted black in places.
Blend everything with a little broth into a thick, slightly grainy sauce.
Add the chicken, potatoes and green beans to the sauce, simmer 20 minutes and serve with rice.

baleada.d: A thick flour tortilla, folded over mashed red beans, crumbled cheese and thick cream — Honduras's simplest street meal, sold at every hour from improvised stalls.
s: Knead flour, baking powder, salt, oil and water into a supple dough, rest 15 minutes.
Shape balls and roll into thick discs, cook dry in a hot pan 2 minutes per side.
Heat the cooked red beans and roughly mash into a thick purée.
Spread each hot tortilla with the bean purée.
Top with crumbled cheese and thick cream, fold in half and serve hot.

pupusas.d: El Salvador's national dish: a thick corn masa cake, filled with cheese, beans or chicharron before cooking on a griddle, always served with curtido, a lightly tangy fermented cabbage slaw.
s: Mix finely shredded cabbage, grated carrot, vinegar, oregano and salt, let ferment at least 2 hours for the curtido.
Knead the corn masa with water and salt into a supple dough that doesn't stick to your hands.
Shape balls, hollow a well in the centre and fill with crumbled cheese, beans or chopped chicharron.
Close by pinching and gently flatten into a thick cake without bursting the filling.
Cook on a lightly oiled hot griddle 4 minutes per side, serve piping hot with the curtido and a tomato sauce.

sancocho-panameno.d: Panama's national dish, a chicken broth scented with culantro, a long-leafed coriander far more pungent than the common kind, in which ñame roots simmer until naturally thickening the soup.
s: Place the chicken pieces in a large pot with onion, garlic and culantro, cover with water.
Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer 45 minutes over low heat.
Add the peeled yam in large chunks and the corn pieces.
Continue cooking 30 minutes until the yam breaks down slightly and thickens the broth.
Adjust the seasoning, add oregano and chopped scallion at the end, serve piping hot with white rice.

mangu.d: A purée of boiled green plantains, mashed with the cooking water until smooth and glossy, crowned with vinegared red onions cooked just enough to soften without melting away. The base of every Dominican breakfast, called "the three hits".
s: Peel the green plantains and cut into chunks, cook 20 minutes in salted water until tender.
Drain, reserving a little cooking water, mash with a potato masher adding the reserved water and butter to a smooth consistency.
Slice the red onion, fry it with the vinegar for 5 minutes until just softened.
Fry slices of salami and eggs to accompany.
Serve the plantain mash crowned with vinegared onions, with fresh cheese, salami and fried egg on the side.

griot.d: Pork cubes marinated for hours in bitter orange juice and spices, boiled then fried twice until almost lacquered outside, served with pikliz, a relish of cabbage and scotch bonnet chilli pickled in vinegar.
s: Cut the pork into large cubes, marinate at least 3 hours with bitter orange juice, crushed garlic, onion, cloves and salt.
Drain and boil the meat 30 minutes in its strained marinade liquid until tender.
Make the pikliz by mixing finely shredded cabbage and carrot, scotch bonnet chilli and vinegar, marinate at least 2 hours.
Drain the boiled pork and fry it in two batches for 8 minutes in very hot oil until golden and crisp.
Serve piping hot with the pikliz and djon-djon or white rice.

salteñas.d: A sweet-savoury pastry filled with a beef and potato stew bound with gelatine before baking, so it turns back into scalding broth inside the oven. Eaten standing in the morning, never pierced before the first bite.
s: Fry onion and diced beef with paprika and sugar until browned.
Add potato in small dice and broth, simmer 25 minutes.
Dissolve the gelatine in the hot stew broth, cool then chill until set into firm jelly.
Knead flour, melted butter, egg and warm water into a supple dough, rest 30 minutes.
Roll the dough, fill with diced jellied stew, a pea, an olive and a raisin, close into a twisted turnover and bake 25 minutes at 200°C.

encebollado.d: An albacore tuna and cassava soup drowned under a mountain of lime-marinated red onions, famed as a Sunday-morning hangover cure across Guayaquil, eaten with plantain chips.
s: Cook the peeled cassava in salted water 25 minutes until tender, reserve the broth.
Poach the tuna in this same broth for 10 minutes, roughly flake it.
Fry tomato and cumin in a little oil, add to the broth with the cassava and flaked tuna.
Very finely slice the red onion, marinate it in lime juice and mustard for at least 20 minutes.
Serve the scalding soup crowned generously with marinated onions and coriander, with plantain chips on the side.

sopa-paraguaya.d: Despite its name, this is not a soup but a savoury cornmeal cake with melted onion and cheese, born from a kitchen accident at President Carlos Antonio López's court in the 19th century, when a too-thick porridge was baked by mistake.
s: Melt the sliced onions in butter and oil until translucent, without browning.
Mix the cornmeal with the milk, let it swell for 10 minutes.
Stir in the beaten eggs, crumbled cheese and melted onions.
Pour into a buttered tin, the batter should be pourable like a thick cake batter.
Bake 40 minutes at 180°C until golden on top and a knife comes out clean, let cool slightly before cutting into squares.

doubles.d: Two small fried, turmeric-leavened flatbreads stacked around a spiced chickpea curry, hence the name: "doubles". Trinidad and Tobago's most popular street breakfast, sold from carts from dawn.
s: Knead flour, yeast, turmeric, cumin, water and salt into a supple dough, let rise 2 hours.
Cook the soaked chickpeas until tender, mash part of them to thicken.
Season the chickpea curry with crushed garlic, minced scotch bonnet and coriander.
Divide the risen dough into small balls, flatten each into a thin disc and fry 1 minute per side in hot oil until they puff.
Stack two fried discs, fill generously with chickpea curry and fold closed, serve warm.

conch-salad.d: Conch, a large firm-fleshed shellfish, pounded then diced small and "cooked" only by lime acidity, prepared and served in minutes right on the docks of the fish markets.
s: Pound the conch flesh with a mallet to tenderise, rinse well.
Cut into very small even dice.
Mix with tomato, bell pepper, onion and scotch bonnet, all diced small.
Season generously with lime juice and orange juice, salt.
Marinate 15 minutes chilled, stirring once, serve very cold scattered with coriander.

texas-brisket.d: A whole beef brisket smoked twelve hours over oak wood, seasoned with nothing but a rub of salt and cracked black pepper, until a black crust called bark forms around meat smoked pink to the core.
s: Trim the brisket leaving a thin fat cap, rub generously with salt and cracked pepper all over.
Rest at room temperature 1 hour before placing in a smoker preheated to 110°C.
Smoke over oak wood 10 to 12 hours, keeping a steady temperature, never opening the smoker needlessly.
Wrap the meat in butcher paper once the bark is well formed, continue cooking until a probe slides in with no resistance, about 93°C internal.
Rest wrapped at least 1 hour before slicing thin against the grain, serve with white bread, pickles and barbecue sauce.

mumu.d: A pit dug in the earth, lined with stones heated over a wood fire for hours, where pork, sweet potato and leafy greens wrapped in banana leaves are stacked, covered with earth to steam-cook all afternoon.
s: Dig a pit and heat volcanic stones in a large wood fire for 2 hours.
Arrange the burning stones at the bottom of the pit, cover with a layer of banana leaves.
Wrap the pork, sweet potato and cassava in separate banana-leaf parcels, salt them.
Stack the parcels on the stones, drizzle with coconut milk, cover with leaves then earth to seal tightly.
Let it steam-cook 2h30 without opening, dig it up and serve straight from the opened leaves.

palusami.d: Tender young taro leaves layered into small parcels around fresh coconut cream and sometimes onion and corned beef, tied and steam-cooked until the leaves melt into a texture close to spinach.
s: Wash the young taro leaves carefully, stack five in a star shape to form a wide base.
Place a little chopped onion and crumbled corned beef in the centre.
Fold the leaves closed into a tight parcel, tie with a leaf strip or kitchen string.
Arrange the parcels in a pot, cover generously with coconut milk and salt.
Cook covered over low heat 45 minutes to 1 hour until the leaves are meltingly soft, serve hot.

lap-lap.d: Vanuatu's national dish: a grated yam, cassava or taro batter, drowned in coconut milk and topped with chicken or fish, cooked for hours in a leaf-wrapped stone oven until it becomes a dense, melting loaf.
s: Peel and finely grate the yam until you get a moist batter.
Mix it with half the coconut milk to a thick cake-batter consistency.
Spread the batter over a wide bed of overlapping banana leaves, in an even layer.
Arrange the chicken pieces and leafy greens on top, drizzle with the rest of the coconut milk.
Fold the leaves to wrap everything well, steam-cook over hot stones or in a very low oven for 2 hours, serve cut into portions.

mulgipuder.d: A peasant mash of barley and potato boiled together until they merge, crowned with grilled pork bits and their melted fat drizzled on scalding hot just before serving.
s: Soak the barley 2 hours, drain.
Cook barley and peeled potatoes together in salted water 35 minutes until fully tender.
Mash everything with a potato masher without aiming for smoothness, the texture should stay rustic.
Cut the bacon into small lardons, fry them dry with the sliced onion until nicely crisp.
Serve the mash topped with the bacon bits and their cooking fat poured on scalding hot.

pelekie-zirni.d: Grey peas, an heirloom variety grown for centuries around the Baltic, simmered until tender then mixed with rendered pork lardons and caramelised onion. Latvia's quintessential Christmas dish, served with fermented milk.
s: Soak the grey peas overnight, drain.
Cook covered 45 minutes in lightly salted water until tender but holding their shape.
Dice the bacon small, render it in a pan until it crisps up.
Add the sliced onion and let it caramelise slowly in the bacon fat.
Mix the drained peas with the bacon and caramelised onion, serve hot with fermented milk on the side.

tave-kosi.d: Albania's national dish: browned lamb drowned under a yoghurt and egg sauce that puffs up in the oven like a soufflé, then settles into a golden, faintly tangy crust.
s: Brown the lamb pieces in butter with crushed garlic.
Add the rice and a little water, simmer 30 minutes until the meat is tender.
Spread the meat and rice in a buttered baking dish.
Whisk the yoghurt with the eggs and flour until smooth, pour over the meat.
Bake 30 minutes at 190°C until puffed and golden on top, let rest 10 minutes before serving.

tavce-gravce.d: North Macedonia's national dish: white beans simmered then finished in the oven in a clay dish with smoked paprika and dried mint, until a thin skin forms on top.
s: Soak the white beans overnight, drain.
Cook 1 hour in fresh water until nearly tender.
Fry onion and pepper in oil, add flour and smoked paprika, moisten with tomato.
Mix the drained beans into this sauce, pour into a clay dish.
Bake uncovered 30 minutes at 200°C, scatter with dried mint at the end until a golden skin forms on top.

kacamak.d: A cornmeal and potato porridge beaten with a wooden paddle until elastic, drowned in melting fresh cheese and clotted cream, a shepherd's dish from the Montenegrin mountains.
s: Cook the peeled, chunked potatoes in salted water until tender, roughly mash them in their water.
Pour the cornmeal into the mashed potatoes in a stream, beating constantly with a wooden paddle.
Continue cooking and beating for 15 minutes over low heat until an elastic dough forms that pulls from the sides.
Fold in the crumbled fresh cheese and half the cream, mix until they melt into the hot porridge.
Serve immediately, topped with the rest of the cream and a little melted butter.

draniki.d: Pancakes of raw grated potato, pressed to remove excess water then fried until the edges turn lacy and crisp, served with well-chilled sour cream.
s: Finely grate the potatoes and onion, press firmly to remove excess liquid.
Mix with the egg, flour and salt into a thick batter.
Heat a generous layer of oil in a wide pan.
Drop flattened spoonfuls of batter, fry 3 minutes per side until the edges are lacy and golden.
Drain on paper towel, serve piping hot with well-chilled sour cream.

placinta.d: A dough stretched by hand into an almost transparent circle, rolled spiral-fashion around fresh cheese and dill before being flattened and pan-fried dry until it blisters into golden pockets.
s: Knead flour, water, egg and salt into a supple dough, rest 30 minutes under a cloth.
Divide into balls and stretch each by hand on an oiled surface until nearly transparent.
Mash the fresh cheese with chopped dill, spread over the whole stretched dough.
Roll into a tight log then coil the log onto itself into a spiral, gently flatten with a rolling pin.
Cook in a dry pan 4 minutes per side over medium heat, brush with melted butter on coming out.

flija.d: Up to twenty thin layers of batter, each brushed with cream and baked separately under a metal dome called a sač covered in embers, stacked one on another into a cake striped like a tree trunk.
s: Make a liquid batter with flour, water and salt, thin like crêpe batter.
Pour a thin layer into a large buttered round dish, bake in a very hot oven 5 minutes until lightly coloured.
Brush with cream, pour a new thin layer of batter on top without mixing the layers.
Repeat fifteen to twenty times, alternating baking and brushing with cream between each layer.
Finish with a pass under the grill to brown the top, let cool slightly then cut into striped triangular portions.

machboos.d: Basmati rice scented with the Gulf's own bezar spice blend, cooked in meat juices and dried black lime, inherited from the sea routes linking Emirati ports to India and East Africa.
s: Brown the chicken with sliced onion and garlic in oil.
Add crushed tomato, whole spices and pierced black limes, cover with water and simmer 40 minutes.
Remove the chicken, reserve the strained fragrant broth.
Fry the rinsed rice for 2 minutes, moisten with the hot broth and cook covered 18 minutes without lifting the lid.
Grill the chicken briefly to crisp the skin, serve over the rice scattered with golden raisins.

harees.d: Cracked wheat and meat simmered for hours then beaten at length into a perfectly smooth, velvety porridge, served during Ramadan and at weddings across the Gulf.
s: Soak the cracked wheat 2 hours in water, drain.
Place wheat and chicken in a large pot, cover generously with water and bring to the boil.
Simmer covered 2h30 over very low heat until the chicken falls apart completely.
Remove the bones, beat vigorously with a whisk or mixer until a smooth, even porridge forms.
Serve piping hot, topped with melted butter and dusted with cinnamon.

shuwa.d: A whole lamb marinated for several days in a spice and vinegar paste, wrapped in banana leaves then buried in an ember-heated pit for twenty-four hours, until meltingly tender enough to shred on its own.
s: Blend garlic, vinegar and all the spices into a thick paste.
Rub the whole lamb generously with this paste, working it into knife slits, marinate 2 days in the fridge.
Wrap the meat in several layers of banana leaves, tie securely.
Steam-cook it 8 to 10 hours in a very low oven or an ember pit, until extremely tender.
Unwrap and shred the meat with a fork, serve with basmati rice.

jireesh.d: Coarsely cracked wheat simmered with chicken and spices until it thickens into a rustic porridge, coarser than the neighbouring harees, traditionally eaten on cool Kuwaiti winter nights.
s: Soak the cracked wheat 1 hour, drain.
Brown the sliced onion and chicken in butter.
Add the wheat, cinnamon, cardamom and dried limes, cover with water and bring to the boil.
Simmer covered 1h30 over low heat, stirring regularly to prevent sticking.
Lightly mash with a spoon at the end to thicken, serve hot.

kibbeh.d: A shell of fine bulgur and raw meat pounded into a smooth paste, hand-shaped into a hollow torpedo, stuffed with spiced minced meat and pine nuts then fried to a deep, crisp brown.
s: Soak the fine bulgur 20 minutes in cold water, squeeze out firmly.
Blend half the minced meat with the bulgur, one onion and the spices until a smooth, pliable paste forms.
Fry the remaining onion with the rest of the meat and pine nuts for the filling, let cool.
Shape the paste into small hollow torpedoes with wet fingers, fill with the filling and pinch the ends closed.
Fry at 170°C until deep brown and crisp, drain and serve hot.

musakhan.d: Roast chicken set over taboun bread soaked in olive oil and a mountain of onions slow-cooked with sumac for hours, until they turn into an almost jammy, tangy purple mass.
s: Rub the chicken with olive oil, sumac and spices, roast 45 minutes in a 200°C oven.
Finely slice a large quantity of onions.
Slow-cook them in olive oil over very low heat for 45 minutes, until soft and lightly caramelised.
Add the sumac to the confited onions at the end, mix.
Spread the taboun bread on a platter, cover generously with sumac onions, top with the roast chicken and scatter with pine nuts toasted in butter.

muhammar.d: Basmati rice sweetened with date syrup and saffron, an unexpected contrast served alongside salty grilled fish, in a Bahraini culinary tradition where sweet and savoury answer each other on the same plate.
s: Cook the rinsed basmati rice in salted water until nearly tender, drain.
Heat the date syrup with butter and cardamom until fluid.
Pour the syrup over the drained rice, gently mix to coat without crushing it.
Cover and steam-cook 15 minutes over very low heat until fully absorbed.
Salt and grill the whole fish with lemon, serve alongside the sweetened rice.

lagman.d: Hand-pulled noodles, stretched and slapped on the worktop to the right thickness, topped with a cumin-spiced beef and vegetable stew, inherited from the Silk Road routes that crossed Central Asia.
s: Knead flour, water and salt into a very supple dough, rest 1 hour under oil.
Stretch the dough into long ropes, pull and slap them against the worktop to thin them into noodles.
Brown the beef strips with onion and garlic in oil.
Add pepper, carrot and tomato in strips, cumin and soy, moisten and simmer 25 minutes.
Cook the noodles in boiling water 3 minutes, drain and top with the hot beef stew.

qurutob.d: Tajikistan's national dish: fatir bread torn into pieces, drowned under a dried yoghurt reconstituted into sauce, with raw tomato and onion on top. Traditionally eaten by hand from one large communal dish.
s: Dissolve the dried yoghurt balls in warm water until a smooth, tangy sauce forms.
Tear the fatir bread into irregular pieces directly into a large dish.
Pour the yoghurt sauce over the torn bread, mix gently to soak it well.
Finely slice tomato and onion, arrange on top.
Drizzle with olive oil, scatter with coriander and serve immediately at room temperature.

gutap.d: A half-moon pastry filled with pumpkin or wild leafy greens, cooked dry in a cast-iron pan without a drop of oil, until the dough puffs into small crisp pockets.
s: Knead flour, water and salt into a supple dough, rest 30 minutes.
Grate the raw pumpkin, mix with sliced onion, cumin and salt.
Roll the dough thin, cut discs and fill each with the pumpkin filling.
Fold into a half-moon and pinch the edges firmly to seal well.
Cook dry in a hot pan 4 minutes per side, covered, brush with melted butter on coming out.

kabuli-palaw.d: Afghanistan's national dish: basmati rice cooked in lamb broth, coloured with caramelised sugar and crowned with fine carrot juliennes and raisins sautéed until lightly caramelised.
s: Brown the lamb with sliced onion, cover with water and simmer 1 hour until tender, reserve the broth.
Cut the carrots into fine julienne, sauté with the sugar until lightly caramelised, add the raisins at the end.
Fry the rinsed rice in a little oil, moisten with the lamb broth scented with cardamom and cumin.
Cook covered 18 minutes over low heat without lifting the lid.
Plate the rice, arrange the lamb on top and crown with the caramelised carrots and raisins.

mas-huni.d: The Maldivian national breakfast: hand-flaked smoked dried tuna, mixed raw with freshly grated coconut, red onion and chilli, eaten wrapped in roshi, a thin flatbread.
s: Finely flake the smoked dried tuna by hand, removing any bones.
Freshly grate the coconut.
Very finely slice the red onion and chilli.
Mix the flaked tuna, grated coconut, onion and chilli, drizzle with lime juice and salt.
Serve at room temperature with warm roshi to wrap each bite.

ambuyat.d: Brunei's national dish, a viscous, almost flavourless sago starch paste, wound onto forked bamboo sticks called candas and dipped into a tangy tamarind and chilli sauce.
s: Loosen the sago starch with a little cold water to form a smooth paste.
Bring the rest of the water to the boil, pour in the sago paste in a stream, stirring constantly.
Keep stirring over low heat until the mixture turns translucent and viscous, like thick glue.
Blend tamarind, chilli, sugar and dried shrimp with a little water for the dipping sauce.
Wind the ambuyat around forked sticks and dip each mouthful into the sauce before swallowing it whole, without chewing.

ikan-sabuko.d: A whole mackerel brushed with a paste of chilli, tamarind and lemongrass, grilled over wood embers until the skin cracks, eaten with rice and pounded cassava leaves, an everyday dish along the shores of Dili.
s: Gut and scale the mackerel, score the skin two or three times on each side.
Blend chilli, tamarind, lemongrass and garlic into a thick paste.
Brush the fish generously with this paste, including in the cuts, marinate 30 minutes.
Grill over wood embers 5 to 6 minutes per side until the skin cracks.
Boil then pound the cassava leaves, serve with the grilled fish, rice and a lime wedge.

solomon-cassava-fish.n: Fish in coconut cream with cassava
solomon-cassava-fish.d: White fish barely simmered in fresh, hand-pressed coconut cream, served with boiled cassava and sweet potato, the everyday meal of most households across the Solomon Islands.
s: Peel and chunk the cassava and sweet potato, boil 20 minutes until tender.
Cut the fish into large pieces, salt lightly.
Warm the coconut milk to a bare simmer with the sliced onion.
Add the fish and poach gently for 8 minutes, never letting it boil hard.
Serve the fish in coconut milk with the cassava, sweet potato and a squeeze of lime, alongside boiled leafy greens.

lu-pulu.d: Corned beef or stewed beef wrapped in several layers of taro leaves with coconut milk, tied and steam-cooked until the thick leaves melt into a texture close to wilted spinach.
s: Cut the beef into pieces, mix with the crumbled corned beef and sliced onion.
Stack four to five taro leaves in a star shape to form a wide base.
Place the meat filling in the centre, fold the leaves into a tight parcel, tie.
Arrange the parcels in a pot, cover generously with coconut milk.
Cook covered 1h30 to 2 hours over low heat until the leaves are meltingly soft, serve hot with rice or boiled taro.

bougna.d: The Kanak festive dish: fish, chicken or lobster wrapped with yam, sweet potato and plantain in banana leaves, drenched in coconut milk and cooked for hours in an earthen pit oven heated with volcanic stones.
s: Peel and chunk the yam, sweet potato and plantain.
Layer several banana leaves to form a wide, sturdy base.
Arrange the fish and vegetables in the centre, drench generously with coconut milk, salt.
Fold the leaves to wrap everything into one large parcel, tie securely.
Steam-cook 2 hours over hot stones or in a very low oven, unwrap and serve straight from the leaves.

dambou.d: Steamed millet semolina mixed with pounded cabbage or spinach leaves, scented with peanut oil and dried chilli, a Nigerien family dish varying with whatever greens are found at the day's market.
s: Moisten the millet semolina and fluff it by hand, steam it 20 minutes in a couscoussier.
Boil the cabbage and spinach 10 minutes, drain and roughly pound in a mortar.
Fry onion and tomato in peanut oil with the chilli.
Mix the pounded greens into the tomato-onion sauce.
Fold the cooked semolina into the greens, fluff with a fork, reheat 5 minutes over steam and serve hot.

riz-gras.d: Rice cooked directly in an oil-rich tomato sauce with meat and vegetables, which gives it its orange colour and its name: "fatty rice". Burkina Faso's quintessential festive dish, made in huge batches for big occasions.
s: Brown the beef pieces with onion and garlic in oil.
Add crushed tomato, bay, cover with water and simmer 40 minutes until tender.
Add carrot and cabbage in chunks, cook a further 10 minutes.
Remove the meat and vegetables, cook the rinsed rice directly in the remaining tomato sauce and its oil.
Once the rice is cooked and coloured, return the meat and vegetables, warm through together and serve.

soupe-kandia.d: An okra sauce pounded until stringy and viscous, simmered with smoked fish and palm oil until it thickens into an almost sticky texture, poured over hot white rice.
s: Slice the okra into thin rounds, pound half of it in a mortar into a stringy paste.
Fry onion, garlic and tomato in palm oil.
Add the whole and pounded okra, the flaked smoked fish and chilli, moisten with water.
Simmer 30 minutes over low heat, stirring regularly, until the sauce is thick and viscous.
Serve over a bed of hot white rice.

cassava-leaf-stew.d: Cassava leaves pounded at length in a mortar into a fine paste, simmered for hours with smoked fish, meat and palm oil until nearly black and deeply fragrant.
s: Pound the cassava leaves at length in a mortar into a fine, smooth paste.
Boil the beef pieces 30 minutes until tender.
Add the cassava paste, flaked smoked fish, onion, chilli and pounded crayfish.
Pour in the palm oil and simmer 45 minutes over low heat, stirring often, until the mixture darkens and thickens.
Serve generously over hot white rice.

palava-sauce.d: Finely chopped sweet potato or amaranth leaves, simmered with fish, smoked meat and peanut butter into a thick green sauce, whose name is said to come from the animated palavers exchanged while cooking it.
s: Finely chop the sweet potato leaves.
Boil the beef pieces 25 minutes until tender.
Add the flaked smoked fish, onion, chilli and chopped leaves.
Loosen the peanut butter with a little hot broth, stir into the sauce with the palm oil.
Simmer 25 minutes over low heat, stirring, until a thick green sauce forms, serve over rice.

amiwo.d: Cornmeal batter beaten until smooth and firm, tinted red by a very spicy tomato sauce, served with grilled fish or chicken at Cotonou's street stalls.
s: Make a well-spiced tomato sauce with onion, chilli and palm oil, let it reduce 20 minutes.
Mix a third of the cornmeal with a little cold water, pour into boiling water whisking.
Stir in the rest of the flour, beating vigorously with a wooden paddle.
Add half the tomato sauce directly into the corn batter while still beating, until a smooth, firm red dough forms.
Grill the whole fish, serve the amiwo with the fish and the rest of the tomato sauce.

ablo.d: Small fermented rice cakes steamed in banana leaves until soft and faintly tangy, sold in the evening on Lomé's streets with a fiery pepper-tomato sauce.
s: Mix rice flour, water, yeast and sugar into a semi-liquid batter, let ferment at room temperature 4 to 6 hours.
Cut squares of banana leaf, pour a ladle of fermented batter into the centre of each.
Fold into small closed parcels and steam 20 minutes until the cakes are firm.
Blend tomato, chilli and onion into a fresh, fiery sauce, salt.
Serve the cakes warm, unwrapped, with the hot sauce.

domoda.d: A beef stew simmered in a thick peanut paste and tomato sauce, with cabbage and sweet potato, Gambia's national dish, often compared to a mafé but always more concentrated in peanut.
s: Brown the beef cubes with onion and garlic in oil.
Add crushed tomato, cover with water and simmer 30 minutes.
Loosen the peanut butter with a little hot broth, stir into the stew.
Add cabbage, sweet potato and a whole chilli, cook a further 30 minutes over low heat, stirring regularly.
Adjust seasoning once the sauce is thick and creamy, serve with white rice.

mechoui.d: A whole lamb basted with butter and spices, slowly turned over wood embers for hours until the skin becomes crackling and golden, a dish of hospitality offered on great family occasions.
s: Blend melted butter, crushed garlic, cumin, paprika, lemon juice and salt into a thick marinade.
Rub the whole lamb generously with this marinade, including inside, let rest 2 hours.
Skewer the lamb onto a long, sturdy metal or wooden rod.
Turn slowly over moderate embers 3 to 4 hours, basting regularly with the remaining marinade.
Check the meat pulls easily off the bone before carving and serving with bread and a fresh salad.

gozo.d: A cassava paste beaten until smooth and elastic, the Central African staple, served with a thick peanut and leafy greens sauce, torn into small balls for dipping.
s: Pour the cassava flour into the boiling water in a stream, beating constantly with a wooden paddle until a smooth ball forms.
Fry onion, tomato and chilli in palm oil.
Loosen the peanut butter with a little hot water, add to the tomato sauce.
Stir in the shredded spinach, simmer 15 minutes until thickened.
Serve the gozo as a ball alongside the peanut sauce, tearing off pieces by hand to dip.

poulet-nyembwe.d: Gabon's national dish: chicken simmered in a palm nut cream extracted and pounded by hand, whose deep orange colour and richness echo the Congolese moambe, spiked with more chilli.
s: Brown the chicken pieces in a pot, set aside.
Fry sliced onion, garlic and ginger, add crushed tomato and chilli.
Return the chicken, stir in the palm nut cream and bay, cover with water.
Simmer covered 45 minutes until the sauce thickens and the oil rises to the surface.
Serve with white rice or boiled cassava.

saka-saka.d: Finely pounded cassava leaves, simmered in palm oil with eggplant and smoked fish, served with chikwangue, a fermented cassava loaf wrapped and cooked in leaves, with a sticky, faintly tangy texture.
s: Make the chikwangue by fermenting grated cassava for 2 days, then wrapping it in banana leaves and boiling 2 hours.
Finely pound the cassava leaves, boil 20 minutes, drain.
Fry onion, garlic and chilli in palm oil, add the diced eggplant.
Stir in the pounded cassava leaves and flaked smoked fish, simmer 25 minutes over low heat.
Serve the saka-saka hot with slices of warm chikwangue.

pepesoup.d: A clear fish broth with fiery chilli and locally bitter tree bark, reputed to cure colds and rough mornings after, served scalding hot in small bowls along the Gulf of Guinea.
s: Cut the fish into pieces, rinse well.
Bring the water to the boil with sliced onion, garlic and ginger.
Add the fish and the chilli, whole or crushed depending on the desired heat.
Simmer 20 minutes over low heat until the fish is cooked and the broth fragrant.
Add the chopped aromatic leaves at the end, serve scalding hot in small individual bowls.

skoudehkaris.d: Djibouti's national dish: rice cooked in the lamb's own juices, coloured with turmeric and cardamom, inherited from the trading crossroads between the Arabian peninsula, India and the Horn of Africa.
s: Brown the lamb pieces with onion and garlic in oil.
Add crushed tomato, turmeric, cardamom and cinnamon, cover with water and simmer 40 minutes.
Remove the meat, reserve the fragrant broth.
Fry the rinsed rice for 2 minutes, moisten with the hot broth and cook covered 18 minutes.
Return the meat onto the rice, warm through together a few minutes and serve hot.

zigni.d: A beef stew simmered in berbere, a blend of chillies and toasted spices unique to the Horn of Africa, served on injera, the large spongy flatbread made of fermented teff, which doubles as cutlery.
s: Make the injera by mixing teff flour and water, let ferment 2 days then cook into large thin flatbreads in a hot dry pan.
Slowly melt down the sliced onions dry in a pot until they reduce and brown, 20 minutes.
Add the butter, garlic, ginger and berbere, fry 5 minutes until the oil turns red.
Add the cubed beef and tomato, moisten and simmer 45 minutes over low heat until tender.
Serve the stew on the injera, tearing off pieces of bread to scoop up the meat.

bariis-iskukaris.d: Long basmati rice scented with the Somali xawaash spice blend, tinted with a thread of saffron, often served with a sliced banana on the side, in a sweet-savoury pairing typical of the Horn of Africa.
s: Brown the chicken with onion and garlic in oil.
Dust with xawaash, moisten and simmer 30 minutes until tender.
Remove the chicken, reserve the strained fragrant broth.
Fry the rinsed rice, moisten with the hot saffron broth, cook covered 18 minutes.
Serve the rice with the chicken, raisins and slices of fresh banana on the side.

ibiharage.d: Red beans simmered at length in red palm oil with onion and tomato, until forming an almost creamy thick sauce, the everyday staple of most Burundian households, served with boiled plantain.
s: Soak the red beans overnight, drain.
Cook 1 hour in fresh water until tender.
Fry onion, garlic and tomato in palm oil.
Add the drained beans to the sauce, simmer 20 minutes, lightly mashing some to thicken.
Boil the peeled plantains, serve alongside the beans.

nsima-chambo.d: A ball of cornmeal beaten until firm, served with chambo, a tilapia caught in Lake Malawi and fried whole until the skin cracks, a fish so prized it appears on the country's banknotes.
s: Mix a third of the cornmeal with cold water, pour into boiling water whisking.
Stir in the rest of the flour, beating vigorously with a wooden paddle until a smooth, firm ball forms.
Gut and scale the tilapia, salt and fry whole in hot oil 5 minutes per side until the skin cracks.
Fry tomato and onion for a fresh sauce to serve alongside.
Serve the nsima as a ball with the fried chambo, the tomato sauce and a lemon wedge.

ifisashi.d: Local leafy greens simmered in a thick pounded peanut sauce, served with nshima, the same beaten cornmeal ball that accompanies almost every Zambian meal, whatever the day.
s: Dry-roast the peanuts then coarsely pound them in a mortar.
Fry onion and tomato, add the pounded peanuts and a little water to form a sauce.
Add the chopped leafy greens, simmer 15 minutes until tender.
Make the nshima by beating the cornmeal into boiling water until a smooth, firm ball forms.
Serve the nshima with the hot ifisashi on the side.

kapana.d: Beef grilled hot on a scorching plate right in the heart of Katutura market, sliced in front of the customer and dipped into a ground chilli-and-spice mix, eaten standing with no plate.
s: Cut the beef into wide, thin strips.
Heat a cast-iron plate or very wide pan over high heat.
Grill the beef strips 2 to 3 minutes per side, turning often to sear all sides well.
Blend chilli, paprika, garlic and salt into a dry mix for dipping.
Slice the grilled meat into small pieces in front of the guests, serve with the spice mix and a lemon wedge.

motoho.d: A sorghum porridge fermented for a few days before cooking, which gives it a natural tang, eaten by the spoonful or poured into a cup like a thick Basotho breakfast drink.
s: Mix the sorghum flour with a little warm water, let ferment at room temperature 2 to 3 days in a jar covered with a cloth.
Bring the rest of the water to the boil.
Pour the fermented flour in a stream into the boiling water, stirring constantly.
Cook 15 minutes over low heat, whisking regularly, until a fluid, faintly tangy porridge forms.
Sweeten lightly, salt and serve warm, by the spoonful or poured into a cup.

sidvudvu.d: Pumpkin boiled then mashed directly into the cornmeal it cooks alongside, forming a sweet, orange porridge, a comforting dish of the Swazi kingdom.
s: Peel and chunk the pumpkin, boil 20 minutes until fully tender.
Mash the pumpkin directly in its cooking water.
Add the cornmeal in a stream, beating constantly with a wooden paddle.
Continue cooking 10 minutes over low heat until a thick, even porridge forms.
Sweeten lightly, add the butter and salt, serve hot.

kari-pwason.d: A fish curry with coconut milk and massalé, the Creole spice blend unique to the Seychelles, simmered with fresh tamarind for a tangy edge, served with rice and a breadfruit salad.
s: Fry onion, garlic, ginger and curry leaves in oil.
Add the massalé and toast briefly until fragrant.
Add tomato and tamarind, moisten with the coconut milk and simmer 15 minutes.
Add the fish cut into pieces, let it barely simmer 10 minutes without boiling hard so it doesn't break apart.
Boil the breadfruit in chunks, serve the curry with rice and the breadfruit.

dholl-puri.d: A thin flatbread filled with ground, cooked yellow split peas, rolled barely thicker than a crêpe, served folded with a curry and chilli sauce. Mauritius's most eaten Indian heritage food, sold on every street corner.
s: Soak the split peas 2 hours, cook until tender then drain and let dry.
Grind the cooked split peas with cumin and turmeric into a fine powder.
Knead flour, water and salt into a supple dough, rest 20 minutes, divide into balls.
Flatten each ball, fill with split pea powder, close and roll out again very thin.
Cook on a lightly oiled hot griddle 2 minutes per side, serve folded with a garlic chilli sauce.

langouste-vanille.d: Lobster from the Comorian lagoons flambéed then simmered in a coconut cream sauce infused with local vanilla pods, the archipelago being one of the world's top producers of this spice.
s: Split the lobsters in half lengthwise, lightly shell the tail.
Sear them in butter 2 minutes per side, flambé with rum.
Remove the lobsters, sweat onion and garlic in the same butter.
Add the coconut milk and scraped vanilla seeds, let reduce 10 minutes into a velvety sauce.
Return the lobsters to the sauce, warm through 3 minutes, serve with a squeeze of lime.

cachupa.d: Cape Verde's national dish, cracked corn and beans simmered for hours with pork and vegetables until nearly a purée, even better reheated and pan-fried the next day, then called cachupa refogada.
s: Soak the cracked corn and white beans overnight, drain.
Brown the pork and smoked sausage with onion, garlic and tomato.
Add the drained corn and beans, cover generously with water and simmer 2h30 over low heat.
Add cabbage and sweet potato in chunks, cook a further 30 minutes until everything is very tender.
Serve hot, or set aside and pan-fry the next day for the refogada version.

muzongue.p: São Tomé, São Tomé and Príncipe
muzongue.d: A fish soup spiced with local red chilli and palm oil, thickened with grated green plantain, a São Toméan festive dish made for big family gatherings by the ocean.
s: Cut the fish into pieces, salt lightly.
Fry onion, garlic and tomato in palm oil.
Finely grate the raw green plantains, add to the sauce with water to thicken.
Add the fish and chilli, simmer 20 minutes over low heat until the fish is cooked and the soup has thickened.
Serve scalding hot with a squeeze of lime.

belize-rice-beans.n: Rice and beans with stewed chicken
belize-rice-beans.d: Belize's quintessential Sunday meal: rice cooked in coconut milk and the soaking water of red beans, served with chicken slow-simmered in a recado sauce, a deep-red achiote condiment.
s: Soak the red beans overnight, drain reserving the soaking water.
Rub the chicken with achiote paste, garlic and salt, brown then simmer 40 minutes with onion and pepper.
Cook the beans in their soaking water until tender.
Add the rinsed rice and coconut milk to the cooked beans, cook covered 18 minutes.
Serve the rice and beans with the stewed chicken and its sauce.

oil-down.d: Grenada's national dish: breadfruit, vegetables and salted meat layered and simmered in coconut milk until the liquid fully evaporates and the coconut oil rises to the surface, hence the name.
s: Desalt the salted pork 2 hours in cold water, drain and cut into pieces.
Peel and cut the breadfruit into large wedges.
Layer in a large pot: pork, sausage, onion, then breadfruit, salting each layer.
Mix the coconut milk with turmeric, pour over the layers, add the whole chilli.
Cover and simmer 45 minutes without stirring until the liquid nearly fully evaporates, add the leafy greens for the last 10 minutes.

cou-cou-flying-fish.d: Barbados's national dish: a cornmeal and okra mash beaten with a wooden spoon until smooth, served with flying fish poached in a Creole tomato sauce, a fish that even appears on the country's coins.
s: Slice the okra into rounds, boil 10 minutes in salted water, drain reserving the water.
Pour the cornmeal into the boiling okra water in a stream, beating constantly with a wooden spoon.
Fold in the cooked okra, keep beating 10 minutes until a smooth, supple mash forms, add the butter.
Marinate the flying fish with lime and thyme, poach 15 minutes in a tomato and onion sauce.
Serve the cou-cou as a dome with the fish and its sauce on the side.

green-fig-saltfish.d: Saint Lucia's national dish: green bananas, called "figs" in the English Caribbean, boiled, flaked and mixed with desalted saltfish sautéed with tomato, onion and chilli.
s: Desalt the cod 24 hours, changing the water several times, then poach 10 minutes and flake.
Boil the unpeeled green bananas 20 minutes until tender, peel and slice.
Fry onion, pepper, garlic and chilli in oil.
Add crushed tomato and flaked cod, simmer 10 minutes.
Gently mix with the sliced bananas, scatter with scallion and serve hot.

fungee-pepperpot.d: Antigua's national dish: a firm cornmeal and okra ball called fungee, served with a thick stew of leafy greens, okra and salted meat called pepperpot, as old as the settlement of the eastern Caribbean.
s: Desalt the salted pork 2 hours, drain and cut into pieces.
Simmer it with pumpkin, spinach, onion and chilli in water for 40 minutes until everything is tender and the sauce thick.
Slice the okra into rounds, boil in a little water, drain reserving the water.
Pour the cornmeal into the boiling okra water in a stream, beat with a paddle, fold in the cooked okra until a firm ball forms.
Serve the fungee as a ball with the hot pepperpot on the side.

dominica-bouyon.d: A hearty broth of local roots — yam, dasheen, green banana — and salted meat, thickened with flour dumplings, made every Sunday in nearly every household on the island of a thousand rivers.
s: Desalt the salted pork 2 hours, drain and cut into pieces.
Simmer it with onion and thyme in water for 30 minutes.
Peel and chunk the yam, dasheen and green banana, add to the broth and cook a further 20 minutes.
Knead flour and water into a firm dough, shape small elongated dumplings, add to the broth 10 minutes before the end.
Adjust seasoning, scatter with scallion and serve scalding hot in large bowls.

pom.d: A bake of shredded chicken and grated pomtajer root, tied to Surinamese-Jewish heritage with a bitter orange sauce, oven-baked until golden on top, an unmissable dish for big family celebrations.
s: Poach the chicken 30 minutes until tender, shred it, reserving the broth.
Finely grate the raw pomtajer root.
Fry onion and garlic, add tomato and bitter orange juice, let reduce 10 minutes.
Mix shredded chicken, grated pomtajer and sauce, pour into a buttered baking dish, dust with breadcrumbs.
Bake 45 minutes at 180°C until the top is well browned and crisp.

guyana-pepperpot.d: Guyana's national Christmas dish, a beef and pig tail stew simmered for hours in cassareep, a black boiled bitter cassava syrup that acts as a natural preservative, letting the pot be reboiled daily for weeks.
s: Desalt the pig tail 2 hours, drain.
Place beef and pig tail in a large pot with onion, cinnamon and cloves.
Add the cassareep and cover with water, bring to the boil then simmer covered 2h30 over low heat.
Add the whole scotch bonnet pepper without piercing it to only lightly flavour, and the sugar.
Continue cooking until the sauce is black and thick and the meat is meltingly tender, serve with bread.

appam-stew.d: A fermented rice and coconut milk pancake, thin and crisp at the edges but thick and spongy in the middle, cooked in a curved pan called an appachatti, served with a mild coconut milk chicken curry, without excessive chilli.
s: Soak the rice 6 hours, blend with a little coconut milk into a smooth batter.
Add yeast and sugar, let ferment at room temperature overnight until the batter doubles and foams.
Pour a ladle of batter into a hot appachatti, swirl to spread thin edges and leave the centre thick, cover 2 minutes.
Fry onion, garlic, ginger and spices, add the chicken and brown it.
Moisten with the rest of the coconut milk, simmer 25 minutes until tender, serve with the warm appams.

sarson-da-saag.n: Sarson da saag with makki di roti
sarson-da-saag.d: Mustard leaves simmered for hours then pounded into a velvety green purée with clarified butter, paired with a thick cornmeal flatbread, a Punjabi winter speciality eaten with a knob of butter melting at the centre.
s: Boil mustard leaves and spinach with ginger, garlic and chilli for 40 minutes until very tender.
Drain, reserving a little water, pound or roughly blend into a thick purée.
Fry the sliced onion in ghee until browned, stir into the green purée, simmer 10 minutes.
Knead the cornmeal with warm water into a supple dough, shape thick discs by hand.
Cook the roti dry in a hot pan, brush with ghee, serve with the saag topped with a knob of butter.

macher-jhol.d: A light, watery freshwater fish curry, scented with panch phoron, a five-whole-seed spice blend unique to Bengal, with potato and turmeric, eaten daily with rice by millions of Bengali households.
s: Rub the fish with turmeric and salt, lightly fry in mustard oil, set aside.
Heat a little oil, add the panch phoron and let it crackle a few seconds.
Add potato in chunks and tomato, fry then moisten with water.
Simmer 15 minutes until the potato is nearly tender, add the split green chillies.
Return the fish to the broth, let it barely simmer 8 minutes without boiling hard, scatter with coriander and serve with rice.
