s: Take the steak out of the fridge 45 minutes before cooking so it reaches room temperature.
Season generously with coarse salt and cracked pepper on both sides.
Heat a cast-iron pan over very high heat until smoking.
Sear the steak 3 to 4 minutes per side depending on thickness, basting with garlic and thyme butter at the end of cooking.
Let rest 5 minutes under foil before slicing and serving.

nanaimo-bars.d: A cold, no-bake three-layer square, with a crumbled coconut biscuit base, pale yellow buttercream custard, and a crackling dark chocolate topping, a mining town's dessert that became a national emblem.
s: Blitz the biscuits into crumbs, mix with coconut, cocoa and melted butter, add the beaten egg and cook 3 minutes in a bain-marie, stirring.
Press this mixture into a paper-lined square pan, chill 20 minutes.
Beat butter, icing sugar and custard powder until light, spread over the cooled base.
Chill another 20 minutes until firm.
Melt the dark chocolate, pour over the custard layer, chill until hardened before cutting into small squares.

bc-spot-prawns.d: Large spot prawns caught in the cold Pacific waters, available for only a few weeks each spring, simply grilled whole in their shells to preserve their sweet, delicate flesh.
s: Leave the prawns whole with their shells on, do not peel.
Mix olive oil, crushed garlic and sliced chilli, brush generously over the prawns.
Heat a grill or griddle over high heat.
Grill the prawns 2 minutes per side until the shell turns pink and the flesh turns opaque.
Drizzle with a squeeze of lemon, scatter with parsley and serve immediately, to be shelled with fingers.

arctic-char-grilled.d: A fish from the icy waters of the Canadian Arctic, a salmon cousin with delicate pink-orange flesh, caught by Inuit communities and simply grilled whole over a wood fire with salt, letting its exceptional freshness speak for itself.
s: Gut and rinse the whole fish, dry thoroughly.
Salt generously inside and out, tuck a few sprigs of dill and lemon rounds into the cavity.
Heat a grill or wood embers until hot but stable.
Grill the whole fish 6 to 7 minutes per side depending on thickness, until the flesh flakes easily.
Drizzle with melted butter and a squeeze of lemon just before serving.

bannock.d: A traditional unleavened flatbread of the Indigenous peoples of northern Canada, cooked in a pan or on a hot stone, sometimes even wrapped around a stick and cooked over a campfire, an essential staple of bush cooking.
s: Mix flour, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
Gradually add water, mixing until a supple but non-sticky dough forms.
Knead briefly, let rest 10 minutes under a cloth.
Flatten the dough into one or several thick discs about 2 cm.
Cook in an oiled pan over medium heat, 8 minutes per side until golden and cooked through.

montreal-smoked-meat.d: A beef brisket cured in spices then smoked and steamed, less sweet than its New York pastrami cousin, hand-sliced in front of the customer and piled high between two slices of rye bread with mustard.
s: Rub the beef brisket with a mix of coarse salt, crushed garlic and spices, cure chilled 10 days, turning regularly.
Rinse thoroughly, coat with a generous crust of cracked pepper and coriander.
Cold-smoke then hot-smoke for several hours until a black crust forms.
Steam 4 hours until extremely tender.
Hand-slice in front of guests, pile generously between two slices of rye bread spread with mustard.

beavertails.d: A yeasted dough hand-stretched into a flat oval shape resembling a beaver's tail, fried until golden and crackling, covered in cinnamon sugar, sold hot to skaters on the frozen Rideau Canal every winter.
s: Knead flour, yeast, warm milk, egg, sugar and a pinch of salt into a supple dough, let rise 1 hour.
Divide the dough into balls, hand-stretch each into a flat, elongated oval shape.
Fry in hot oil at 180°C 1 minute per side until golden and crackling.
Drain quickly on paper towel.
Brush with melted butter and dust generously with cinnamon sugar, serve immediately, piping hot.

tire-erable.d: Pure maple syrup heated until it thickens into a concentrated syrup, poured in long streams directly onto fresh snow where it sets instantly, rolled around a wooden stick and eaten still warm-cold right at the sugar shack.
s: Pour the pure maple syrup into a large heavy-bottomed pan.
Heat over medium heat until reaching 112°C on a candy thermometer, never stirring.
Prepare a large tray of clean, freshly fallen snow, or crushed ice as a substitute.
Immediately pour long streams of hot syrup onto the packed snow.
Quickly roll each set stream around a wooden stick before it hardens too much, eat right away.

bagna-cauda.d: A hot bath of garlic, anchovy and oil set in the middle of the table, where everyone dips raw vegetables. The dish of the Piedmont grape harvest: eaten slowly, in company, on an autumn evening.
s: Peel the garlic, remove the green germ and poach it gently in the milk for 30 minutes: this takes away its bite.
Drain the garlic and crush it with a fork together with the rinsed anchovy fillets.
Pour in the olive oil, add the butter, and melt over very low heat for 30 minutes, never letting it bubble.
The sauce is ready when smooth and pale gold; keep it warm over a table burner.
Serve with raw vegetables cut into batons, cardoon and Jerusalem artichoke first among them.

vitello-tonnato.d: Poached veal served cold in near-transparent slices under a sauce of tuna and capers. The pairing sounds improbable until the first mouthful: it has opened Piedmontese Sunday lunches for two centuries.
s: Tie the veal and poach it for 1½ hours in a broth of white wine, carrot, celery, onion and bay, never letting it boil.
Let it cool completely in its broth: this is what keeps it tender.
Whisk a firm mayonnaise with the yolks, oil and lemon juice.
Blend the drained tuna, anchovies and half the capers, fold into the mayonnaise and loosen with a little broth.
Slice the veal very thinly, coat with the sauce, scatter the remaining capers and chill for two hours before serving.

pizzoccheri.d: Buckwheat tagliatelle boiled with cabbage and potato, then drowned in melted casera cheese and garlic butter. The Lombard mountains on a plate, with no concession whatsoever to lightness.
s: Knead both flours with the warm water, rest for 30 minutes, then roll out and cut strips 1 cm by 7.
Boil the diced potatoes for 5 minutes in plenty of salted water, then add the shredded cabbage.
Five minutes later drop in the pizzoccheri: they take about 8 minutes.
Meanwhile turn the garlic and sage golden in the butter without letting it burn.
Drain, layer pasta, vegetables and cheeses in the dish, pour over the sizzling butter and serve at once.

casoncelli.d: Sweet-wrapper-shaped ravioli whose filling mixes meat, amaretti and raisins — a survival of medieval cooking, where sweet and savoury shared a plate without embarrassment. Served with butter, pancetta and sage.
s: Knead the flour and eggs into a firm dough, wrap and rest for an hour.
Brown the minced beef and sausage, let cool, then mix with the crushed amaretti, raisins, grated pear, breadcrumbs and parmesan.
Roll the dough very thin, place hazelnut-sized mounds of filling every 5 cm, fold over and pinch both ends into sweet-wrapper shapes.
Crisp the pancetta in the butter with the sage.
Cook the casoncelli for 4 minutes in barely simmering water, drain and spoon over the pancetta butter.

tortelli-di-zucca.d: Roast pumpkin meets Cremona mostarda and amaretti: sweet, mustardy and bitter all at once. Served on Mantuan tables on Christmas Eve since the Renaissance.
s: Roast the pumpkin in chunks for 45 minutes at 180°C: it should dry out as much as cook.
Mash the flesh with the powdered amaretti, chopped mostarda, parmesan and nutmeg; rest overnight in the fridge.
Knead flour and eggs, rest for an hour, then roll into very thin sheets.
Form 6 cm squares around a spoonful of filling and seal the edges carefully.
Cook for 4 minutes, drain and serve with sage butter and grated parmesan.

polenta-concia.d: Here the polenta is only a pretext for the fontina. Stirred for a full hour, then loaded with cheese and butter until it pulls into threads. The dish of Aosta Valley mountain refuges.
s: Bring the salted water to the boil and rain in the cornmeal, whisking constantly.
Turn the heat to its lowest and stir with a wooden spoon for 50 minutes: the polenta should pull away from the sides.
Slice the fontina and fold it in off the heat, a handful at a time.
Add the butter in pieces and the parmesan, stirring until the mass is glossy and stringy.
Serve scalding hot, straight from the pot, with a turn of the pepper mill.

risi-e-bisi.d: Neither quite soup nor quite risotto: in Venice they say it must run off the spoon. It was served to the Doge on 25 April, Saint Mark's day, with the first peas of the lagoon.
s: Pod the peas and boil the pods in the broth for 20 minutes, then strain: that is where the flavour lives.
Soften the onion and pancetta in half the butter.
Add the peas and parsley, moisten with a ladle of broth and stew for 10 minutes.
Pour in the rice, cover with boiling broth and cook for 15 minutes without stirring much: this is not a risotto.
Off the heat, beat in the remaining butter and the parmesan. It should stay loose enough to pour.

baccala-alla-vicentina.d: Norwegian stockfish stewed for four and a half hours in milk and oil, never once stirred. The brotherhood that guards the recipe insists on this stillness: one spoonful too many and the flesh falls apart.
s: Soak the stockfish for three days, changing the water morning and evening, then cut into pieces without removing the skin.
Soften the sliced onions very slowly in the oil, add the crushed anchovies and the parsley.
Flour the fish pieces and pack them tightly into a casserole, alternating with onion and parmesan.
Cover with milk and oil, bring to a bare simmer and cook uncovered for 4½ hours, never stirring.
Serve warm with a thick polenta: the dish is better still reheated the next day.

tiramisu.d: Six ingredients, no cooking, a 1960s invention that became the most copied Italian dessert in the world. The Treviso rule: no whipped cream, no alcohol, no gelatine — only eggs, mascarpone and strong coffee.
s: Make the coffee and let it cool completely: while hot it would soak the biscuits through.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar to the ribbon stage, then fold in the mascarpone with a spatula.
Whip the whites to firm peaks and fold them into the cream, lifting rather than stirring.
Dip each biscuit for one second per side in the coffee — no longer — and line the base of the dish.
Alternate two layers of biscuits and cream, smooth the top, chill for 6 hours and dust with cocoa just before serving.

frico.d: A cake of montasio and potato fried until it forms a lace-like crust. Born of thrift: Friulian shepherds melted down the rinds rather than throw them away.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins, peel and crush them roughly with a fork.
Soften the sliced onion in the butter without colouring it.
Grate the montasio — one third young, two thirds aged — and mix it with the potato and onion.
Tip the mixture into a hot pan, press it down and let it set for 12 minutes over medium heat without touching it.
Flip it using a plate and brown the second side for 10 minutes. Serve cut into wedges, crust upwards.

farinata-genovese.d: A chickpea flatbread baked in a copper pan in a wood oven, crisp at the edge and creamy at the centre. Three ingredients and a long wait: the batter must rest five hours to lose its bitterness.
s: Whisk the chickpea flour into the water until lump-free, and salt it.
Rest for 5 hours at room temperature, skimming off the foam that rises: that foam carries the bitterness.
Stir in half the oil; the batter should stay very liquid.
Oil a wide pan generously, pour in a layer barely 5 mm deep and scatter over the rosemary.
Bake at 250°C with top heat for 12 to 15 minutes: the surface should be blistered brown. Pepper it and cut into uneven pieces.

passatelli.d: Vermicelli of stale bread, parmesan and egg pushed through a perforated plate and cooked for two minutes in broth. Romagna's cooking of leftovers raised to its highest point.
s: Mix the fine breadcrumbs, grated parmesan, eggs, nutmeg and lemon zest.
Work by hand to a compact, dry dough that no longer sticks; rest it for 30 minutes.
Bring the broth to a bare simmer — it should be fragrant, it is half the dish.
Push the dough through a coarse potato ricer directly over the broth.
The passatelli rise in 2 minutes: serve immediately, with extra parmesan on the side.

piadina-romagnola.d: An unleavened flatbread cooked on a terracotta griddle, folded over squacquerone cheese and rocket. Pascoli called it 'the national bread of the Romagnoli'; seafront kiosks still sell it at all hours.
s: Rub the lard into the flour with your fingertips, then add the salt and bicarbonate.
Pour in the warm water little by little and knead for 10 minutes to a supple dough; rest for 30 minutes under a cloth.
Divide into six balls and roll them into 3 mm discs.
Cook on a very hot dry griddle, 2 minutes a side, pricking the bubbles with a fork.
Fill while hot with the soft cheese, ham and rocket, then fold in half.

pappa-al-pomodoro.d: Stale unsalted Tuscan bread melted into tomato and olive oil until it becomes a thick porridge. A poor man's dish turned regional emblem: eaten lukewarm, never piping hot.
s: Turn the crushed garlic golden in half the oil, then remove it.
Add the peeled and chopped tomatoes, salt, and reduce for 20 minutes.
Cut the stale bread into thick slices and drop them into the pan with the hot broth.
Crush with a wooden spoon and cook 20 minutes more: the bread should vanish into the sauce.
Off the heat, add the torn basil and the remaining raw oil. Serve lukewarm, never scalding.

bistecca-alla-fiorentina.d: A five-centimetre-thick Chianina T-bone seared over embers and served rare — asking for it well done is, in Florence, a breach of taste. Salt, pepper, raw oil: nothing else.
s: Take the meat out of the fridge two hours ahead: a bistecca cold at the centre will never cook properly.
Build a fierce fire and let the embers turn white with ash.
Lay the steak on the grill and do not touch it for 5 minutes, then turn it for 5 minutes more.
Stand it upright on the bone for 5 minutes to sear the rim, never piercing the meat.
Salt, pepper, pour over raw oil and rest for 5 minutes before carving along the bone.

olive-ascolane.d: Large green olives stoned in a spiral, stuffed with three meats, breaded and fried. A work of patience invented in the 19th century by cooks in noble households to use up their leftovers.
s: Stone the olives by turning the knife around the pit so as to keep one continuous ribbon.
Brown the meats with the diced vegetables, deglaze with white wine and cook for 30 minutes.
Chop everything finely, bind with an egg, the parmesan and the nutmeg.
Re-form each olive around a hazelnut of stuffing, then coat in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs.
Fried for 3 minutes at 175°C they should be golden and crisp. Serve scalding hot.

strangozzi-al-tartufo.d: Water-and-flour pasta, no egg, rolled by hand and served under a shower of raw grated Norcia black truffle. The sauce is three things: oil, garlic, anchovy — anything more would mask the scent.
s: Knead the flour and salted water for 15 minutes to a very firm dough; rest for an hour.
Roll out to 2 mm, flour it, roll the sheet on itself and cut thick strips, unrolling them at once.
Warm the oil gently with the whole garlic cloves and the anchovies until the latter dissolve; discard the garlic.
Grate two thirds of the truffle into the warm oil off the heat: it must never cook.
Cook the pasta for 3 minutes, toss with the sauce and a ladle of cooking water, and grate the rest of the truffle at the table.

amatriciana.d: Guanciale, tomato, pecorino: the trinity of Amatrice, an Apennine village whose recipe conquered Rome. Guanciale is not pancetta, and the distinction is no quibble — the cheek gives that melting fat.
s: Cut the guanciale into thick lardons and render it over low heat, with no added fat, until golden.
Lift it out and keep it crisp; deglaze the pan with white wine.
Add the crushed tomatoes and chilli, salt lightly and reduce for 15 minutes.
Cook the bucatini very al dente and drain, keeping a ladle of the water.
Combine pasta, sauce and guanciale off the heat, then beat in the grated pecorino, stirring briskly.

saltimbocca-alla-romana.d: 'Jump in the mouth': a veal escalope, a sage leaf, a slice of raw ham, ten minutes in a pan. The speed is part of the recipe — overcooked, the veal toughens and the dish loses its point.
s: Flatten the escalopes between two sheets of paper to 4 mm.
Lay two sage leaves and a slice of ham on each, fixing them with a cocktail stick.
Flour very lightly, on the veal side only.
Sear ham-side down for 1 minute in foaming butter, then turn for 2 minutes.
Keep warm, deglaze with white wine, reduce by half and pour this buttery juice over the saltimbocca.

arrosticini.d: One-centimetre cubes of mutton threaded onto wooden skewers and grilled over a long narrow brazier, the 'canala'. Eaten by hand, by the dozen, pulling the meat off with your teeth.
s: Cut the meat and fat into even 1 cm cubes: this is the only technical point of the dish.
Thread them alternating lean and fat, five or six pieces per 20 cm skewer.
Prepare a bed of red embers in a narrow hearth, longer than it is wide.
Lay the skewers tightly side by side and turn them every 30 seconds, 4 minutes in all.
Salt as they come off the fire and serve on country bread drizzled with oil, which catches the juices.

parmigiana-di-melanzane.d: Fried aubergine, tomato, basil and two cheeses, stacked and baked. The name comes not from Parma but from Sicilian 'parmiciana', the slats of a shutter — which overlap exactly as the slices do.
s: Cut the aubergines into 6 mm slices, salt them and let them drain for an hour under a weight.
Pat them thoroughly dry, flour them and fry until golden; drain on paper.
Make a sauce by reducing the tomatoes with the garlic and olive oil for 20 minutes.
Layer sauce, aubergine, drained mozzarella, basil and parmesan in a dish, four storeys high.
Bake for 45 minutes at 180°C and let it settle for 30 minutes before cutting: that rest is what holds it together.

sfogliatella.d: A shell of pastry in a hundred leaves, crisp enough to shatter, filled with a semolina and ricotta cream scented with cinnamon. Born in a convent on the Amalfi coast, perfected by a Neapolitan pastry cook in 1818.
s: Knead the flour, water, honey and salt for 15 minutes into a very hard dough; rest for 2 hours.
Pass it through a pasta roller, thinner and thinner, into a translucent sheet several metres long. Brush with melted lard and roll it up tightly into a log. Chill overnight.
Cook the semolina in the milk, let it cool, then mix in ricotta, sugar, yolks, candied fruit, cinnamon and orange blossom water.
Slice the log into 1 cm rounds and push each into a cone with your thumbs; fill with cream and seal.
Bake for 25 minutes at 200°C. The leaves fan open. Dust with icing sugar and eat warm.

pasta-alla-norma.d: Named after the opera by Bellini, a son of Catania: to call a dish 'a Norma' was to say it approached perfection. Fried aubergine, tomato, basil and grated salted ricotta on top.
s: Dice the aubergines, salt them and let them drain for 30 minutes.
Fry them in hot oil until golden and melting, then drain.
Make a short sauce with the garlic, olive oil and crushed tomatoes, 20 minutes over a lively flame.
Cook the pasta al dente and toss it with the sauce and half the aubergine.
Plate up, crown with the remaining aubergine, the basil and a generous shower of grated salted ricotta.

caponata.d: Aubergine, celery, olives and capers bound by a sweet-and-sour of vinegar and sugar. Every Sicilian family defends its own version; all agree on one point: eat it the next day, at room temperature.
s: Cut the aubergines into large dice, salt for 30 minutes, pat dry and fry until coloured.
Blanch the celery for 5 minutes, then sweat it in olive oil with the sliced onion.
Add tomatoes, stoned olives, rinsed capers, pine nuts and raisins; stew for 15 minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and sugar, raise the heat and let it evaporate for 3 minutes: that is the sweet-sour strike.
Fold in the aubergines, cut the heat, add the basil and rest overnight before serving at room temperature.

seadas.d: A fried semolina turnover stuffed with barely sour fresh pecorino, poured over with bitter strawberry-tree honey. Sweet and savoury meet head-on — it began life as a main course, not a dessert.
s: Knead the semolina, lard, warm water and salt into a smooth dough; rest for an hour.
Melt the fresh pecorino gently with the lemon zest until it pulls into threads, spread it 1 cm thick and let it set.
Cut 8 cm discs of cheese and 10 cm discs of dough.
Seal each cheese disc between two rounds of pastry, crimping with a fluted wheel and pushing out the air.
Fried 2 minutes a side at 170°C, they puff up. Drain and pour over the warm honey.

koenigsberger-klopse.d: Veal dumplings poached in broth and served under a white sauce of capers and lemon. They came from East Prussia with the refugees of 1945 and became a staple of Berlin canteens.
s: Soak the bread roll in water, squeeze it out and mix into the minced veal with the softened onion, crushed anchovies and egg.
Shape golf-ball dumplings and poach them for 15 minutes in broth with bay and allspice, never boiling.
Lift them out and strain the broth.
Make a pale roux with the butter and flour, whisk in half a litre of broth and cook for 10 minutes.
Off the heat, bind with the yolk beaten into the cream, add the capers and lemon juice, then return the dumplings. Serve with steamed potatoes.

maultaschen.d: Big Swabian ravioli whose nickname says everything: Herrgottsbscheißerle, 'little cheaters of the Lord'. The monks of Maulbronn hid meat under spinach so they could eat it during Lent.
s: Knead the flour and eggs into a firm dough and rest it for an hour.
Blanch the spinach, squeeze it thoroughly dry and chop it with the bacon and the soaked bread rolls.
Combine with the minced pork, softened onion, parsley, marjoram and nutmeg.
Roll the dough into long strips, pipe the filling along them, fold over and press every 6 cm before cutting.
Poach for 12 minutes in simmering broth and serve in that broth — or fried in butter the next day.

kaesespaetzle.d: Fresh noodles scraped from a board into boiling water, layered with mountain cheese and crowned with fried onions. Swabian lore said you judged a woman by her Spätzle — the saying has aged badly, the recipe has not.
s: Beat the flour, eggs, sparkling water and salt hard until the batter blisters and pulls away from the spoon.
Rest for 20 minutes, then scrape it in small batches into a large pan of boiling salted water.
The Spätzle are done the moment they float: drain and barely refresh them.
Fry the sliced onions slowly in the butter until golden and lightly crisp.
Layer Spätzle and grated cheeses in a warm dish, cover and let melt for 5 minutes, then top with the onions and chives.

schweinshaxe.d: A pork knuckle roasted for two and a half hours, its rind turned into a glassy shell you have to crack with a knife. The dish of Munich beer halls, basted with dark beer during cooking as much as poured beside it.
s: Score the rind into diamonds without cutting into the meat, rub with salt, crushed garlic and caraway.
Set the knuckles on a bed of onion and carrot and pour half the beer into the dish.
Roast for 2 hours at 160°C, basting every 20 minutes with the juices and the rest of the beer.
Raise to 220°C for the last 20 minutes: the rind blisters and hardens.
Rest for 10 minutes, deglaze the roasting juices and serve with sauerkraut and potatoes.

weisswurst.d: A white sausage of veal and parsley, poached and never grilled. Munich lore says it must not hear the noon bells: made without preservatives, it was eaten the very morning it was made.
s: Blend the very cold veal and fat with the iced water in several stages, never letting the mixture warm.
Fold in the chopped parsley, cooled softened onion, lemon zest, white pepper and nutmeg.
Fill the casings and twist every 12 cm; prick any air bubbles.
Poach for 12 minutes in water at 75°C: it must never boil, or the sausages burst.
Serve in their water with sweet mustard and a pretzel. You suck out the meat and leave the skin.

brezel.d: The knot of dough dipped in an alkaline bath before baking: that is what gives the brown crust and the unmistakable taste. The belly cracks, the arms stay soft — a good pretzel is known by that contrast.
s: Knead flour, water, yeast, butter, malt and salt for 10 minutes into a firm dough; prove for 45 minutes.
Divide into eight, roll long ropes tapered at the ends and swollen in the middle.
Form the knot: cross the two arms twice and fold them back onto the belly.
Let them dry uncovered in the fridge for 30 minutes, then dip each pretzel for 20 seconds in a litre of boiling water with the bicarbonate.
Slash the belly, scatter coarse salt and bake for 15 minutes at 220°C.

rinderrouladen.d: A slice of beef rolled around mustard, bacon, onion and a gherkin, braised for two hours in its own juices. The German Sunday lunch par excellence, with red cabbage and potato dumplings.
s: Flatten the beef slices, season and spread them with mustard.
Lay bacon, sliced onion and a halved gherkin on each, roll up and tie with string.
Sear the rolls on all sides in hot butter and set aside.
Sweat carrot and onion in the same pot, add the tomato paste and deglaze with red wine.
Return the rolls, pour in the broth, add the bay and braise covered for 1¾ hours. Thicken the sauce with the slaked flour.

labskaus.d: A bright pink hash of salt beef, potato and beetroot, served with a fried egg, a pickled herring and a gherkin. Deep-sea sailors' food: everything in it was salted or pickled, and therefore imperishable.
s: Boil the potatoes in salted water with the bay leaf, then crush them roughly.
Soften the onion in the lard, add the shredded salt beef and the cooked beetroot in small dice.
Fold into the potato, moisten with the pickle brine and heat through for 10 minutes, stirring: the hash should stay coarse.
Fry the eggs, whites set and yolks running.
Mound the hash on the plate, set the egg on top, herring and gherkin alongside.

gruenkohl-pinkel.d: The kale waits for the first frost before it is picked: cold turns its starch into sugar. It is stewed for two hours with bacon and Pinkel, a smoked oat sausage, during the ritual outings of January.
s: Strip the kale from its stalks, blanch for 5 minutes and chop it coarsely.
Soften the onion and bacon in the lard, add the kale and let it sweat for 10 minutes.
Moisten with broth, bury the smoked pork and simmer covered for 1 hour.
Lay the Pinkel sausages on the kale without pricking them and continue for 45 minutes: their fat perfumes the whole dish.
Thicken with the oats, sharpen with mustard and serve with fried potatoes.

handkaese-mit-musik.d: A translucent sour cheese married to a marinade of raw onion and vinegar. The 'music' of the name is not poetic: it is what the onions produce a few hours later, and the Hessians still find it funny.
s: Slice the onions as finely as you can and salt them lightly.
Mix them with the vinegar, oil, caraway and a little pepper.
Lay the cheeses in a deep dish and cover them entirely with this marinade.
Rest in the fridge for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight: the cheese should soak without falling apart.
Serve with buttered rye bread and plenty of chives. A glass of apple cider is obligatory.

thueringer-rostbratwurst.d: Recorded as early as 1404 in the accounts of a convent in Arnstadt, it is grilled over pine-cone embers and eaten standing, in a roll too short for it, with brown mustard.
s: Mince the meat and fat on a medium plate, keeping everything very cold.
Season with caraway, marjoram, garlic, nutmeg, salt and pepper, and work the mixture until it turns tacky.
Fill the casings loosely and twist every 20 cm; rest overnight in the fridge.
Grill over medium embers for 12 to 15 minutes, turning often: the skin should brown without splitting.
Serve in a split roll with a spoonful of brown mustard.

spargel-hollandaise.d: From April to Midsummer, Germany stops for white asparagus. At Beelitz it is cut before it breaks the sand, which keeps it white and sweet. Butter, ham, steamed potatoes: nothing more.
s: Peel the asparagus from tip to base, twice rather than once, and snap off the fibrous end.
Simmer the peelings for 15 minutes in salted water with the sugar: this broth will cook the spears.
Poach them 12 to 18 minutes depending on thickness; they should bend without snapping.
Clarify the butter. Whisk the yolks with the wine over a bain-marie to the ribbon, then trickle in the warm butter, whisking without pause.
Season the sauce with lemon, salt and nutmeg, and serve the asparagus with the ham and steamed potatoes.

saumagen.d: A pig's stomach stuffed with meat and potato, poached then sliced and pan-fried. Helmut Kohl served it to Gorbachev, Thatcher and Reagan: the most diplomatic peasant dish in Germany.
s: Clean the stomach thoroughly in vinegared water and soak it overnight.
Cut the pork and boiled potatoes into large dice, mix with the softened onion, eggs, marjoram and spices.
Fill the stomach only three quarters full — the stuffing swells — and sew the opening shut.
Poach for 2½ hours in water at 80°C, never boiling, pricking it two or three times so it does not burst.
Cool, cut into thick slices and fry them golden in lard. Serve with sauerkraut cooked in white wine.

himmel-und-erde.d: Heaven is the apples that grow above; earth is the potatoes below. Mashed together and crowned with fried black pudding and onions, they make a Rhineland dish recorded since the 18th century.
s: Boil the potatoes in salted water. Meanwhile stew the quartered apples with the sugar and vinegar.
Mash the two together with a fork, keeping some texture, and season with nutmeg.
Fry the sliced onions in the butter until golden, along with the diced bacon.
Cut the black pudding into thick slices and fry for 2 minutes a side, turning no more than once.
Spoon out the mash, lay on the pudding and cover with the onions and crisp bacon.

stollen.d: A Christmas loaf heavy with fruit and butter, its shape recalling the swaddled child. Until 1491 butter was forbidden in it during Advent: it took a papal bull to allow it.
s: Steep the raisins in the rum for at least one night, two if you can.
Make a starter with the yeast, warm milk and a little flour; let it froth for 20 minutes.
Knead with the remaining flour, 200 g of butter, the sugar and the spices, then work in the fruit and almonds without tearing the dough.
Prove for an hour, flatten, lay a rope of marzipan down the middle and fold the dough over it, off-centre.
Bake for 60 minutes at 160°C, brush with melted butter as it comes out and bury it in icing sugar. Wait three weeks before slicing.

rote-gruetze.d: A barely thickened compote of red fruit, served ice cold beneath a veil of cold cream or vanilla sauce. The summer dessert of the North, where the berry season is short and nothing is wasted.
s: Hull the fruit and stone the cherries; keep a quarter of the raspberries back for the end.
Bring the water, sugar and lemon juice to the boil, add the currants and cherries and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the strawberries and raspberries and take off the heat almost at once: they must not collapse.
Slake the cornstarch in a little cold water, stir it into the hot fruit and let it thicken for barely a minute.
Add the vanilla and the reserved raspberries, cool, then chill for 4 hours. Serve with cold cream on the side.

tafelspitz.d: The most prized cut of beef in Vienna, poached for three hours and served in its broth with two sauces: horseradish with apple, and chive. It was Franz Joseph's favourite dish, eaten almost daily.
s: Brown the halved onions dry, cut side down on the pan: this is what gives the broth its golden colour.
Bring the meat and bones to a bare simmer in plenty of water, skimming carefully for twenty minutes.
Add the vegetables, bay and peppercorns, and poach for 2½ hours, never boiling.
Grate the horseradish into cooked apple and a little broth for the first sauce; blend chives, cream and soaked bread for the second.
Carve the meat against the grain, serve it in a tureen with the broth and vegetables, the two sauces alongside.

kaiserschmarrn.d: A thick pancake torn into golden shreds with a spatula, caramelised in sugar and served with plum compote. The 'Emperor's scramble': legend has a cook botching his pancake in front of Franz Joseph.
s: Plump the raisins in the warm rum.
Whisk the yolks, milk, flour, vanilla and a pinch of salt to a smooth batter; rest for 15 minutes.
Beat the whites to soft peaks with half the sugar and fold them in gently.
Pour into a large buttered pan, scatter the raisins over and let it set for 4 minutes, then flip it in one piece.
Tear the pancake into pieces with the spatula, sprinkle with the remaining sugar and caramelise for 3 minutes, stirring. Dust with icing sugar and serve with the compote.

apfelstrudel.d: The dough must be stretched by hand over a tablecloth until you can read a newspaper through it — the Viennese rule allows no appeal. It came from Turkey by way of Hungary, a distant cousin of baklava.
s: Knead flour, warm water, oil and salt for 10 minutes until the dough is elastic and glossy; oil it and rest it for an hour under a warm bowl.
Toast the breadcrumbs in half the butter: they will absorb the apple juices.
Peel and thinly slice the apples, mix with the sugar, cinnamon, rum-soaked raisins, walnuts and lemon.
Stretch the dough by hand over a floured cloth until translucent, brush with melted butter and scatter the crumbs.
Lay the apples along one third, roll up using the cloth, seal the ends and bake for 40 minutes at 190°C, brushing twice with butter.

tiroler-groestl.d: The leftover meal, made in a pan: yesterday's potatoes, Sunday's boiled beef, onion, all fried together and crowned with a fried egg. The refuge lunch after a morning in the mountains.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins the day before: cold, they will not fall apart in the pan.
Peel them, cut into thick rounds and fry them in lard until golden.
Add the bacon and sliced onion, letting them colour without stirring too often.
Fold in the sliced boiled beef, the caraway and the marjoram, and heat through for 5 minutes.
Fry four eggs and lay them on the gröstl, parsley over the top. Serve in the pan.

steirisches-backhendl.d: A jointed chicken, breaded and fried in lard, served warm with potato salad dressed in roasted pumpkin-seed oil. In the 18th century only the Viennese aristocracy could afford a whole chicken for one person.
s: Joint the chicken into eight pieces, salt them and rest for 30 minutes.
Coat each piece in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, without pressing: the crumb must stay loose so it puffs in the fat.
Heat the lard to 165°C and fry the pieces for 12 to 15 minutes depending on size.
Drain on a rack, never on paper, to keep the crust crisp.
Make the warm potato salad with onion, vinegar and pumpkin-seed oil, and serve with lemon wedges.

roesti.d: A cake of grated potato browned in butter, originally the breakfast of Bernese farmers. The imaginary line dividing French- from German-speaking Switzerland is still called the 'Röstigraben'.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins the day before and leave them to cool overnight: this is the only rule that matters.
Peel and grate them on the coarse side of the grater, without crushing them.
Salt at the last moment, never before: salt would draw out water and the cake would stay soft.
Tip into a hot buttered pan, press down lightly and let it set for 15 minutes over medium heat.
Turn it with a plate, add the remaining butter and brown the other side for 12 minutes. The crust should be even and brittle.

zuercher-geschnetzeltes.d: Veal cut into fine strips, seared very fast and coated in a cream and white wine sauce. In Zurich the kidneys go in; elsewhere they are left out. It is always served with rösti.
s: Cut the veal into finger-width strips and flour them very lightly.
Sear them in two batches in sizzling butter, barely 90 seconds, and keep them warm: they will finish cooking in the sauce.
Sweat the shallot, add the sliced mushrooms and let them release their water.
Deglaze with white wine, reduce by half, pour in the cream and let it thicken for 5 minutes.
Return the meat and its juices, heat through without boiling, and sharpen with lemon and parsley.

raclette-valaisanne.d: Half a wheel held to the fire, its melting face scraped onto the plate — hence the name. Valais herdsmen did this from the Middle Ages; the electric grill arrived only six centuries later.
s: Choose firm-fleshed potatoes of even size and boil them in their skins for 25 minutes.
Keep them warm under a cloth: they must stay scalding throughout the meal.
Hold the half-wheel under the grill, or lay slices in individual pans.
Scrape the cheese the moment it blisters and runs, without waiting for it to colour.
Serve at once over the crushed potato, with gherkins, pickled onions and air-dried beef. Grind pepper over.

aelplermagronen.d: Macaroni, potatoes, cream and cheese cooked in one pan, with fried onions and apple sauce on the side. Alpine herdsmen had one fire and little crockery: everything goes in together.
s: Dice the potatoes to the size of the macaroni: they must cook together.
Start them in salted water for 5 minutes, then add the pasta for its stated time.
Meanwhile fry the sliced onions slowly in the butter until deep golden.
Drain, return to the pan with the cream and milk, and reduce for 3 minutes.
Off the heat, stir in the grated gruyère and the nutmeg, cover with the fried onions and serve with cold apple sauce.

souvlaki-pita.d: Cubes of pork marinated in lemon and oregano, grilled over embers and rolled in a warm pita with tomato, red onion, tzatziki and a few chips. The standing meal of Athenians, always has been.
s: Cut the pork into 3 cm cubes and marinate for 4 hours in lemon juice, oil, oregano, crushed garlic and pepper.
Grate the cucumber, squeeze it hard and mix into the yogurt with a little garlic and oil: that is the tzatziki.
Thread the meat onto skewers and grill for 10 to 12 minutes over lively embers, turning often.
Deep-fry the potatoes as chips and salt them as they come out.
Warm the pitas 30 seconds a side, fill with meat, tzatziki, tomato, onion and chips, then roll tightly in paper.

horiatiki.d: No lettuce and no dressing: horiatiki, the 'village salad', is nothing but tomato, cucumber, onion, pepper, olives and a whole slab of feta laid on top. Olive oil and oregano do the rest.
s: Cut the tomatoes into large irregular wedges — never dice — and salt them at once.
Peel the cucumber in stripes, slice it thick, and cut the onion and pepper into rings.
Combine the vegetables in a deep dish with the olives and capers, without crushing them.
Lay the slab of feta whole on top, unbroken.
Pour over plenty of olive oil, scatter oregano and serve with bread to mop the bottom of the dish.

spanakopita.d: The pie of Epirus, land of great pies: spinach, wild herbs and feta between pastry leaves so thin they are counted by the dozen. Every village had its own version, according to what the mountain gave.
s: Salt the shredded spinach and let it drain for 30 minutes, then squeeze it out by the handful: this is the step people wrongly skip.
Sweat the leek and spring onions in a little oil, then let them cool.
Combine spinach, leek, chopped herbs, crumbled feta and beaten eggs. Pepper it; the feta usually salts it enough.
Oil the tin, layer seven sheets of pastry brushing each one, dust with semolina and spread the filling.
Close with seven more sheets, score the portions before baking and bake for 50 minutes at 180°C. Let it cool before cutting.

pastitsio.d: Three storeys: fat macaroni standing on end, a meat sauce with cinnamon and clove, and a thick béchamel browned in the oven. The Greek cousin of baked pasta, marked by that note of sweet spice.
s: Brown the onion and meat, deglaze with red wine, add tomato, cinnamon, cloves and bay, then reduce for 40 minutes.
Cook the macaroni very al dente, drain and bind with a beaten egg and a little cheese.
Make a thick béchamel with the butter, flour and milk; off the heat stir in two eggs, the nutmeg and half the cheese.
Lay half the pasta in the dish, cover with the meat, then the rest of the pasta.
Pour over the béchamel, dust with the remaining cheese and bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. Wait 30 minutes before cutting.

gemista.d: Tomatoes and peppers hollowed out, filled with herbed rice and baked slowly until they slump. A summer dish made in the morning and eaten warm in the afternoon, never hot.
s: Cut a lid off the tomatoes and peppers, hollow them out and keep the tomato pulp.
Soften the onion in oil, add the raw rice, the blended pulp, herbs, pine nuts and raisins; let it absorb for 5 minutes.
Salt the inside of the vegetables, sugar the tomatoes lightly and fill them three quarters full: the rice swells.
Wedge them tightly in a dish, slip quartered potatoes between them and pour over oil and a glass of water.
Bake for 1¼ hours at 180°C with the lids back on. Serve warm, ideally the next day.

fasolada.d: The white bean soup that Greeks call their national dish, long before moussaka. Nothing but vegetables, a great deal of olive oil, and a long cooking that does all the work.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then bring them to the boil in fresh water and throw that first water away.
Cover with cold water and simmer for 45 minutes with the bay leaves.
Add the carrot, celery and onion in large pieces, along with the tomato purée.
Pour in all the olive oil at once — it is what gives the broth its body — and continue for 40 minutes.
Salt only at the end, add the oregano and parsley, and serve with olives and a wedge of lemon.

loukoumades.d: Small round fritters drenched in honey and cinnamon. They were given to victors of the ancient Games as 'honey cakes' — which would make them the oldest sweet in Europe still sold in the street.
s: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm water and let it froth for 10 minutes.
Whisk in the flour and salt: the batter should be very slack, almost pourable, halfway between dough and cream.
Cover and prove for 1½ hours somewhere warm, until doubled and pitted with bubbles.
Scoop the batter with a wet spoon and drop it into oil at 175°C; the fritters turn themselves once golden.
Drain, pile them up while still hot, pour over warm honey and scatter cinnamon, crushed walnuts and sesame.

kleftiko.d: 'In the manner of thieves': the klephts cooked stolen lamb in a sealed pit oven so that neither smoke nor smell would betray them. Today's parcel keeps the principle, minus the clandestinity.
s: Stud the lamb shoulder with slivers of garlic and marinate for 3 hours in lemon, oil and oregano.
Line a large dish with two crossed sheets of baking paper, long and overhanging.
Lay the lamb on a bed of quartered potatoes, add tomatoes, bay and white wine.
Crumble the feta over, fold the paper into a sealed parcel and tie it.
Bake for 3½ hours at 160°C without ever opening it. Open the parcel at the table: the trapped steam is what makes the dish.

burek-mesni.d: A long snake of hand-stretched pastry rolled around a filling of beef and onion, then coiled into a round tin. Eaten in the morning with drinking yogurt, standing outside the bakery.
s: Knead flour, warm water, a little oil and the salt for 15 minutes until very elastic; oil the dough and rest it for an hour.
Mix the raw beef with grated onion, paprika, salt and pepper: the filling is not pre-cooked.
Stretch the dough by hand on a floured cloth until translucent, drizzle with oil and let it dry for 5 minutes.
Lay the filling in a rope along one edge, roll loosely and coil that rope into an oiled round tin.
Brush with beaten egg and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C; splash with sparkling water halfway so the pastry stays soft inside.

punjene-paprike.d: Sweet white peppers filled with meat and rice, stewed standing upright in a roux-thickened tomato sauce. The dish of Vojvodina, the paprika plain where peppers come in by the cartload in September.
s: Hollow the peppers through the stalk without piercing them, and keep the tops.
Soften the onion, let it cool and mix with the meat, raw rice, egg, paprika and parsley.
Fill the peppers three quarters full and close them with their tops.
Stand them upright, packed tightly in a pot, cover with tomato purée let down with water and add the bay.
Simmer covered for 1 hour, then thicken the sauce with a roux of lard, flour and paprika stirred in at the last moment.

peka-dalmate.d: Meat and vegetables cooked under a cast-iron bell buried in embers. You must order it a day ahead in Dalmatian konobas: two hours of slow cooking, and the bell is lifted only once.
s: Joint the chicken into eight and marinate for 2 hours in oil, crushed garlic and rosemary.
Cut all the vegetables into large pieces: small ones would collapse over two hours.
Arrange meat and vegetables in a wide cast-iron dish in a single layer, pour over the white wine and oil.
Cover with a bell or a heavy lid and bake for 1 hour at 220°C.
Take off the lid, stir once only and continue for 45 minutes uncovered to brown everything.

crni-rizot.d: An ink-black risotto, coloured by the cuttlefish's own sacs. It stains the lips and teeth of everyone who eats it, which is part of the pleasure on the Istrian quaysides.
s: Clean the cuttlefish, keeping the ink sacs aside, and cut the flesh into strips.
Sear them hard in oil with the garlic, then lower the heat and let them release their water for 15 minutes.
Add the onion and the rice, and toast for 2 minutes before deglazing with white wine.
Moisten ladle by ladle with hot broth, stirring, for 18 minutes; stir in the ink and tomato paste halfway through.
Off the heat, beat in the butter and parsley. The risotto should stay loose: neither dry nor soupy.

zagorski-strukli.d: Squares of stretched dough folded over fresh cheese, poached then baked under cream. Savoury at dinner, sweet for pudding: the same parcel, and people in Zagreb happily eat both versions on the same day.
s: Knead flour, warm water, one egg, the oil and salt for 12 minutes, then rest for an hour under a warm bowl.
Mix the drained fresh cheese with two eggs, half the sour cream and salt.
Stretch the dough by hand on a cloth until translucent, brush with melted butter and spread the cheese.
Roll it up, cut 8 cm squares pressing the edges, and poach them for 5 minutes in simmering water.
Set them in a buttered dish, pour over the remaining sour cream and the cream, and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C.

ajvar.d: The 'red caviar' of the Balkans: roasted peppers, peeled one by one, crushed and cooked for hours in oil. Making it is a collective autumn ritual, outdoors, in large copper cauldrons.
s: Roast the whole peppers in the oven or over embers until the skin blackens and blisters.
Shut them in a sealed bag for 20 minutes: the steam will lift the skin by itself.
Peel and seed them, then let them drain for an hour in a colander — water would ruin the cooking.
Roast the aubergines too, scoop out the flesh, then chop everything coarsely by knife.
Cook for 2 hours over low heat, stirring often and trickling in the oil; add the garlic, vinegar and sugar at the end. It is ready when the spoon leaves a furrow.

pljeskavica.d: A meat patty as wide as a plate, grilled and served in a lepinja bread that soaks up the juices. Nothing to do with the hamburger: it descends from the Ottoman kebab, and is eaten with kajmak and ajvar.
s: Mix the two meats with grated onion, garlic, paprika, bicarbonate and sparkling water.
Work the mixture by hand for 10 minutes until smooth and tacky, then rest it overnight in the fridge.
Shape wide patties 1.5 cm thick and 15 cm across, wetting your hands so they do not stick.
Grill over lively embers for 6 minutes a side, never pressing the meat.
Slide each patty into a warm flatbread, spread with kajmak and top with raw sliced onion.

shopska-salata.d: White, green and red: the colours of the Bulgarian flag on a plate, and no accident — it was invented in the 1950s by the state tourist board. The grated sirene forms a thick snow on top.
s: Grill the peppers until the skin blackens, peel them and cut into strips.
Cut the tomatoes and cucumber into one-centimetre dice, slice the onion finely.
Toss with the chopped parsley, oil, vinegar, salt and pepper.
Let it stand for 10 minutes so the vegetables give up a little juice.
Grate the salted white cheese over the top in a thick even layer, without mixing it in: it must stay on the surface.

tarator.d: A cold soup of yogurt, cucumber, dill and walnuts, served with ice cubes in the glass. In Bulgaria it is drunk more than eaten, in summer, when the Black Sea heat puts you off everything else.
s: Grate the cucumber coarsely, salt it and let it weep for 10 minutes; do not squeeze it.
Pound the garlic with a little salt and half the walnuts into a paste.
Whisk the yogurt with this paste, then let it down with iced water to the consistency of a light soup.
Fold in the cucumber and chopped dill, adjust the salt and chill for an hour.
Serve very cold with ice cubes, a thread of olive oil and the rest of the walnuts, crushed.

kavarma.d: A stew of pork and peppers, simmered then served in an individual clay pot, often with an egg cracked on top. The earthenware keeps it scalding from oven to table.
s: Sear the pork in large cubes in the lard until well coloured, then set aside.
Soften the onion and sliced peppers in the same fat, without rushing them.
Add the mushrooms, let them release their water, then return the meat.
Pour in the wine, crushed tomatoes, paprika and savory; cover and simmer for 1 hour.
Divide between clay pots, crack an egg onto each and bake for 12 minutes at 200°C, until the white sets.

fergese.d: Peppers, tomatoes and fresh cheese melted together in an earthenware dish into an orange-red cream. You dip bread straight into it, and that is the whole meal on a Berat evening.
s: Grill the peppers until the skin blisters, peel them and cut into strips.
Melt the butter, add the flour and cook for 2 minutes, then pour in the milk for a short béchamel.
Add the crushed tomatoes and garlic and reduce for 10 minutes over a lively flame.
Fold in the peppers and both cheeses crushed with a fork, without smoothing: the dish should stay lumpy.
Pour into an earthenware dish and bake for 15 minutes at 200°C, until the surface browns in patches. Serve with country bread.

pastrmajlija.d: A long boat of dough topped with diced salt pork and an egg cracked over it at the end. Its name comes from pastrma, the dried meat kept for winter; Štip devotes a festival to it each autumn.
s: Salt the diced pork generously and refrigerate for 12 hours: this salting stands in for the pastrma.
Knead flour, warm water, yeast, oil and salt, and prove for 1½ hours.
Roll the dough into long ovals, raising the edges to hold the juices.
Scatter over the rinsed and dried meat, dust with paprika and bake for 15 minutes at 250°C.
Crack an egg into the centre of each pastrmajlija and return for 4 minutes. Serve with a grilled chilli.

halaszle.d: The fishermen's soup of the Tisza, red with paprika and cooked in a cauldron over a wood fire. In Szeged the broth of small fish is strained before the good carp pieces are poached in it: two cookings for one dish.
s: Fillet the carp and set the fillets aside; keep the head, bones and trimmings for the broth.
Cook these trimmings for 45 minutes with half the sliced onions, never stirring with a spoon: you shake the pot instead.
Pass the broth through a fine sieve, pressing hard, then return it to the heat.
Add the sweet and hot paprika off the heat — it would scorch and turn bitter — then the pepper and tomato.
Salt the fish, slide the pieces into the simmering broth and poach for 12 minutes without touching them.

langos.d: A round of risen dough thrown into hot fat, rubbed with garlic and heaped with sour cream and grated cheese. Once baked against the wall of the bread oven; the fryer made it the staple of every Budapest swimming pool.
s: Mash the cooked potato and work it into the flour: it is what keeps the dough soft for hours.
Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm milk, pour onto the flour with the salt and knead for 10 minutes.
Prove for 1½ hours, until the dough has doubled.
Stretch each piece by hand into an uneven 20 cm disc, thinner at the centre than at the edge.
Fried 90 seconds a side at 180°C, they balloon. Rub with crushed garlic and cover with sour cream and grated cheese.

paprikas-csirke.d: A great deal of onion, a great deal of Kalocsa paprika, a little sour cream: the simplest Hungarian dish and the hardest to spoil. The absolute rule is never to boil the cream once it is in.
s: Soften the finely sliced onions in the lard for 20 minutes, until they collapse into a golden purée.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the paprika at once: above 120°C it turns bitter.
Return to the heat, add the chicken, pepper and tomato, pour in broth to come halfway up and cover.
Simmer for 45 minutes; the sauce should coat without any flour in it yet.
Slacken the sour cream with the flour and a ladle of warm sauce, stir into the pan off the heat and never let it boil again.

dobos-torta.d: Five discs of sponge, a chocolate buttercream, and a lid of hard caramel cut into wedges while still hot. József Dobos presented it in 1885 and refused to give up the recipe for twenty years.
s: Whip the whites, fold in the yolks beaten with 120 g of sugar, then the sifted flour.
Spread the batter into five thin 22 cm discs on baking paper and bake each for 7 minutes at 200°C.
Make the cream: cook a custard with the yolks, milk and 100 g of sugar, cool it, then beat it with the softened butter and melted chocolate.
Build the cake, alternating discs and cream, keeping the most even disc back for the caramel.
Make a pale caramel with the remaining sugar, coat the reserved disc and cut it into ten wedges with an oiled blade before it sets. Fan them over the cake.

lecso.d: Peppers, tomatoes, onion and lard cooked down until everything collapses. Made by the basin in August, when peppers cost nothing, and frozen for winter. With or without egg, with or without sausage: everyone has a version.
s: Slice the onions and soften them in the lard for 15 minutes without colouring.
Add the smoked sausage in rounds and let it render its fragrant fat.
Off the heat stir in the paprika, then return to the heat with the peppers cut into wide strips.
Cover and sweat for 15 minutes, then add the peeled tomatoes and continue uncovered for 15 minutes.
Crack the eggs straight into the lecsó and barely scramble them: they should stay in visible ribbons.

bigos.d: The 'hunter's stew': sauerkraut, fresh cabbage, several meats and dried plums, stewed then reheated three days running. Mickiewicz gives it twenty lines in Pan Tadeusz — which says something.
s: Rinse the sauerkraut if it is very sour, squeeze it dry and chop it; shred the fresh cabbage.
Fry the bacon and onion in the lard, then brown the pork in large cubes and the sausage in rounds.
Bring everything together in a large pot with the soaked mushrooms, prunes, wine, tomato paste and spices.
Simmer for 3 hours over very low heat, stirring now and then so nothing catches.
Let it cool, then reheat it the next day and the day after: bigos only becomes itself on the third day.

zurek.d: A sour soup made from rye starter fermented for five days, served at Easter with white sausage and a hard-boiled egg. The sourness comes from a household lactic ferment once kept in a stoneware crock.
s: Five days ahead, mix the rye flour, warm water and two garlic cloves in a jar; cover with a cloth and ferment at room temperature.
On the day, make a broth with the bacon, onion, bay and allspice for 40 minutes.
Poach the white sausages in it for 20 minutes, lift them out and cut into rounds.
Shake the starter, pour it into the broth in a thin stream and cook for 10 minutes without boiling: it clears and thickens the soup.
Add cream, marjoram, horseradish and crushed garlic. Serve with the sausage, half a hard-boiled egg and potatoes.

barszcz-czerwony.d: A beetroot broth as clear as wine, served scalding in a cup on Christmas Eve with tiny mushroom dumplings. Nothing like Ukrainian borscht: this one is strained, limpid, almost a drink.
s: Soak the dried mushrooms for an hour and carefully keep their liquid.
Roast half the beetroot whole for 50 minutes: this is what gives the broth its depth.
Boil the other half, grated, with the vegetables, spices and mushroom liquid for 45 minutes over low heat.
Strain very carefully through a cloth, without pressing, to keep it clear.
Balance it sweet-sour with the vinegar and sugar, add the garlic and marjoram, and serve scalding in cups.

kotlet-schabowy.d: The Sunday breaded pork chop of Poland, served with dill potatoes and a cabbage salad. It is supposed to hang over the edge of the plate: that is a criterion, not an exaggeration.
s: Cut the loin into 2 cm slices and beat them out to 8 mm, working from the centre outwards.
Season, then coat in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, without pressing.
Heat the lard half a centimetre deep and fry the cutlets 4 minutes a side over medium heat.
Shake the pan as they cook: the fat should run under the crumb and puff it up.
Serve at once with dill potatoes and a cabbage salad dressed with cream and lemon.

oscypek-grille.d: A smoked ewe's-milk cheese pressed in carved wooden spindle moulds, grilled until it blisters and served with cranberry jam. Its making is protected and reserved to Tatra shepherds.
s: Slice the smoked cheese lengthways into pieces a centimetre thick.
Oil the grill very lightly — the cheese sticks easily — and prepare medium embers, never fierce ones.
Grill 3 minutes a side: the surface should stripe and swell without the centre running.
Take it off the moment the edges start to sag: a few seconds more and the cheese pours into the fire.
Serve scalding with a spoonful of cranberry jam and toasted country bread.

paczki.d: The doughnuts of Fat Thursday, filled with rose jam or plum. Tradition says you must eat at least one that day or face a year of bad luck: Poles get through a hundred million of them.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, warm milk and a little flour; let it froth for 20 minutes.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar to the ribbon, then knead with the flour, starter, rum and salt for 15 minutes.
Work in the soft butter last and prove for 1½ hours: the dough should be very slack.
Shape 60 g balls, fill each with a spoonful of jam and seal carefully; prove for 40 minutes.
Fry 2 minutes a side at 175°C, covered for the first side: that is what makes the pale ring around the middle.

vepro-knedlo-zelo.d: The Czech national dish comes in three words: roast pork, bread dumplings sliced with a thread, sweet-sour caraway cabbage. Eaten with a Plzeň beer, which is not optional.
s: Rub the pork with salt, crushed garlic and caraway, set it on a bed of onions and pour over the beer.
Roast for 2 hours at 160°C, basting regularly, then 15 minutes at 220°C for the crackling.
For the knedlíky, knead flour, warm milk, yeast, eggs and salt, work in the diced bread rolls, and prove for an hour.
Shape two large logs and poach them for 20 minutes in simmering water, turning halfway. Slice them with a thread, never a knife.
Fry the sauerkraut with onion, caraway and sugar for 30 minutes, and serve everything under the roasting juices.

kulajda.d: A white soup of potato and mushroom, sharpened with sour cream and vinegar, with a poached egg set in it. The dill is heavy-handed — that is what tells kulajda apart from any other Bohemian soup.
s: Cook the diced potatoes in a litre of salted water with the caraway and bay.
Fry the sliced mushrooms in butter and add them to the pan halfway through.
Slacken the sour cream with the flour, stir it into the soup in a thin stream and thicken for 5 minutes without boiling.
Poach the eggs separately in vinegared water for 3 minutes, yolks running.
Sharpen the soup with vinegar, sugar and a great deal of chopped dill, then set a poached egg in each bowl.

trdelnik.d: A ribbon of dough wound around a wooden roller, turned over embers and rolled in sugar and nuts. It came from Transylvania in the 18th century and conquered the streets of Prague — to the irritation of Praguers.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, warm milk and a spoonful of sugar; let it froth for 15 minutes.
Knead with the flour, eggs, 60 g of sugar, the soft butter and salt for 12 minutes, then prove for an hour.
Cut 2 cm strips and wind them in a spiral around buttered wooden rollers, edges just touching.
Brush with melted butter, roll in sugar and turn over the embers for 12 minutes, never stopping.
While still hot, roll in the sugar, crushed walnut and cinnamon mixture, then slide the cylinder off the roller.

bramborak.d: A cake of grated potato with garlic and marjoram, fried in lard until brittle. Sold at village fairs with nothing but a scrap of paper to hold it.
s: Grate the potatoes finely and let them drain in a colander for five minutes, without pressing.
Mix with the eggs, flour, milk, crushed garlic, marjoram and caraway.
Salt only at the last moment; the batter should stay thick and barely pourable.
Heat the lard and drop in flattened spoonfuls 12 cm across; let them set for 4 minutes untouched.
Turn, brown for 3 minutes on the other side and drain on a rack. Eaten scalding, with your fingers.

kapustnica.d: The sauerkraut soup of the Slovak Christmas Eve, with smoked sausage, dried mushrooms and prunes. Every family has its own; some add cream, others call that sacrilege.
s: Soak the mushrooms for an hour and keep the soaking liquid.
Bring the smoked ribs to a simmer in two litres of water with the bay and allspice for 45 minutes.
Add the rinsed and squeezed sauerkraut, the mushrooms with their liquid, the prunes and the sliced sausage; continue for 30 minutes.
Make a pale roux of lard, flour and paprika off the heat, and stir it into the soup to thicken it.
Pull the meat from the bones, return it, adjust the seasoning and serve with a spoonful of sour cream — or not, depending on your camp.

mamaliga-branza.d: Romanian polenta, poured onto a board and cut with a thread, served with salted sheep's cheese, cream and an egg. It fed the countryside for two centuries, when wheat bread was a luxury.
s: Bring the salted water to the boil and rain in the cornmeal, whisking constantly.
Lower the heat and stir with a wooden spoon for 30 minutes, until the mass pulls away from the sides.
Turn the mămăligă out onto a damp wooden board and let it firm for two minutes before cutting it with a thread.
Fry the diced bacon and cook the eggs in the rendered fat.
Serve the mămăligă with the crumbled cheese, sour cream, egg and crisp bacon.

ciorba-de-burta.d: A white, sharp tripe soup thickened with egg yolk and cream, lifted with garlic and vinegar at the table. Romanians hold it to be the sovereign cure for a difficult morning after.
s: Clean the tripe thoroughly with coarse salt and vinegar, rinse it well, then blanch it for 10 minutes.
Cook it for 2½ hours with the veal foot, whole vegetables, bay and peppercorns, until tender to a fork.
Lift out the tripe, cut it into fine strips and strain the broth.
Pound the garlic with a little salt and a little broth, and stir this liquor into the soup.
Beat the yolks with the cream, loosen with a ladle of hot broth and stir in off the heat. Serve with vinegar and chilli on the side.

mici.d: Small skinless meat rolls, made springy by bicarbonate and sparkling water, grilled wherever there are embers in Romania. Eaten with mustard and bread, never with cutlery.
s: Pound the garlic with a little salt and a little broth to draw out a fragrant liquid.
Mix the meats, spices, bicarbonate, garlic liquid and broth, then work the mass for 10 minutes.
Add the sparkling water little by little: it is what gives the characteristic springiness.
Rest overnight in the fridge, then pipe or shape 8 cm logs with wet hands.
Grill 6 to 8 minutes over lively embers, turning often. Serve with mustard and bread.

papanasi.d: A fresh cheese doughnut shaped like a ring, capped with its own little ball, drowned in sour cream and blueberry jam. The Romanian restaurant dessert par excellence, served scalding.
s: Drain the fresh cheese for an hour in a cloth: too wet and the dough would drink the oil.
Mix it with the eggs, sugar, semolina, zest and vanilla, then add the flour and baking powder without overworking.
Rest for 30 minutes, then shape four 10 cm rings and four small balls.
Fry 3 minutes a side at 165°C — no hotter, or the outside browns before the centre cooks.
Stack the ring, sour cream, jam and then the ball, and serve at once.

kibinai.d: Mutton turnovers brought in the 14th century by the Crimean Karaites, settled at Trakai by Grand Duke Vytautas. Six centuries on, the community numbers only a few dozen; the kibinai, meanwhile, are all over Lithuania.
s: Rub the cold butter into the flour, add the sour cream, one egg and the salt, and bring together without kneading. Chill for an hour.
Chop the mutton by knife into small dice — never in a processor, the texture would be lost.
Mix with finely chopped onion, the fat, salt and plenty of pepper.
Roll the pastry, cut 14 cm discs, fill them and seal the edge in a plaited crimp.
Pierce a small hole on top, pour in a spoonful of broth, glaze with egg and bake for 35 minutes at 190°C.

sklandrausis.d: A rye tartlet layered with potato then carrot, sweetened with honey and scented with caraway. It comes from the Livonians, a Finno-Ugric people of the Latvian coast whose language has almost no speakers left.
s: Knead the rye flour, melted butter, warm water and salt: the dough is short and does not rise.
Roll it thin and line 10 cm rings, raising the edges by hand like a basket.
Mash the boiled potatoes with a little cream, salt and caraway.
Do the same with the boiled carrots, adding the honey and one egg.
Spread the potato first, then the carrot, glaze with egg and bake for 30 minutes at 200°C. Eaten cold.

kama-dessert.d: A flour of four roasted grains — rye, barley, oat and pea — beaten into buttermilk and sweetened. Once travelling food that kept for months, it is now the childhood taste of every Estonian.
s: Whisk the buttermilk with the sour cream until perfectly smooth.
Rain in the kama flour, whisking without pause: tipped in at once it forms lumps you will never recover from.
Sweeten with the sugar and honey, and add a pinch of salt that wakes up the roasted grain.
Rest for 30 minutes in the fridge: the kama swells and the mixture thickens by itself.
Serve very cold in glasses, with sliced strawberries at the bottom and a thread of honey.

verivorst.d: The Estonian Christmas blood sausage, made with pearl barley rather than onion alone, served with lingonberry jam and braised cabbage. It is waited for all year: it appears in shops only from December.
s: Cook the pearl barley in salted water for 25 minutes, then drain and let it cool a little.
Render the diced fat and turn the finely chopped onions golden in it.
Mix the barley, onions, strained blood, marjoram, allspice, salt and plenty of pepper.
Fill the casings loosely — the barley swells further — and poach for 25 minutes in water at 80°C, pricking any bubbles.
Brown them in the oven for 20 minutes at 200°C and serve with lingonberry jam and butter-braised sauerkraut.

varenyky.d: Dumplings of soft dough filled with sour cherries, served with cream and sugar. Savoury with potato the rest of the year, sweet in July when the cherry trees of Poltava are heavy with fruit.
s: Knead the flour, warm water, egg and salt for 10 minutes into a supple dough; rest for 40 minutes under a cloth.
Stone the cherries and let them macerate for an hour with half the sugar; keep the juice.
Drain them and roll them in the starch: without it the juice would pierce the dough as it cooks.
Roll the dough to 2 mm, cut 7 cm discs, fill with three cherries each and seal carefully.
Poach for 4 minutes in simmering water, drain, toss in butter and serve with the sour cream, sugar and reduced juice.

salo-lviv.d: Back fat cured for a week in coarse salt and garlic, sliced thinly onto rye bread. Far more than a food in Ukraine: a national symbol, to which Lviv devotes an entire museum.
s: Choose thick back fat with a fine rind and pearly white flesh, with no streak of lean.
Stud it with slivers of garlic all over, at regular intervals.
Rub it hard with a mixture of coarse salt, cracked pepper, crumbled bay and coriander.
Wrap it in a cloth and leave it a week in the fridge, turning it daily.
Rinse, pat dry, roll in paprika and keep it in the freezer: it only slices paper-thin when very cold. Serve on rye bread with raw onion.

banosh.d: The polenta of Hutsul shepherds, cooked not in water but in sour cream, until the butter rises to the surface. Served with brynza and pork scratchings; tradition holds that a man should stir it.
s: Bring the salted sour cream to a bare simmer in a cauldron, never letting it boil properly.
Rain in the cornmeal very finely, stirring in one direction and always the same one.
Stir without pause for 25 minutes: the mass thickens then, suddenly, beads of butter rise to the surface. That is the sign.
Take it off the heat at once: a few minutes more and the banosh grains irretrievably.
Serve in the pot with the crumbled brynza, the scratchings and the fried mushrooms.

kotleta-po-kyivsky.d: A chicken breast rolled around herb butter, breaded and fried: when cut, the melted butter should spurt out. The whole difficulty lies there — sealing it well enough that it does not escape before the plate.
s: Beat the soft butter with the chopped herbs, crushed garlic, lemon zest and salt; shape four logs and freeze them hard.
Butterfly the breasts and flatten them between two sheets to 5 mm, without piercing.
Set a frozen butter log at the centre, fold in the sides then roll tightly; wrap and firm up for 30 minutes in the fridge.
Bread them twice — flour, egg, crumb, then egg and crumb again: the double coat is what holds the butter.
Fry for 8 minutes at 165°C, then 8 minutes in the oven at 180°C. Serve immediately, knife at the ready.

machanka.d: A creamy pork stew into which large buckwheat pancakes are dipped — machatsi means 'to dip'. The Belarusian Sunday breakfast, which sees you through to the evening.
s: Brown the pork in large dice and the sausage in the lard, add the onion and let it soften.
Moisten with a glass of water, add the bay and simmer covered for 35 minutes.
Slake two spoonfuls of flour in the sour cream, stir it into the pot and thicken for 5 minutes without boiling.
For the pancakes, mix both flours, the warm milk, eggs, yeast and salt; prove for 40 minutes.
Cook large thick pancakes in a pan and serve them beside the stew, for dipping. Scatter with dill.

zeama.d: A hen broth with home-made noodles, soured with borș — a fermented wheat bran liquor, not Russian beetroot. Lovage is compulsory: without it, Moldovans say, it is not a zeamă.
s: Bring the hen to a bare simmer in three litres of cold water and skim patiently for twenty minutes.
Add the whole carrot, onion and pepper, and cook for an hour without boiling.
Meanwhile knead the flour and eggs into a hard dough, roll it very thin and cut fine noodles; let them dry on a cloth.
Lift out the bird, bone it, strain the broth and return it to a simmer with the crushed tomatoes.
Drop in the noodles for 5 minutes, return the meat, sharpen with vinegar and cover with chopped lovage off the heat.

gravlax.d: Raw salmon pressed for three days between salt, sugar and dill. The name means 'buried salmon': medieval fishermen sank it in the sand above the tide line and let it ferment.
s: Choose a skin-on fillet, pin-boned, and run your hand against the grain to check nothing is left.
Mix the salt, sugar and cracked pepper; rub it into the flesh and sprinkle over the akvavit.
Cover with a thick layer of roughly chopped dill and lay the fillet skin down in a dish.
Wrap, weight it with two kilos and leave three days in the fridge, turning morning and evening and pouring off the brine.
Rinse barely, pat dry and slice on the bias, very thinly. Serve with a mustard, honey and vinegar sauce and rye bread.

janssons-frestelse.d: A gratin of matchstick potatoes, onion and pickled sprats, drowned in cream. The name is said to come from a Swedish preacher who abandoned his asceticism at the sight of it — the story is probably false and much retold.
s: Cut the potatoes into fine matchsticks, but never rinse them: their starch is what binds the gratin.
Soften the sliced onions in the butter for 15 minutes without colouring them.
Layer potatoes, onions and sprat fillets in the dish, finishing with potatoes.
Pour over half the cream and the milk, keeping the rest for halfway through.
Scatter breadcrumbs, bake for 50 minutes at 200°C, add the remaining cream partway and let it brown.

toast-skagen.d: North Sea prawns bound with mayonnaise and dill, piled on buttered toast and crowned with fish roe. Created in 1956 by the restaurateur Tore Wretman, aboard his boat.
s: Peel the prawns and keep them cold; pat them thoroughly dry.
Mix the mayonnaise, sour cream, mustard, lemon zest and juice, chopped dill and finely diced red onion.
Fold in the prawns gently with a spatula, without crushing them. Adjust the salt.
Fry the bread slices golden in foaming butter on both sides and blot them.
Mound the mixture on each toast, top with a spoonful of salmon roe and a frond of dill.

kanelbullar.d: The cinnamon buns of fika, the Swedish break that is not a coffee break but an institution. The cardamom in the dough is what sets them apart from every other rolled bun in the world.
s: Warm the milk to 37°C, dissolve the yeast in it, add 100 g of sugar, freshly ground cardamom and the salt.
Work in the flour then 100 g of soft butter, knead for 12 minutes and prove for 45 minutes.
Roll the dough into a 5 mm rectangle and spread with the remaining softened butter mixed with sugar and cinnamon.
Fold in three, cut 2 cm strips, twist them and knot them on themselves; prove for 45 minutes.
Glaze with egg, scatter pearl sugar and bake for 12 minutes at 225°C. Take them out the moment they turn golden: five minutes more and they dry out.

raggmunk.d: A pancake of grated potato in a milk batter, served with crisp bacon and lingonberry jam. Sweet, salt and sour in the same mouthful: the complete Swedish logic.
s: Whisk the flour, milk and eggs to a smooth batter and rest it for 20 minutes.
Grate the potatoes coarsely at the very last moment, without rinsing, and fold them into the batter.
Season and work quickly: the batter darkens if it waits.
Cook wide pancakes in the butter, 4 minutes a side, until the edges turn lacy and brittle.
Grill the bacon separately and serve it on the pancakes, with lingonberry jam alongside.

surstromming.d: Herring fermented for six months in a weak brine, whose tin bulges and whose smell defies description. Opened outdoors, under water, and eaten in late summer on flatbread with potato and onion.
s: Open the tin outdoors and submerged in a bucket of water, without exception: pressure has built up during fermentation.
Rinse the fillets in cold water, remove skin and bones, then pat them dry.
Boil small yellow-fleshed potatoes and crush them roughly with a fork.
Slice the red onion very finely and stir the chives and dill into the sour cream.
Butter the flatbread, top with potato, onion, a piece of herring and a spoonful of cream. Roll and eat at once.

rakfisk.d: Trout fermented for two or three months in cold brine, eaten raw in thin slices. Valdres farms prepared it in autumn to last until spring; Fagernes devotes a November festival to it.
s: Lift the fish from its brine, rinse it briefly and let it drain for an hour on a rack.
Fillet it and remove the skin in one movement, starting from the tail.
Slice on the bias into 3 mm strips, with a long thin blade.
Boil the potatoes in salted water and let them cool a little.
Serve on buttered flatbread with crushed potato, raw onion, sour cream, dill and a turn of pepper.

kjottkaker.d: Large beef patties with nutmeg and ginger, served in their brown gravy with peas, potatoes and lingonberry jam. Not the Swedish köttbullar: these are bigger, plainer, more rustic.
s: Work the minced beef with the salt and starch until it turns tacky — it is the salt that binds, not egg.
Beat in the very cold milk in three additions, then the grated onion, nutmeg and ginger.
Shape large oval patties the size of your palm and brown them in butter for 4 minutes a side.
Lift them out, make a brown roux with the remaining butter and the flour, whisk in the broth and thicken for 5 minutes.
Return the patties to the gravy and simmer covered for 25 minutes. Serve with peas, potatoes and lingonberry jam.

brunost-vafler.d: Heart-shaped waffles, soft rather than crisp, served with brunost — the brown caramel-tasting cheese made by boiling down whey until its lactose browns.
s: Whisk the eggs and sugar, then stir in the sour cream and warm milk.
Add the flour, baking powder, cardamom and salt without overworking, then the melted butter.
Rest for an hour: the batter relaxes and the waffles come out softer for it.
Cook in a hot heart-shaped waffle iron for about 3 minutes, to a pale gold rather than brown.
Stack them under a cloth — they should stay soft — and serve with thin slices of brunost shaved off with a cheese plane, and jam.

skrei-poche.d: The migratory Barents cod that comes to spawn in the Lofoten from January to April. Its flesh, firmed by two thousand kilometres of swimming in icy water, flakes into large pearly leaves. Barely poached, in heavily salted water.
s: Bring three litres of water to a bare simmer with the coarse salt: it should be frankly briny, almost unpleasant to taste.
Cut the cod into thick skin-on steaks, leaving the bones in.
Slide them into the barely trembling water and turn off the heat: they cook in 8 minutes of residual warmth.
Melt the butter until it just turns nutty and stir in the crisp bacon and chopped hard-boiled egg.
Serve the fish with steamed potatoes and carrots, the hot butter poured over, and a spoonful of lingonberry.

flaeskesteg.d: The Danish Christmas pork roast, whose rind must become a chequerboard of crackling hard enough to snap. A roast with soft rind is considered a failure, and there is no arguing about it.
s: Score the rind every 5 mm, through to the fat but not into the meat — ask the butcher if need be.
Rub coarse salt into every cut and push in pieces of bay leaf and cloves.
Set the roast on a rack over a dish of water, the rind perfectly horizontal: that is the condition for even crackling.
Roast for 1½ hours at 160°C, then raise to 220°C for 25 minutes, watching constantly.
Meanwhile braise the red cabbage for an hour with the vinegar and sugar. Serve with potatoes and a gravy thickened with the juices.

frikadeller.d: The flat patties every Dane ate weekly as a child, shaped with a spoon rather than by hand. Served hot with potatoes, or cold on rye bread the next day.
s: Combine the meats, grated onion, egg, flour, salt and pepper, and beat the mixture with a wooden spoon for 5 minutes.
