Add the milk little by little until the mixture is soft but still holds on a spoon.
Rest for 30 minutes in the fridge: that rest is what gives frikadeller their texture.
Scoop with a tablespoon dipped in water and drop into hot butter, flattening slightly.
Cook 6 minutes each side over medium heat. Serve with potatoes, red cabbage and gherkins.

stegt-flaesk.d: Slices of pork belly grilled until brittle, served with potatoes and a parsley sauce. Voted Denmark's national dish in 2014 by popular ballot, ahead of all the others.
s: Have the belly sliced 5 mm thick, rind on: any thicker and it will never crisp.
Lay the slices flat on a tray, salt them and roast for 25 minutes at 220°C without turning.
Boil the potatoes in salted water, in their skins.
Make a white roux with the butter and flour, whisk in the hot milk and cook for 8 minutes.
Off the heat, add a great deal of finely chopped parsley and the nutmeg. The sauce should turn properly green.

rodgrod-med-flode.d: The red fruit compote with cream whose name serves as a pronunciation test for foreigners — three silent d's, two ø's, and the certainty of getting it wrong. The Danish summer pudding, served warm or chilled.
s: Cook the redcurrants with the water and sugar for 10 minutes, then pass through a sieve to remove skins and seeds.
Return the juice to the heat, add the raspberries and strawberries and simmer for barely 3 minutes.
Slake the potato starch in a little cold water and pour it in off the heat.
Return to low heat for one minute only: potato starch loses its thickening power if boiled.
Pour into a dish, dust with a little sugar to stop a skin forming, cool and serve with cold cream and flaked almonds.

wienerbrod.d: The 'Vienna bread' that the rest of the world calls a danish. It arrived in 1850 with Austrian bakers hired during a strike; the Danes added butter, egg and remonce, and never gave it back.
s: Briefly knead the flour, warm milk, yeast, one egg, sugar, cardamom and salt; chill for an hour.
Flatten 250 g of cold butter into a square between two sheets, enclose it in the dough and give three single turns, resting 30 minutes between each.
Make the remonce by beating the marzipan with the remaining butter and a little sugar.
Roll out to 4 mm, cut 10 cm squares, fill with remonce, pastry cream or jam, and fold two corners to the centre.
Prove for 45 minutes, glaze with egg and bake for 18 minutes at 200°C. Ice them and scatter with chopped almonds.

kalakukko.d: A rye loaf sealed around whole small fish and pork fat, baked for five hours in a slow oven until the bones dissolve. The crust serves as the vessel: you cut into it like a lid.
s: Knead the flours, warm water, melted butter and salt into a dense, unelastic dough; rest for 30 minutes.
Gut and scale the small fish but keep them whole, bones included: they will dissolve during baking.
Roll the dough into a thick oval, lay a layer of salted fish, a layer of pork fat, then fish again.
Close the dough, sealing the edges carefully: the smallest leak would dry out the inside.
Bake for 1 hour at 200°C to set the crust, brush with butter, wrap in paper and continue for 4 hours at 150°C.

lohikeitto.d: A creamy salmon soup with potato and leek, the dill going in right at the end. The salmon cooks for only eight minutes: that restraint is what keeps the pieces whole and melting.
s: Sweat the sliced leek and carrot in the butter, without colouring them.
Add the diced potatoes, the broth, bay and allspice; cook for 15 minutes.
Pour in the cream and bring to a bare simmer, without boiling.
Cut the salmon into large 3 cm cubes, salt them and slide them into the soup. Turn off the heat.
Let it poach for 8 minutes off the heat, then add a large handful of chopped dill and serve at once.

korvapuusti.d: Literally 'a slap on the ear': the Finnish cinnamon bun is cut on the slant then pressed down the middle with a finger, which gives it that flattened ear shape and its dense sweet heart.
s: Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk, add 100 g of sugar, one egg, ground cardamom and the salt.
Work in the flour, knead for 10 minutes, then add 80 g of soft butter and knead 5 minutes more. Prove for 1 hour.
Roll into a large rectangle and spread with the remaining butter mixed with sugar and cinnamon.
Roll into a tight log and cut slices on the slant: wide on one side, narrow on the other.
Set them wide side down and press the centre with two fingers. Prove for 40 minutes, glaze, scatter pearl sugar and bake for 12 minutes at 225°C.

poronkaristys.d: Reindeer shaved into curls with a plane while still frozen, seared in butter then stewed in beer. Served with mashed potato and lingonberry jam, it is the dish of the whole Finnish North.
s: Plane the meat into very fine shavings while still frozen: thawed, it would be impossible to cut this way.
Sear it in small batches in very hot butter, without crowding the pan.
Add the sliced onion, let it soften, then pour in the beer and broth.
Add juniper berries and bay, cover and simmer for 25 minutes over low heat.
Serve on milky mashed potato, with lingonberry jam and gherkins.

kjotsupa.d: The Icelandic lamb soup, with swede, carrot, cabbage and a little oatmeal to thicken it. The lamb tastes distinctive: Icelandic sheep roam entirely free in summer, over moors of wild thyme and angelica.
s: Cut the lamb on the bone into large pieces and bring it to a simmer in cold water.
Skim patiently for twenty minutes: this is what gives a clear broth.
Add the bay, peppercorns and thyme, and cook covered for an hour.
Add the swede and carrot in large dice, then twenty minutes later the potato, cabbage and leek.
Rain in the oats and give it another 15 minutes: they bind the broth without really thickening it. Salt at the end.

hangikjot.d: The smoked Christmas lamb, hung for weeks over a fire of dried sheep dung and birch — Iceland having few trees to spare. Served cold in thin slices, or hot with a pea béchamel.
s: Rub the leg with salt, sugar, crushed juniper and bay, and dry-cure it for a week in the cold, turning daily.
Rinse, pat dry, then cold-smoke it for three days over birch — or buy it ready-smoked, which is what Icelanders do themselves.
Poach it for 2 hours in water at 80°C, never boiling, and let it cool completely in its liquor.
Make a béchamel with the butter, flour and milk, and fold in the cooked peas.
Slice the hangikjöt very thinly and serve cold on buttered flatbread, or hot with potatoes and béchamel.

skerpikjot.d: Mutton wind-dried for nine months in a hjallur, a slatted shed beaten by the salt Atlantic air. Neither salt nor smoke: only wind, constant damp and time.
s: The leg must have dried for nine months: too soon and the meat stays soft and spoils; too long and it turns crumbly.
Cut away the outer crust, darker and harder, and keep it — it is eaten too, but separately.
Slice the meat against the grain, as thinly as you possibly can, with a well-sharpened knife.
Boil small potatoes in their skins and let them cool a little.
Serve on buttered rye bread with a potato and a glass of akvavit. Never cook this meat.

lutefisk.d: Stockfish rehydrated in a lye of wood ash, which swells and turns translucent as jelly. The method dates from the Middle Ages; it still divides Norwegians between Christmas devotion and frank horror.
s: Soak the stockfish for six days in cold water, changing it daily, then two days in a lightly alkaline solution, and finally two days in fresh water to desalt it.
The fish should have tripled in volume and turned translucent grey and gelatinous.
Lay the pieces skin down in a dish, salt generously and let them drain for 30 minutes.
Cover tightly and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C: it cooks in its own water, without adding a drop.
Serve at once — it collapses quickly — with crisp bacon, pea purée, potatoes, melted butter and flatbread with brunost.

sunday-roast.d: The English Sunday ritual: a beef roast, potatoes crisped in the fat, and those popovers that billow in the oven. Yorkshire pudding was once served first, drenched in gravy, to fill people up before the meat.
s: Take the joint out two hours ahead and rub it with mustard, salt and pepper.
Sear it at 240°C for 20 minutes, then drop to 180°C and allow 15 minutes per 500 g for rare.
Make the Yorkshire batter: flour, eggs, milk and salt, whisked then rested for an hour. It should run like cream.
Get the beef dripping smoking in the tins at 220°C, pour the batter in all at once and do not open the oven for 20 minutes.
Rest the meat for 20 minutes, deglaze the roasting tin with red wine and broth for the gravy, and serve with the roast vegetables and horseradish.

cornish-pasty.d: The tin miners' pasty, whose plaited crimp served as a handle: held there with arsenic-covered fingers, the crest then thrown away. Beef, potato, swede and onion, never pre-cooked.
s: Rub the cold suet and butter into the flour, add the iced water and bring together without kneading. Chill for an hour.
Cut the beef, potato, swede and onion into half-centimetre dice — never grated, never minced.
Season very generously with white pepper: it is the pasty's signature spice.
Cut 20 cm discs, fill one half in layers, add a knob of butter and fold over.
Crimp the edge by pinching and folding it back on itself, glaze with egg, cut a vent and bake 15 minutes at 220°C then 40 minutes at 170°C.

shepherds-pie.d: Minced lamb under a blanket of mashed potato forked into ridges. The name matters: made with beef it would be a cottage pie — shepherds keep sheep, and in England the distinction is no pedantry.
s: Brown the minced lamb in small batches over high heat, so it grills rather than boils.
Add the onion, carrot and celery in small dice and let them soften for 10 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste, Worcestershire sauce, herbs and broth, and reduce uncovered for 30 minutes.
Mash the potatoes with the butter and hot milk into a firm purée: too loose and it would sink into the meat.
Add the peas to the meat, cover with the mash, fork the surface into ridges, dust with cheddar and bake for 35 minutes at 200°C.

full-english-breakfast.d: Eggs, bacon, sausages, beans, tomato, mushrooms, black pudding and toast: nine elements on one plate, cooked separately and brought together scalding. The order of assembly is the subject of sincere debate.
s: Start with the sausages, which need 15 minutes over medium heat, turned regularly.
Add the bacon when they are half done, then the sliced black pudding for 3 minutes a side.
Fry the mushrooms in the rendered fat, and the halved tomatoes cut side down.
Warm the beans with the tomato paste, brown sugar and Worcestershire — that is what brings them close to the tinned flavour.
Fry the eggs last, in the bacon fat, and toast the bread. Plate immediately: cold is the enemy of this dish.

bakewell-tart.d: Shortcrust, a layer of raspberry jam, frangipane and flaked almonds. Born, they say, of a mistake by an inn cook who poured the almond mixture over the jam instead of stirring it into the pastry.
s: Rub 125 g of cold butter into 250 g of flour, add 50 g of sugar, a yolk and a little iced water; chill for an hour.
Line a 24 cm tin, prick the base and blind-bake for 15 minutes at 180°C.
Spread the raspberry jam in an even layer over the cooled base.
Beat 175 g of soft butter with 175 g of sugar, work in three eggs one at a time, then the ground almonds and the extract.
Spread the frangipane, scatter flaked almonds and bake for 30 minutes at 170°C. Ice with sugar and lemon once cool.

sticky-toffee-pudding.d: A date sponge drowned in salted butter toffee sauce, served scalding with cold cream. Invented in a Lake District hotel in the 1970s, in fifty years it has become the best-loved English pudding.
s: Soak the stoned dates in the boiling water with the bicarbonate for 20 minutes, then crush them roughly.
Beat 100 g of butter with 150 g of brown sugar, add the eggs one at a time, then the flour and baking powder.
Fold in the dates and their liquid: the batter will look very loose, which is right.
Bake for 35 minutes at 180°C in a buttered dish.
For the sauce, melt 200 g of butter with 300 g of brown sugar and the cream, boil for 5 minutes and salt it. Pierce the sponge and pour over half the sauce, keeping the rest for serving.

pie-and-mash.d: A beef pie, mash flattened with a palette knife and a green parsley sauce called 'liquor', a survivor of the water in which eels were once poached. East End shops have served this on marble tables since 1890.
s: Brown the beef, coarsely chopped by knife, with the onion, moisten with broth and simmer for 45 minutes until barely any liquid remains.
Rub the suet and butter into the flour, bind with iced water and chill.
Line small oval tins, fill with the cooled meat, cover with a pastry lid and seal.
Bake for 35 minutes at 200°C, until the pastry is pale gold and firm.
For the liquor, thicken 400 ml of cooking water with the cornstarch, add an enormous quantity of chopped parsley and the vinegar. Serve the flattened mash beside it, liquor poured over everything.

haggis-neeps-tatties.d: A sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, oats and onion, served with mashed swede and potato. On 25 January it is piped in and addressed with the ode Burns wrote for it, before being opened with a knife.
s: Simmer the pluck for 2 hours in salted water, letting the windpipe hang out of the pan. Keep the broth.
Chop it coarsely once cool and mix with the dry-toasted oats, chopped onion, fat and spices.
Loosen with the broth to a moist but not runny mass; pepper it heavily.
Fill the stomach two thirds full and sew it up; prick it and poach for 1½ hours in water at 85°C.
Serve with buttery mashed swede, mashed potato, and a thread of whisky poured over the opened haggis.

cullen-skink.d: A thick soup of smoked haddock, potato and onion, born in the fishing village of Cullen. 'Skink' means a shin of beef in old Scots: the name of a broth that became, for want of meat, a fish soup.
s: Poach the smoked haddock in the milk with the bay for barely 8 minutes, then lift it out and strain the milk.
Flake the flesh into large pieces, discarding skin and bones.
Soften the onion and leek in the butter without colouring, then add the diced potatoes.
Pour in the infused milk and cook for 20 minutes; crush half the potatoes to thicken the soup.
Return the fish, add the cream and heat without boiling. Season with white pepper and cover with chives.

cranachan.d: Whipped cream, raspberries, heather honey, whisky and toasted oats, layered in glasses. Served at harvest festivals, each guest mixing for themselves from ingredients brought separately to the table.
s: Toast the oats dry in a pan until fragrant and golden, then let them cool completely.
Crush half the raspberries with a fork and the sugar, and let them give up their juice.
Whip the very cold cream to soft peaks, without tightening it, then fold in the honey and whisky.
Fold three quarters of the toasted oats into the cream in one movement, without working it.
Layer in glasses, alternating cream, crushed and whole raspberries. Scatter the remaining oats at the last moment, so they stay crisp.

scotch-broth.d: A mutton broth with pearl barley and root vegetables, so thick the spoon almost stands up. Samuel Johnson ate three plates of it on his Scottish journey and admitted a liking, which from him was saying a great deal.
s: Soak the split peas overnight; rinse the pearl barley in cold water.
Bring the mutton on the bone to a simmer in cold water and skim patiently for twenty minutes.
Add the barley, split peas, bay and onion, and cook covered for an hour.
Stir in the diced carrot, swede and leek, then the cabbage twenty minutes before the end.
Lift out the meat, bone it, return it in pieces and rest the soup overnight: scotch broth is better reheated. Pepper it and cover with parsley.

cawl.d: The Welsh pot-au-feu: lamb, leek, swede and potato in a clear broth. Eaten in two courses — broth first, meat and vegetables after — with bread and Caerphilly cheese.
s: Cook the lamb on the bone in cold water, skimming carefully for the first twenty minutes.
Add the onion, bay and thyme, and simmer for 1½ hours without fully covering.
Cool overnight and lift off the set fat: that is what gives cawl its clarity.
Reheat, add the swede and carrot for 20 minutes, then parsnip, potatoes and the white of the leeks for 15 minutes.
Add the finely shredded leek greens two minutes before serving, with the parsley. Serve the broth first.

welsh-rarebit.d: Far more than cheese on toast: a thick sauce of cheddar melted with brown ale, mustard and Worcestershire, spread on bread and grilled. The name once mocked the Welsh as too poor to eat rabbit.
s: Make a roux with the butter and flour, then whisk in the brown ale and cook for 3 minutes.
Add the grated cheddar off the heat, a handful at a time, stirring until it strings.
Stir in the mustard, Worcestershire, cayenne and finally the egg yolks, without letting them cook.
Let it cool: the paste should thicken enough to spread with a spoon.
Toast the bread on one side only, spread the paste thickly right to the edges of the untoasted side, and grill fiercely for 3 minutes until it blisters.

soda-bread.d: A bread without yeast, raised by the meeting of bicarbonate and buttermilk. Made in ten minutes and eaten the same day. The deep cross cut on top lets out the steam — and, they say, the fairies.
s: Mix the flours, oats, bicarbonate and salt in a large bowl with your fingertips.
Pour in the buttermilk and honey all at once and mix by hand, in a figure of eight, for thirty seconds only.
Do not knead: the bicarbonate starts working the moment it meets the buttermilk and your time is short.
Shape a flattened round, set it on a floured tray and cut a deep cross, halfway down.
Bake for 45 minutes at 200°C. It is done when it sounds hollow underneath. Cool on a rack under a cloth to keep the crust soft.

colcannon.d: Mashed potato with kale and spring onion, a well of melted butter in the middle. At Halloween a ring was hidden inside: whoever found it was to marry within the year.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins, then peel them while still hot, burning your fingers a little.
Strip the kale, chop it and wilt it for 5 minutes in boiling salted water; drain and squeeze it dry.
Warm the milk and cream with the sliced spring onions, without letting them boil.
Rice the potatoes, work in the infused milk, then the kale, and 100 g of butter.
Mound it up, hollow a well in the centre and fill it with the remaining melted butter. Each forkful is dipped in.

boxty.d: The potato pancake of the Irish north-west, half raw and grated, half boiled and mashed. An old rhyme warns: 'Boxty on the griddle, boxty in the pan, if you can't make boxty, you'll never get a man'.
s: Boil half the potatoes and mash them smooth; grate the other half raw.
Squeeze the grated potato in a cloth over a bowl: keep the liquid and let the starch settle at the bottom.
Pour off the clear water, scrape up the white starch and add it to the mixture: that is what marks out real boxty.
Combine both potatoes, the flour, bicarbonate, salt and buttermilk into a thick batter.
Cook wide pancakes in butter, 4 minutes a side. Serve with grilled bacon and an egg.

bitterballen.d: Round croquettes of set beef ragout, breaded and fried, served with mustard in every brown café. The centre is liquid and scalding: biting into a whole one is a beginner's mistake.
s: Cook the beef for 2 hours in the broth with the bay, until it shreds with a fork. Strain and keep 600 ml of broth.
Make a roux with the butter and flour, cook it for 3 minutes, then add the hot broth in three stages: the sauce must become very thick.
Add the shredded meat, softened onion, parsley and nutmeg, and salt generously.
Spread 2 cm deep in a dish and refrigerate for at least 4 hours: the mass should cut with a knife.
Roll 3 cm balls, bread them twice in egg and crumbs, and fry for 4 minutes at 180°C. Serve with the mustard.

hollandse-nieuwe.d: The herring of the first June catch, gutted but with the pancreas left in: its enzyme ripens the flesh in a light brine. Eaten raw, by hand, held by the tail with the head tipped back.
s: Choose herring with pale pink, firm flesh, never grey: the sign of a short and proper maturation.
Remove the skin by pulling from head to tail in one continuous movement.
Open the herring along the backbone and lift it out, keeping both fillets joined at the tail.
Chop the white onion into very small dice — the Dutch custom, disputed by northern purists.
Serve either by hand, held by the tail and dipped in onion, or in a buttered roll with gherkins.

erwtensoep.d: The winter split pea soup, so thick the spoon must stand up in it — that is the unofficial test. It is called snert, and it is eaten only from the second day, once it has set.
s: Soak the split peas overnight, then put them in three litres of cold water with the knuckle and bay.
Bring to a simmer, skim, and cook for 1½ hours until the peas have collapsed entirely.
Add the celeriac, carrot, leek, onion and potato in dice, and continue for 45 minutes.
Lift out the knuckle, bone it, return the meat with the belly and the sliced smoked sausage for 30 minutes.
Rest overnight before reheating. Serve with buttered rye bread and mustard.

poffertjes.d: Tiny puffed pancakes made with buckwheat flour, cooked in a dimpled iron plate and served under an avalanche of icing sugar and butter. Sold from wooden chalets on the squares in winter.
s: Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk, then whisk with both flours, the eggs and the salt.
Prove for an hour under a cloth: the batter should blister and smell of fermentation.
Butter each dimple of the plate generously and heat it over medium heat.
Fill the dimples three quarters full; as soon as the edges set, flip each poffertje with a fork.
Give them another minute and serve at once, with a knob of cold butter on top and a great deal of icing sugar.

hutspot.d: A mash of carrot, onion and potato served with braised beef. Legend has an orphan finding it still steaming in the abandoned Spanish camp when the siege of Leiden was lifted on 3 October 1574 — and it is still eaten on that day.
s: Cook the brisket for 2½ hours in salted water with the bay and cloves, never letting it boil.
An hour before the end, add the carrots and onions in large pieces to the same broth.
Thirty minutes later, add the potatoes.
Drain the vegetables and crush them roughly with the butter and a little broth: the mash should stay rustic, with lumps.
Slice the beef and serve it on the mash, moistened with a little broth, mustard on the side.

boulets-liegeois.d: Large meatballs under a sauce lapée — sweet and sour, made with sirop de Liège, a concentrate of pears and apples boiled for twenty hours. Served with chips, they are the staple of Walloon friteries.
s: Soak the bread rolls in the milk, squeeze them out and mix with both meats, the eggs and one grated onion.
Work the mixture by hand for 10 minutes, season generously, then shape four meatballs the size of a fist.
Brown them on all sides in the butter, then set aside.
Slowly turn the two remaining sliced onions golden, moisten with broth, and add the syrup, vinegar, sugar, bay and thyme.
Return the meatballs and simmer covered for 45 minutes, turning them halfway. Serve with chips.

stoemp.d: A Brussels mash in which potato is crushed with a vegetable — carrot, leek or kale — and never smoothed out. The word comes from the Dutch stampen, to crush: the gesture gives the dish its name.
s: Boil the potatoes and carrots together in salted water with the bay for 25 minutes.
Meanwhile soften the sliced onion and diced bacon in half the butter, then add the sliced leeks and let them soften for 10 minutes.
Drain the potatoes and carrots and return them to the heat for two minutes to dry out.
Crush them roughly with a fork along with the remaining butter, the cream and the nutmeg: stoemp should stay lumpy.
Fold in the leeks and bacon, pepper it, and serve with pan-fried sausages and parsley.

waterzooi.d: A creamy stew of chicken and julienned vegetables, halfway between soup and main course, thickened with egg yolk and cream. Once made with fish from the Scheldt; pollution of the river turned it to poultry.
s: Poach the whole chicken for 45 minutes in the broth with the thyme and bay, without boiling.
Lift it out, let it cool a little and pull the meat into large pieces; strain the broth.
Cut all the vegetables into fine julienne — carrot, leek, celery, celeriac — and sweat them in butter for 10 minutes.
Moisten with the broth, add the potatoes in batons and cook for 20 minutes.
Beat the yolks with the cream, loosen with a ladle of hot broth and stir in off the heat. Return the chicken, sharpen with lemon and cover with parsley.

anguilles-au-vert.d: Sections of eel poached in a broth of fresh herbs — sorrel, chervil, parsley, tarragon — which gives the sauce a colour of spring. Eaten cold or warm, with bread and beer.
s: Have the fishmonger cut the eel into 5 cm sections, skin removed.
Sweat the shallots in butter, add the eel and let it firm up for 3 minutes without colouring.
Pour in the white wine and as much water again, bring to a simmer and poach for 8 minutes.
Add all the chopped herbs at once and wilt them for two minutes only: any longer and the green turns khaki.
Take off the heat, thicken with the beaten yolks and lemon juice, without boiling. Let it cool: the dish is better cold.

speculoos.d: The brown biscuit of Saint Nicholas, pressed into wooden moulds carved with images. Its colour comes not from chocolate but from brown candi sugar and spices — cinnamon, clove, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg.
s: Beat the soft butter with the brown sugar until the mixture barely lightens.
Add the spices, salt, bicarbonate and milk, then the flour, and bring together without kneading.
Wrap and rest for 24 hours in the fridge: this rest is essential, it lets the spices spread through.
Roll out to 4 mm and press the dough into floured wooden moulds, or cut with a cutter.
Bake for 15 minutes at 160°C. They are still soft when they come out and harden as they cool: do not bake them longer.

chicons-au-gratin.d: Braised endives wrapped in ham and covered in cheese béchamel. The endive was born in Brussels around 1830, from a farmer who forgot chicory roots in his cellar: they had blanched.
s: Cut out the core of each endive with a pointed knife: that is where the bitterness sits.
Braise them for 25 minutes in a little butter, water, sugar and lemon juice, covered, turning halfway.
Drain them thoroughly and press them gently in a cloth: any remaining water would flood the gratin.
Make a béchamel with the butter, flour and milk, and add three quarters of the gruyère and the nutmeg.
Wrap each endive in a slice of ham, pack them tightly, coat with the sauce, dust with the remaining cheese and breadcrumbs, and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C.

lancashire-hotpot.d: Lamb chops and onions under a roof of overlapping potato slices, baked for three hours untouched. Cotton mill workers put it in the oven before their shift; it was waiting for them at night.
s: Flour and sear the lamb pieces and trimmed kidneys hard, in small batches.
Soften the sliced onions and carrot in the same pot, lifting the caramelised juices.
Layer meat and onions in a deep casserole, seasoning each layer, then pour in broth and Worcestershire to come only halfway up.
Slice the potatoes 3 mm thick and lay them in tight overlapping scales on top, in a spiral.
Brush with melted butter, cover and bake for 2½ hours at 150°C, then uncover for 30 minutes at 200°C to brown the roof.

escalivada.d: Aubergines, peppers and onions roasted whole over embers until the skin blackens, then peeled and pulled apart by hand. The Catalan verb escalivar means to cook under ashes.
s: Lay the whole vegetables, unoiled, directly on the embers or under the oven grill at 220°C.
Turn them every ten minutes: the skin must blacken and blister all over, or it will not come away.
Shut them in a covered dish for 20 minutes: the steam lifts the skin by itself.
Peel and pull the flesh apart by hand, along the fibres — never with a knife.
Dress with olive oil and sherry vinegar, salt, and rest for two hours. Serve warm on grilled bread with anchovies.

crema-catalana.d: A milk custard scented with lemon and cinnamon, thickened with starch rather than baked, and burnt with a hot iron just before serving. Eaten on 19 March, Saint Joseph's day.
s: Infuse the milk for 20 minutes with the zests and cinnamon sticks, then strain.
Whisk the yolks with 150 g of sugar to the ribbon, then add the cornstarch without lumps.
Pour the hot milk onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking, then return to low heat.
Stir constantly in figures of eight until it thickens, about 5 minutes, never letting it boil.
Divide between earthenware dishes, cover with film and chill for 4 hours. Dust with the remaining sugar and burn with a red-hot iron at the last second.

suquet-de-peix.d: The fish stew of Catalan fishermen, cooked on board with whatever would not sell. It is thickened with picada — garlic, almonds, fried bread and parsley pounded in a mortar — added in the final minutes.
s: Make a sofregit: sliced onion softened for 20 minutes in oil, then grated tomato cooked down completely.
Add the potatoes in thick pieces broken by hand, and the hot saffron broth.
Cook for 20 minutes, then lay the fish in large sections on top of the potatoes, without burying them.
Pound the garlic, almonds, fried bread and parsley into a paste, loosen it with broth and pour it into the pan.
Add the prawns and mussels, shake the pan in a circular motion — never stir with a spoon — and give it 5 minutes.

bacalao-al-pil-pil.d: Four ingredients — salt cod, oil, garlic, chilli — and an emulsion that is pure sleight of hand: the gelatine from the skin binds the oil into a glossy yellow sauce, achieved by moving the pan alone.
s: Desalt the cod for 48 hours in cold water, changing it six times; keep the skin at all costs.
Turn the sliced garlic and chilli golden in warm oil, lift them out and let the oil cool to 60°C.
Lay the pieces skin down and let them sweat for 8 minutes over very low heat: white beads of gelatine should appear.
Remove the fish, let the oil cool a little, then swirl it round the pan in a slow, continuous circular motion.
The oil suddenly whitens and thickens. Return the cod, garlic and chilli, shake for another minute and serve at once.

txangurro.d: Spider crab picked and stewed in a brandy sofrito, then packed back into its shell and browned. Txangurro is both the crab and the dish — the Basque language makes no distinction.
s: Boil the crabs for 15 minutes in heavily salted water, then cool and pick them clean.
Carefully save the coral and the creamy parts from the shell: that is where all the flavour is.
Soften finely chopped onion, leek and carrot in oil for 25 minutes, then add the grated tomato.
Flame with brandy, moisten with white wine and reduce, then fold in the meat, coral and cayenne.
Fill the cleaned shells, scatter with breadcrumbs and knobs of butter, and brown for 10 minutes at 220°C.

porrusalda.d: Literally 'leek broth': leeks, potatoes, carrots, and nothing else — save sometimes a few flakes of salt cod. Simplicity here is a principle, not a constraint.
s: Desalt the cod for 24 hours and flake it into small pieces.
Turn the sliced garlic golden in the oil, lift it out and keep the flavoured oil.
Sweat the onion and the white of the leeks in lengths, then add the carrot.
Break the potatoes by hand rather than cutting them: the ragged edges release the starch that will thicken the broth.
Cover with water, cook for 30 minutes, add the cod for 5 minutes, then pour in the garlic oil and paprika off the heat.

chilindron-de-cordero.d: A lamb stew with dried red peppers, the choriceros, of which only the pulp scraped out with a spoon is used. That pulp gives the sauce its deep colour, without a scrap of tomato.
s: Soak the dried peppers in hot water for an hour, then scrape out the pulp with a spoon and discard the skin.
Sear the lamb in large pieces in very hot oil, in small batches, until well coloured.
Soften the onion, garlic and diced ham in the same pot, slowly.
Add the fresh peppers in strips, the dried pepper pulp and the grated tomato; stew for 10 minutes.
Return the meat, deglaze with white wine, add the bay and simmer covered for 1¼ hours.

ternasco-asado.d: The Aragonese milk-fed lamb, under three months old, roasted simply with lard, garlic and white wine. No herbs, no spices: the meat is too delicate to carry anything else.
s: Rub the lamb with melted lard, salt and crushed garlic an hour before it goes in the oven.
Lay thick potato slices in the base of an earthenware dish and set the meat on top.
Pour the white wine and half a glass of water into the base, never over the meat.
Roast for 1¾ hours at 170°C, basting every 20 minutes with the juices.
Raise to 220°C for ten minutes to brown, then rest for 15 minutes and squeeze over lemon before carving.

menestra-de-verduras.d: The vegetables of the Navarrese Ribera cooked separately then brought together in a ham broth: artichokes, cardoons, broad beans, white asparagus, each to its own timing. The discipline is the whole recipe.
s: Turn the artichokes and drop them into lemon water; string the cardoons the same way.
Cook each vegetable separately in salted water, taking it out al dente, and refresh in iced water to fix the colour.
Keep a litre of the broad bean cooking water: that will make the broth.
Fry the onion, garlic and diced ham in oil, dust with flour and moisten with white wine then the bean water.
Bring all the vegetables together in this sauce, heat for 5 minutes without boiling, and finish with chopped hard-boiled egg.

piquillos-rellenos.d: Small red peppers roasted over a wood fire, peeled by hand without water, stuffed with a cod brandade and coated in a sauce made from the broken ones. Those from Lodosa carry a protected origin.
s: Desalt the cod for 36 hours, then poach it for 8 minutes in the milk; flake it and keep the milk.
Soften one finely chopped onion and two garlic cloves, add the flaked cod and the cream, and work with a spoon into a bound stuffing.
Fill each piquillo carefully with a piping bag, without tearing it.
For the sauce, fry the second onion, add four broken piquillos, dust with flour, moisten with broth and milk, then blend and sieve.
Arrange the peppers in a dish, coat with the sauce and bake for 15 minutes at 180°C.

patatas-a-la-riojana.d: A potato and chorizo stew of which Paul Bocuse said, after tasting it in 1987, that nothing should be changed. The secret is in the gesture: you break the potatoes, you do not cut them.
s: Push the knife halfway into the potato and snap it off with a twist of the wrist: the fracture releases the starch.
Sweat the onion, garlic and pepper in the oil, without colouring them.
Add the chorizo in thick rounds and let it render its red fat for two minutes.
Stir in the potatoes to coat them, then add the paprika off the heat.
Cover with water, add the bay and dried peppers, and simmer for 35 minutes without stirring — shake the pan instead.

lechazo-asado.p: Aranda de Duero, Castile and León, Spain
lechazo-asado.d: Milk-fed lamb roasted in an earthenware dish in a wood oven, seasoned with nothing but salt and water. Castilian tradition has it carved with the edge of a plate, so readily does the meat fall away.
s: Choose a lamb under thirty days old, fed on milk alone: that is the whole difference.
Lay the quarters skin down in an earthenware dish, rub them with lard and salt generously.
Pour the water into the base of the dish, never onto the skin.
Roast for 1 hour at 180°C, turn skin up and continue for another hour, basting with the juices.
Raise to 230°C for the last 15 minutes to crackle the skin. Serve with a plain lettuce and onion salad.

sopa-de-ajo.d: Stale bread, garlic, paprika and an egg poached in it: the shepherd's soup of the meseta, made from what was left. Also called sopa castellana, and served in scalding earthenware bowls.
s: Turn the sliced garlic gently golden in the oil, without burning it: bitter, it would ruin the whole dish.
Add the diced ham, then the stale bread in pieces, and let it soak up the oil for 3 minutes.
Off the heat, stir in both paprikas briskly — above 120°C they turn acrid.
Moisten with hot broth, add the bay and simmer for 15 minutes: the bread should collapse.
Divide between earthenware bowls, crack an egg into each and bake for 6 minutes at 200°C, until the white sets.

arroz-a-banda.d: The rice is cooked in a rockfish stock and the fish served separately — 'a banda', on the side. Two courses from one dish: fishermen ate the rice on board and sold the fish at the harbour.
s: Make a stock by cooking the rockfish for 25 minutes with the potatoes, then strain it, pressing well.
Fry the soaked ñora pulp, garlic and grated tomato in the paella pan until the sofrito barely darkens.
Add the rice and toast it for 2 minutes, stirring, then pour in the boiling saffron stock — two and a half times the volume of rice.
Cook for 18 minutes over high then low heat, without stirring even once.
Rest off the heat for 5 minutes under a cloth. Serve the rice first, the fish and aioli after.

caldero-del-mar-menor.d: The rice of the lagoon fishermen, cooked in the iron cauldron that gives it its name, red with ñoras and mullet stock. Served with an aioli so stiff it stays on an upturned spoon.
s: Fry the whole ñoras in the oil for a few seconds, without burning them, then pound them in a mortar with two garlic cloves.
Fry the grated tomato in the same oil, add the ñora paste and the paprika.
Moisten with two litres of water, add the gutted fish and cook for 20 minutes; lift them out and strain the broth.
Bring the broth to a rolling boil, tip in the rice and cook for 18 minutes uncovered and unstirred.
Mount the aioli in a mortar with the remaining garlic, the yolk, salt and oil in a thread. Serve the rice, then the fish with the aioli.

pa-amb-oli-sobrasada.d: Country bread rubbed with hanging tomato and oil, spread with sobrassada — the raw, spreadable paprika sausage that the island's damp air prevented from ever fully drying. Melted in the oven with honey.
s: Choose a close-crumbed loaf, cut into one-centimetre slices, and toast it barely.
Rub it with half a garlic clove, then with a halved hanging tomato, pulp against the crumb.
Douse generously with olive oil and salt it.
Spread the sobrassada thickly, drizzle with honey and put it under the grill for 4 minutes: it melts and reddens.
Serve with sheep's cheese, olives and a glass of island wine.

ensaimada.d: A spiral of dough stretched to transparency and brushed with lard — saïm in Mallorcan, hence the name. It still travels in large octagonal boxes seen in every airport on the island.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, warm water and 100 g of flour; let it double for an hour.
Knead with the remaining flour, sugar, eggs and salt for 20 minutes: the dough must become very elastic.
Prove for 2 hours, divide, then stretch each piece by hand on an oiled surface until translucent.
Brush generously with soft lard, roll into a long thin rope and coil it into a loose spiral, leaving space between the turns.
Prove for 12 hours at room temperature, bake for 20 minutes at 180°C and dust heavily with icing sugar.

papas-arrugadas.d: Small potatoes boiled in water saturated with salt until the skin wrinkles and frosts over with white crystals. Dipped into two sauces: red mojo with chilli, green mojo with coriander.
s: Wash the small potatoes without peeling and put them in a pan where they sit tightly packed.
Cover halfway with water and tip in all the coarse salt: the water should be saturated, salty enough to float a potato.
Boil covered for 25 minutes, then pour off the water and return to high heat for two minutes, shaking: the salt crystallises on the skin.
For the red mojo, pound garlic, cumin, chilli, paprika and bread, then mount with oil and vinegar.
For the green mojo, replace the chilli with coriander and green pepper. Serve both on the side.

rancho-canario.d: A thick soup in which short pasta and chickpeas cook together with pork and chorizo. The dish of neighbourhood fiestas, made in hundred-litre pots and handed out in the street.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight with a handful of coarse salt.
Cook them in two litres of water with the pork and bacon for 1 hour at a gentle boil.
Fry onion, garlic and grated tomato in oil for a sofrito, add the paprika off the heat, then tip it all into the pot.
Add the potatoes in large cubes, the sliced chorizo, saffron and thyme, and continue for 20 minutes.
Throw in the short pasta for the last 10 minutes. The rancho should stay thick: the spoon must almost stand up in it.

cocido-montanes.d: White beans and green cabbage stewed with the compango — chorizo, black pudding, bacon and salt ribs. Unlike other Spanish cocidos, this one has no chickpeas and no broth served separately.
s: Soak the beans and desalt the ribs and ear overnight, separately.
Put the beans in cold water with the salt meats, bring to a bare simmer and skim.
Check the boil with cold water twice during the first half hour: this stops the bean skins bursting.
After 1 hour, add the washed and roughly chopped greens, along with the chorizo and black pudding.
Make a refrito of garlic and paprika in the oil, pour it into the pot and give it another 30 minutes. Serve everything together.

rabo-de-toro.p: Jerez de la Frontera, Andalusia, Spain
rabo-de-toro.d: Oxtail braised in sherry for over three hours, until the meat leaves the bone of its own accord. It was made with the animals killed in the ring, on the evening of the bullfight.
s: Flour the oxtail sections and sear them on all sides in very hot oil, in small batches.
Soften onion, carrot, leek and garlic in the same pot for 25 minutes, until golden.
Add the grated tomato, reduce, then deglaze with the red wine and sherry vinegar.
Return the meat, add broth to cover, along with the bay and cloves, and simmer covered for 3 hours.
Lift out the meat, pass the sauce through a sieve pressing the vegetables, reduce it and return the oxtail to it.

arroz-de-cabidela.d: A poultry rice bound with the bird's blood, sharpened with vinegar to stop it setting. The dish of Minho farms, where nothing of the animal was wasted — not even what elsewhere is thrown away.
s: Collect the blood in a bowl already holding the vinegar, and whisk at once: otherwise it would set solid.
Joint the chicken and fry it in the oil with the onion, garlic and bay.
Add the grated tomato and white wine, cover with water and simmer for 30 minutes.
Tip in the rice and cook for 15 minutes, keeping the dish very wet.
Off the heat, pour in the soured blood in a thin stream, stirring constantly: the sauce browns and thickens. Do not let it boil again.

sarrabulho.d: A thick porridge of bread, pork meats and blood, sharpened with cumin and lemon. Served with rojões and a glass of vinho verde; the dish of Minho winter markets.
s: Cook the meats for 1½ hours in water with the onion, garlic, bay and white wine, until they fall apart.
Lift them out, chop them finely by knife and strain the broth.
Crumble the stale bread into the hot broth and let it swell for 15 minutes, then crush it with a wooden spoon.
Return the meat, add the cumin, piri-piri and plenty of pepper, and thicken for 20 minutes over low heat, stirring.
Pour in the blood off the heat, stirring without pause, and finish with lemon juice. It should have the consistency of a loose purée.

caldeirada-de-peixe.d: The fish stew of Nazaré fishermen, built in layers in the pot and never stirred: you only shake the pan. The more different species it holds, the better it is.
s: Cut all the vegetables into rounds of the same thickness: they must cook together.
Build the pot in layers — onion, potato, pepper, tomato, fish — salting and oiling each storey.
Repeat to the top, finishing with vegetables to protect the fish.
Pour in the white wine, water to come only halfway, the bay and paprika, then cover.
Cook for 35 minutes over medium heat without ever stirring: shake the pot in a circular motion every ten minutes.

queijadas-de-sintra.d: Small tartlets of fresh cheese and cinnamon in a hand-pleated crust, recorded in Sintra since the 13th century — they were once used to pay part of the local taxes.
s: Knead 150 g of flour, the warm water, melted butter and salt into a supple dough, and rest it for 30 minutes.
Push the fresh cheese through a sieve to remove every lump — the final texture depends entirely on this.
Mix it with the sugar, eggs, remaining flour, cinnamon and zest into a smooth batter.
Roll the dough very thin and line 6 cm moulds, leaving an overhanging edge that you pleat by hand.
Fill three quarters full and bake for 20 minutes at 220°C: the tops should brown in patches.

arroz-doce.d: The Portuguese rice pudding, yellow with egg yolks, served cold in wide dishes and stencilled with cinnamon. There is no village festa in Portugal without a whole table covered in these dishes.
s: Cook the rice for 10 minutes in salted water with a cinnamon stick and the zest, then drain without rinsing.
Bring the milk to a simmer with the remaining cinnamon and zest, tip in the rice and cook for 30 minutes over low heat, stirring often.
Add the sugar only at this point: any earlier and it would toughen the grain.
Off the heat, stir in the yolks beaten with a little hot rice, then return to very low heat for two minutes without boiling.
Pour into wide dishes, cool, and stencil a pattern with ground cinnamon through cut paper.

pastel-de-tentugal.d: A pastry stretched so thin you can read through it, rolled around an egg cream. The Carmelite nuns of Tentúgal kept the secret; the dough is still worked in rooms without a draught, windows shut.
s: Knead the flour, warm water and salt for 25 minutes: the dough must become smooth and supple as fine leather.
Rest it for 2 hours under a bowl, then stretch it by hand over a large floured cloth until you can see the weave through it.
Make the cream: cook the sugar and water to soft ball, cool a little, stir in the yolks off the heat, then thicken over low heat.
Cut strips of pastry, brush with melted butter, pipe the cream along them and roll loosely.
Fold in the ends, bake for 15 minutes at 220°C and dust with icing sugar and cinnamon.

carne-de-porco-a-alentejana.d: Pork marinated in red pepper paste, sautéed with clams and fried potatoes. The surf-and-turf pairing seems odd until you learn that Alentejo pigs grazed along the estuaries.
s: Cut the pork into 3 cm cubes and marinate for 12 hours in the pepper paste, white wine, crushed garlic and bay.
Purge the clams for 2 hours in salted water so they release their sand.
Drain and dry the meat, then sear it over high heat in olive oil, in small batches.
Pour in the strained marinade, reduce by half, then add the clams and cover: they open in 4 minutes.
Deep-fry the diced potatoes, fold them through, cover with chopped coriander and serve with lemon and gherkins.

arroz-de-lampreia.d: The Minho lamprey, fished from January to April, stewed in its own blood and Alvarinho wine. A prehistoric jawless fish whose taste is closer to game than to the sea.
s: Scald the lamprey to remove the mucus, then collect the blood in a bowl holding the vinegar.
Cut it into 4 cm sections and marinate for 3 hours in the white wine with the bay and cloves.
Soften the onion and garlic in the oil, add the grated tomato and let it cook down.
Pour in the marinade, bring to a simmer and poach the sections for 25 minutes; lift them out and keep warm.
Cook the rice for 15 minutes in that broth, then bind with the blood off the heat, without boiling. Return the fish and serve at once.

maranhos.d: A kid's stomach filled with rice, mint and meats, sewn up and simmered. An Easter preparation in the Portuguese serra, where the animal was killed once a year and nothing was wasted.
s: Clean the stomachs thoroughly with salt, lemon and vinegared water, then cut them into 15 cm pouches.
Dice all the meats small and mix them with the raw rice, onion, garlic, chopped mint and white wine.
Fill the pouches only half full — the rice doubles — and sew them carefully with kitchen thread.
Poach for 1¾ hours in a barely simmering broth with the bay, never boiling, pricking them twice.
Let them cool before slicing: hot, maranhos fall apart. Serve with a squeeze of lemon.

bolo-levedo.d: A flat sweet bread cooked on a griddle, halfway between brioche and English muffin, born in the ovens of Furnas. Eaten warm at breakfast, simply buttered, or split and filled.
s: Dissolve the yeast in the warm milk with a spoonful of sugar and let it froth for 15 minutes.
Knead with the flour, remaining sugar, egg, soft butter and salt for 12 minutes.
Prove for 1½ hours, until the dough doubles.
Divide into eight balls, flatten them into 12 cm discs 1.5 cm thick, and prove for 40 minutes under a cloth.
Cook on a dry griddle over low heat, 7 minutes a side: they should brown without burning and stay soft in the middle.

pudim-abade-de-priscos.d: A custard of fifteen egg yolks, port and — this is its secret — pork fat, which gives it an unmatched silkiness. Father Manuel Rebelo, the greedy priest of Priscos, never gave up the recipe in his lifetime.
s: Make a pale caramel with 150 g of sugar and a little water, pour it into a ring mould and swirl to coat the sides.
Cook the remaining sugar with the water, zest, cinnamon and pork fat into a syrup, 10 minutes at a gentle boil.
Lift out the fat, let the syrup cool a little and strain it.
Beat the yolks without frothing them — bubbles would spoil the texture — then pour in the warm syrup in a thread, and finally the port.
Pass through a sieve, pour into the mould and bake in a bain-marie for 1¼ hours at 180°C. Cool overnight before turning out.

garbure.d: A cabbage and bean soup into which a leg of duck confit is plunged. The Béarn test is well known: a spoon stood in the middle must stay upright on its own, or it is merely soup.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then cook them in three litres of water with the smoked collar for an hour.
Add carrots, turnips and leeks in large pieces, along with the garlic, thyme and bay.
Thirty minutes later, add the potatoes and the cabbage, leaves separated and roughly chopped.
Warm the confit legs in their fat and lay them in the soup for the last twenty minutes.
Serve very thick, over slices of stale bread. Finish in the Béarn manner: a glass of red wine poured into the bottom of the plate.

poule-au-pot.d: A hen stuffed with ham and bread, poached with its vegetables. Henri IV, born in Pau, is said to have wished every ploughman could put one in the pot on Sundays — the phrase may be invented, the dish stayed with him.
s: Make the stuffing: bread soaked in milk and squeezed, chopped ham, the bird's liver, garlic, parsley and eggs.
Stuff the hen without packing it — the stuffing swells — and sew the opening; truss it firmly.
Bring three litres of water to a simmer, lower in the hen and skim patiently for twenty minutes.
Add the clove-studded onion, bay and salt, and poach for 2 hours without ever boiling.
Add the vegetables in large pieces for the last 40 minutes. Serve the broth first, then the hen, stuffing and vegetables.

coq-au-vin.d: A cockerel — a real one, firm and old — marinated then braised overnight in red wine. The sauce is bound with the bird's blood or, failing that, its blended liver: that is what sets it apart from a mere chicken bourguignon.
s: Joint the cockerel into eight and marinate for 24 hours in the red wine with carrot, garlic, thyme and bay.
Drain and dry the pieces thoroughly: wet, they would not colour.
Sear them in butter, flame with marc, dust with flour and cook for two minutes.
Pour in the strained marinade, brought to the boil beforehand, and simmer covered for 2 hours over very low heat.
Glaze the button onions and fry the mushrooms separately, adding them at the end with the browned lardons.

gratin-dauphinois.d: Sliced potatoes cooked in milk and cream with garlic, and nothing else. No cheese, no egg: the recipe recorded in 1788 by the lieutenant general of Dauphiné mentions neither.
s: Choose firm-fleshed potatoes and cut them into 3 mm rounds, never rinsing them: the starch makes the binding.
Rub the dish with a cut garlic clove, then butter it generously.
Heat the milk with the remaining crushed garlic, nutmeg, salt and pepper, and add the potatoes. Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring gently.
Transfer to the dish, pressing the layers down, then pour the cream over.
Bake for 1¼ hours at 150°C. A knife blade should pass through without resistance and the top be golden, not crusted.

socca.d: A chickpea pancake baked in a wood oven on a copper tray, served scalding, peppered and torn by hand. Cousin to Genoese farinata, sold by weight in the markets of the coast.
s: Whisk the chickpea flour into warm water without a single lump, and salt it.
Rest for at least an hour, skimming the foam that rises.
Stir in the olive oil: the batter should stay very liquid, like a crêpe batter.
Heat an oiled tray in the hottest part of your oven, under the grill, then pour in a layer barely 3 mm deep.
Bake for 8 minutes at the very top: the surface should scorch in places. Pepper generously, tear by hand and eat standing up.

daube-provencale.d: Beef marinated in wine and orange, stewed for four hours in a narrow-necked daubière that traps the steam. Black olives and a dried orange peel go in: that is what separates it from a bourguignon.
s: Marinate the beef in large cubes for 24 hours in red wine with carrot, onion, garlic, thyme, bay and orange peel.
Drain and dry the meat, then sear it in very hot oil in small batches.
Fry the lardons and the marinade vegetables in the same pot.
Return everything, pour in the marinade brought to the boil and the tomato, and simmer for 4 hours over very low heat, covered.
Add the stoned olives for the last half hour. Serve with macaroni, as they do in Nice, or cool it for the next day.

tielle-setoise.d: An octopus pie in a spiced tomato sauce, brought by fishermen from Gaeta who settled in Sète in the 19th century. Made only at home for decades, it was not sold until 1937.
s: Cook the octopus for 45 minutes at a gentle boil with the bay, then let it cool in its water and dice it small.
Knead the flour, warm water, yeast, oil and salt, and prove for an hour.
Make a sauce by reducing tomato, onion, garlic, white wine, paprika and chilli for 30 minutes, until very thick.
Mix the octopus into the sauce and let it cool: hot, the filling would sog the pastry.
Line small tins, fill them, cover with a disc of dough, seal by crimping the edge and bake for 30 minutes at 200°C. Eaten warm.

cargolade.d: Snails grilled over a vine-shoot fire, opening upwards, basted drop by drop with melting bacon fat. Less a dish than a gathering: an afternoon spent over aioli and valley wine.
s: Starve the snails for a week, then wash them at length in vinegared water until it runs clear.
Set them opening upwards on a grill, packed tightly together, and salt each opening.
Light a fire of vine shoots and let it fall to embers: an open flame would make them burst.
Grill for 15 minutes, then lay the bacon slices on a rack above: the melting fat drips into the shells.
Mount an aioli in a mortar with the garlic, yolks, salt and oil in a thread. Eat the snails by hand, dipped in it.

mouclade-charentaise.d: Bouchot mussels in a cream sauce with curry and Pineau des Charentes. The curry surprises: it arrived in the 17th century through the port of La Rochelle, on East India Company ships.
s: Scrape and beard the mussels, discarding any that stay open after a tap on the worktop.
Open them over high heat for 4 minutes with the shallots, white wine and bay, then lift them out.
Strain the liquor through a fine cloth: there is always a little sand at the bottom.
Make a pale roux with the butter and flour, add the curry, whisk in the strained liquor and cook for 5 minutes.
Bind with the yolks beaten into the cream, off the heat. Remove one shell from each mussel, coat them and scatter parsley.

lamproie-a-la-bordelaise.d: Garonne lamprey stewed in red wine with leek and bound with its own blood. A spring dish, increasingly rare: the fish is now protected and the fishery closely regulated.
s: Scald the lamprey to remove the mucus, bleed it and keep the blood in a bowl with a glass of wine.
Pull out the dorsal nerve by tugging the white cord near the head: without this, the dish would be bitter.
Cut into sections and fry with the onion, garlic and ham in butter, then flame with marc.
Add the white of the leeks in lengths, dust with flour, pour in the red wine and simmer for 1½ hours over low heat.
Bind with the blood off the heat, never boiling again. Serve on garlic-rubbed croutons — better still reheated the next day.

mique-du-perigord.d: A large ball of leavened bread poached in the broth of a salt-pork stew. It swells as it cooks and is sliced at the table; the poor man's bread, baked without an oven, in the pot.
s: Desalt the pork for 12 hours, then cook it in three litres of water with the bay for an hour.
Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in warm milk, the eggs, duck fat and salt; prove for 2 hours.
Add the vegetables in large pieces to the broth.
Shape the dough into a large ball without reworking it, and lower it gently onto the simmering broth.
Cover and poach for 45 minutes, turning it halfway: it doubles in size. Slice it at the table, with the stew.

tourin-a-l-ail.d: A garlic soup threaded with egg white and finished with a yolk beaten with vinegar. It was brought to newlyweds in the middle of their wedding night, in a tureen, with an insistence whose motive one can guess.
s: Peel two whole heads of garlic, remove the green germ and crush the cloves with the flat of a knife.
Soften them very gently in the duck fat for 10 minutes, never letting them colour: burnt garlic would make the soup bitter.
Dust with flour, pour in the boiling water and simmer for 20 minutes.
Trickle the beaten whites into the simmering broth, stirring: they set into threads.
Off the heat, bind with the yolks beaten with vinegar. Serve over stale bread, with parsley.

estofinado.d: Dried cod rehydrated and crushed with potatoes, garlic and walnut oil. Norwegian stockfish came up the Lot by barge as far as Decazeville: which is why this sea dish is eaten three hundred kilometres inland.
s: Soak the stockfish for four days in cold running water, or changing the water morning and evening.
Poach it for 20 minutes without boiling, then flake it patiently, removing skin and bones.
Boil the potatoes in salted water and rice them while still hot.
Combine the fish, potatoes, crushed garlic, chopped hard-boiled eggs and pounded walnuts.
Work in the walnut oil and cream with a wooden spoon over very low heat, until the mass turns silky. Sharpen with lemon and cover with parsley.

truffade.d: Fried potatoes crushed with fresh Cantal tomme until the cheese pulls into long ribbons. This is not aligot: here the potatoes stay in pieces, and there is no cream.
s: Cut the potatoes into 5 mm slices and fry them in duck fat for 20 minutes, covered then uncovered.
Add the lardons and crushed garlic, and let everything colour.
Crush roughly with a spatula, keeping whole pieces: truffade is not a purée.
Slice the fresh tomme thinly and fold it in off the heat, lifting the mass.
Return to low heat and work with the spatula until the cheese pulls into threads. Serve at once, in the pan.

rillettes-du-mans.d: Pork cooked for five hours in its own fat then pulled apart with forks, never ground. Those of Le Mans are brown and fibrous, unlike the rillettes of Tours, paler and fattier.
s: Cut the meats into large 5 cm strips and salt them the day before with the pepper and aromatics.
Melt the fat in the base of a cast-iron pot, then add the meats without colouring them.
Moisten with white wine, cover and cook for 5 hours at 120°C, stirring every hour.
The meat should fall apart on its own: shred it with two forks along the fibres, never in a machine.
Adjust the salt when cold — hot fat masks it — then pot them up and seal with melted fat.

far-breton.d: A thick dense custard, between clafoutis and pudding, studded with steeped prunes. Far comes from the Latin far, spelt flour: it began as a savoury porridge, served with bacon.
s: Steep the prunes in warm rum for at least two hours, ideally overnight.
Whisk the eggs and sugar, add the sifted flour and salt without working it, then the warm milk little by little.
Stir in the melted butter and vanilla; the batter should be as fluid as crêpe batter.
Rest for an hour, then pour into a buttered dish and scatter over the drained prunes.
Bake for 50 minutes at 200°C: the far rises then sinks as it cools, which is normal. Eat it warm or cold, never hot.

teurgoule.d: A rice pudding baked for five hours in a bread oven, until it forms a thick brown skin. The name is said to come from 'tord-gueule', a mouth-twister: children burnt themselves trying to eat it too soon.
s: Mix the rice, sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg and a pinch of salt in a tall narrow dish, preferably stoneware.
Pour the cold milk over and stir once only: that is the last gesture, it will not be touched again.
Bake at 150°C for an hour, then lower to 130°C.
Cook for four more hours without ever opening or stirring: a thick brown skin forms on the surface.
The teurgoule is ready when that skin is almost black and the rice a deep beige. Eat it warm, with fallue brioche if you can find it.

paris-brest.d: A ring of choux pastry filled with praline mousseline cream, its shape recalling a bicycle wheel. Created in 1910 for the Paris-Brest-Paris cycle race, from which it takes its name.
s: Make the praline: caramelise 100 g of sugar, pour it over the roasted hazelnuts, let it set and blend at length into a flowing paste.
Make choux pastry: bring the water, 125 ml of milk, 100 g of butter and the salt to the boil, tip in the flour, dry it out, then beat in the eggs one at a time.
Pipe a 22 cm ring with a fluted nozzle, double it with a second circle and a third on top, and scatter flaked almonds.
Bake for 40 minutes at 180°C without opening the oven for the first 25 minutes.
Make a pastry cream with the remaining milk, yolks, sugar and cornstarch; once cold, beat it with 250 g of soft butter and the praline. Fill the ring, split in two.

flammekueche.d: Dough rolled paper-thin, spread with cream, onion and bacon, and baked for two minutes against the floor of a bread oven. It was used to judge the oven's heat before the loaves went in.
s: Knead flour, water, oil and salt for 10 minutes into a supple yeastless dough, then rest it for 30 minutes.
Mix the sour cream and drained fromage blanc, season with salt, pepper and nutmeg: the mixture must be thick, never runny.
Slice the onions thinly and cut the bacon into large lardons; do not cook them, they cook on the tart.
Roll the dough until you can see the table through it, into a rectangle that fits your oven.
Spread the cream, scatter onion and bacon, and bake in the hottest part of the oven on a hot floor for 8 to 10 minutes. The edges should blacken in places.

matelote-au-riesling.d: Four river fish — eel, pike, zander, trout — poached in Riesling and coated in a cream sauce. The inns along the Ill have long made it their feast dish, served with noodles.
s: Sweat the sliced shallots in half the butter, add the Riesling and bay, and bring to a simmer.
Poach the fish from firmest to most delicate — eel first, trout last — 4 to 8 minutes each, then keep them warm.
Strain the broth and reduce it by half over high heat.
Make a roux with the remaining butter and the flour, whisk in the reduced broth and cook for 8 minutes.
Add the sautéed mushrooms and the cream, bind with the yolks off the heat, coat the fish and serve with buttered noodles.

coq-au-riesling.d: The white cousin of coq au vin: the wine is dry and mineral, the sauce stays pale, and morels replace the bacon. Served with spätzle, never with potatoes.
s: Soak the morels for an hour in warm water; strain that water carefully and keep it.
Brown the chicken pieces in the butter without scorching them: the sauce must stay pale.
Flame with marc, dust with flour, then pour in the Riesling and the morel liquid.
Add thyme and bay, cover and simmer for 50 minutes over low heat.
Lift out the chicken, add the cream and mushrooms to the sauce, reduce for 10 minutes, then return the pieces. Serve with spätzle.

bouchee-a-la-reine.d: A vol-au-vent filled with chicken, quenelles and mushrooms in a white sauce. It bears the name of Marie Leszczyńska, queen of France and daughter of the Duke of Lorraine, who is said to have had it served at Versailles.
s: Cut twelve discs of puff pastry, hollow the centre from six of them to make rings, stack and glaze with egg.
Bake for 25 minutes at 200°C, then carefully lift the lid and hollow out the inside.
Poach the chicken and veal for 25 minutes in the broth, then cut into one-centimetre dice.
Make a velouté with the butter, flour and strained broth, and cook it for 15 minutes over low heat.
Add the sautéed mushrooms and the meats, bind with the yolks beaten into the cream off the heat, sharpen with lemon, and fill the scalding cases.

gougeres.d: Small comté choux buns, served warm as an aperitif in every Burgundy cellar. They were offered to buyers during tastings: the cheese rounds out the wine and makes the tannins seem softer.
s: Bring the water, butter and salt to the boil, tip in the flour all at once and beat briskly.
Dry the paste out for two minutes over the heat, until it forms a ball that leaves the pan.
Off the heat, work in the eggs one at a time: the paste should form a soft beak on the spatula.
Add three quarters of the grated comté, the nutmeg and the white pepper.
Pipe well-spaced mounds, dust with the remaining cheese and bake for 30 minutes at 180°C without opening the oven.

oeufs-en-meurette.d: Eggs poached in red wine, served on a crouton under a sauce of lardons and button onions. The poaching wine becomes the sauce: nothing is wasted, and the whites take on a disconcerting purple tint.
s: Fry the lardons, button onions and mushrooms in the butter, then set them aside.
Sweat the shallots, dust with flour, pour in the red wine and broth, add thyme and bay, and reduce for 25 minutes.
Strain the sauce and set a good glassful aside in a small pan for poaching the eggs.
Break the eggs one at a time into that simmering wine and poach for 3 minutes; drain them on a cloth.
Rub the toasted croutons with garlic, set the eggs on them, coat with sauce and cover with the garnish.

jambon-persille.d: Ham cooked on the bone, pulled apart and set in a jelly of white wine and parsley. The Burgundian Easter terrine, whose green and pink appear at the cut like marble.
s: Desalt the ham for 12 hours in cold water, changing it three times.
Simmer it for 3 hours with the veal foot, white wine, vegetables and aromatics.
Let it cool in the broth, then pull the meat apart by hand into large pieces, without chopping it.
Strain the broth, cool it and check that it sets; if not, reduce it further.
Layer ham and parsley mixture — parsley, garlic, shallot, tarragon — in a terrine, pour over the warm jelly and press overnight in the fridge.

poulet-de-bresse-a-la-creme.d: The only poultry in the world with a protected designation of origin, cooked in butter and drowned in Étrez cream. The dish is disarmingly simple: the bird does all the work.
s: Joint the bird into eight, salt it and let it colour skin-side down in foaming butter, without browning it hard.
Add the sliced shallots, cover and stew for 25 minutes over very low heat.
Take out the breasts, which cook faster, and continue for 15 minutes with the legs.
Deglaze with white wine, reduce until dry, then pour in the cream and let it coat for 10 minutes.
Return all the chicken, add the sautéed mushrooms, the tarragon and a dash of vin jaune. Sharpen with lemon at the last moment.

quenelles-sauce-nantua.d: Pike quenelles that swell in the oven until they treble in size, under a pink sauce of crayfish butter. Lake Nantua supplied both: the fish and the red-clawed crayfish.
s: Make a panade: bring the milk and 100 g of butter to the boil, tip in the flour, dry it out, then cool completely.
Blend the very cold pike flesh, work in the panade then the eggs one at a time, and finally 100 g of softened butter. Chill for 3 hours.
Fry the crayfish with shallot and carrot, flame with marc, add the tomato paste, cover with water and cook for 20 minutes. Strain, pressing hard, then enrich with the cream.
Shape the quenelles with two spoons and poach them for 10 minutes in simmering salted water: they should rise.
Arrange them in a dish, coat with the Nantua sauce and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C. They swell and brown.

tablier-de-sapeur.d: Tripe marinated in white wine, breaded and grilled, served with sauce gribiche. Marshal de Castellane, governor of Lyon and a former sapper, is said to have given his nickname to this cut, flat as a leather apron.
s: Marinate the pre-cooked tripe for 12 hours in the white wine with salt and pepper.
Pat it dry, spread mustard on both sides, then coat in beaten egg and breadcrumbs.
Let the crumb dry for 30 minutes in the fridge: it will hold better during cooking.
Cook in clarified butter over medium heat, 6 minutes a side, until the crust is golden and crisp.
Make the gribiche by combining mayonnaise, chopped hard-boiled egg, gherkins, capers and herbs. Serve with a lemon wedge.

gratinee-a-l-oignon.d: The soup of Les Halles, swallowed scalding at five in the morning by market porters and night owls. It is all patience: the onions must melt for a full hour before they take on their mahogany colour.
s: Slice the onions very finely and melt them in the butter, covered, for 30 minutes without colouring.
Uncover and continue for 40 minutes, stirring often: they should turn brown and jammy, never burnt.
Dust with flour, deglaze with white wine and marc, then pour in the hot broth.
Add thyme and bay and simmer for 25 minutes; salt late, as the broth reduces.
Divide between bowls, lay on the garlic-rubbed croutons, cover with a thick layer of gruyère and grill for 8 minutes.

hachis-parmentier.d: Beef from the pot-au-feu, chopped and topped with golden mash. The name honours Antoine Parmentier, who got the French to accept the potato by having it guarded by soldiers — so that it would be stolen.
s: Cook the beef for 2 hours as a pot-au-feu, or use yesterday's leftovers — that is the spirit of the dish.
Chop it by knife, never in a machine: a blade crushes the fibres and makes the filling pasty.
Soften onion, carrot and garlic, add the meat, tomato paste, wine and broth, and stew for 20 minutes.
Rice the potatoes with the butter and hot milk, then bind with the egg yolk.
Spread the meat, cover with the mash, fork the surface, dust with gruyère and bake for 35 minutes at 200°C.

navarin-d-agneau.d: A lamb stew with spring vegetables, each turned by hand and glazed separately so they stay distinct. The name may come from the turnip, or from the battle of Navarino — cooks have never settled it.
s: Sear the lamb in large pieces over high heat, in small batches, until well coloured.
Sprinkle with sugar and let it caramelise for a minute: this is what gives the sauce its colour.
Dust with flour, add the tomato paste and garlic, pour in the broth and simmer for 1 hour.
Turn the turnips and carrots into olive shapes and glaze them in butter and sugar in a separate pan.
Add the potatoes and glazed vegetables for the last 25 minutes; the blanched peas and beans only at the very end.

sole-normande.d: Sole poached in cider, crowned with mussels, prawns and mushrooms under a cream sauce. Created around 1830 at the Rocher de Cancale in Paris, it was the dish that made Norman cooking famous.
s: Open the mussels in the cider with a shallot for 4 minutes, then shell them and strain the liquor through a cloth.
Fillet the sole, roll the fillets and lay them in a buttered dish with the remaining shallots.
Moisten with the strained mussel liquor, cover with buttered paper and bake for 12 minutes at 180°C.
Pour off the cooking juices, reduce them by half, then thicken with a white roux and the cream.
Off the heat, add the yolks and lemon. Coat the fillets and surround them with the mussels, prawns and sautéed mushrooms.

andouille-de-vire.d: An andouille made of strips of pig's stomach threaded by hand and then smoked for six weeks over beech. Served cold in thin slices, or warm with apples softened in cider.
s: Choose a genuinely smoked andouille, black-skinned with a visible grain in the slice: the stomach strips should be distinguishable.
Peel the apples, cut them into thick wedges and fry them in butter until golden.
Flame with calvados, moisten with cider and reduce by half, covered.
Add the cream and mustard, and let it coat for 5 minutes.
Fry the andouille slices for 2 minutes a side, no longer — it is already cooked — and serve on the apples, with toast.

canard-a-la-rouennaise.d: A duck smothered rather than bled, roasted rare, its carcass then pressed to extract the blood that will bind the sauce. The ritual of the silver press, at the table, belongs to the grand cooking of the 19th century.
s: Roast the duck for only 20 minutes at 220°C: the flesh must stay frankly pink at the centre.
Carve off the breast slices and legs, keep them warm, and break up the carcass.
Press the carcass — failing a press, crush it firmly in a sieve — to collect the blood and juices.
Reduce the red wine by half with the chopped shallots and cracked pepper.
Off the heat, work in the crushed liver, the carcass juices and the butter in pieces, never boiling. Sharpen with lemon and coat the breast slices.

cotriade.d: The soup of Breton sailors, made on board with the share of the catch that was theirs. The broth is eaten first over bread, then the fish and potatoes, dressed with a sharp vinaigrette.
s: Melt the sliced onions in the salted butter, then add the garlic, thyme and bay.
Cover with two litres of water, salt it, and cook the potatoes in large pieces for 20 minutes.
Add the fish from firmest to most delicate, in three stages, allowing 5 to 10 minutes each.
Lift out the fish and potatoes with a slotted spoon and keep them warm on a platter.
Serve the broth as a soup over slices of bread, then the fish dressed with a mustardy vinaigrette and parsley.

coquilles-saint-jacques-bretonne.d: Scallops in their shell under a parsley crust of salted butter and breadcrumbs. The bay of Saint-Brieuc is France's largest bed: fishing there is limited to forty-five minutes a day.
s: Shuck the scallops, separate the white from the coral and wash the deep shells thoroughly.
Cream the salted butter with very finely chopped shallot and garlic, the parsley and a little lemon.
Sweat the remaining shallots in white wine and reduce until dry.
Set a scallop and its coral in each shell, cover with a knob of parsley butter and dust with breadcrumbs.
Bake for 8 minutes at 240°C at the top of the oven: the scallops should stay pearly at the centre.

gateau-breton.d: A dense cake of salted butter and egg yolks, cross-hatched with a fork before baking. It kept for weeks: sailors took it to sea, where it lasted better than bread.
s: Take the butter out an hour ahead: it must be soft, never melted.
Beat it at length with the sugar, until the mixture pales and nearly doubles in volume.
Work in seven yolks one at a time, then the rum and vanilla.
Fold in the flour and a pinch of salt, lifting rather than beating: the cake should stay short.
Spread 3 cm deep in a buttered tin, glaze with the last yolk and score diamonds with a fork. Bake for 45 minutes at 170°C.

rillons-de-tours.d: Large cubes of pork belly confited in lard then caramelised in Vouvray wine, crisp outside and melting within. Balzac, a son of Touraine, cites them in Le Lys dans la vallée as a childhood memory.
s: Cut the belly with its rind into 5 cm cubes and salt them for 12 hours in coarse salt.
Rinse, dry thoroughly, then colour them on all sides in the melted lard.
Turn the heat to its lowest, add garlic, thyme and bay, and confit for 2½ hours covered: the fat must never bubble hard.
Take off the lid, raise the heat and let the rind crisp for 15 minutes.
Deglaze with the white wine and sugar, let it caramelise while stirring, and serve warm with a lamb's lettuce salad.

sandre-au-beurre-blanc.p: Nantes, Pays de la Loire, France
sandre-au-beurre-blanc.d: A Loire fish under an emulsion of butter, shallot and Muscadet. Clémence Lefeuvre, a cook at Saint-Julien-de-Concelles, is said to have invented beurre blanc around 1890 by botching a béarnaise.
s: Chop the shallots as finely as you can and reduce them with the wine and vinegar until dry.
Two spoonfuls of moist, almost syrupy compote should remain: that is the base of the emulsion.
Add the cream — it stabilises the sauce — then whisk in the very cold butter, cube by cube, off the heat.
The sauce must stay warm: too hot it splits, too cold it sets. Never let it boil.
Cook the zander fillets skin-side down for 6 minutes, turn for a minute, and coat with the beurre blanc.

gateau-nantais.p: Nantes, Pays de la Loire, France
gateau-nantais.d: An almond cake soaked in rum under a white icing. It was born of the triangular trade, which brought sugar and rum from the Caribbean up to Nantes — an origin the city now faces squarely.
s: Cream the softened butter with the sugar until the mixture pales.
Add the ground almonds, then the eggs one at a time, the flour, vanilla and half the rum.
Pour into a buttered tin and bake for 40 minutes at 170°C; the cake should stay moist at the centre.
As it comes out, prick it and soak it with the remaining rum, then let it cool in the tin.
Make a thick icing with the icing sugar and a spoonful of water, spread it over the top and let it set for two hours.

mogettes-au-jambon.d: The white bean of the Vendée, cooked in plain water and served under a grilled slice of ham, on bread rubbed with garlic. Nothing else: the mogette has a skin so fine it melts, and needs no help.
s: Soak the beans for two hours only — any longer and they would burst.
Put them in cold unsalted water with onion, carrot, garlic, thyme and bay; salt only halfway through.
Simmer for 1½ hours without ever boiling: a hard boil would loosen the skins.
Drain, keeping a little of the liquor, and enrich with the salted butter and cream.
Toast the bread, rub it with garlic, spoon the beans on top and crown with a slice of just-seared ham.

cagouilles-charentaise.d: Small grey snails stewed in the Charente manner, with ham, sausage meat and a great deal of garlic. The people of Charente call themselves cagouillards: slow as the snail, and proud of it.
s: Starve the snails for a week, wash them in vinegared water until it runs clear, then blanch them for 10 minutes.
Take them from their shells, remove the black coil and rinse once more.
Fry the diced ham, sausage meat and shallots in the oil, then dust with flour.
Add the snails, crushed garlic, tomato, white wine, thyme and bay; cover with water.
Simmer for 1¼ hours over low heat, add a great deal of parsley and serve with country bread.

ttoro.d: The fish soup of Basque cod fishermen, sharpened with Espelette pepper and thickened with bread. Made on board with hake heads and bones; ashore, it became a feast dish.
s: Make a stock with the hake heads and bones for 30 minutes, then strain it, pressing well.
