Set the meat on the salad, crown with a fried egg and serve with rice and the pepper sauce.

lamprais.d: Rice cooked in stock, three meats in curry, a candied aubergine and a shrimp rissole, all folded into a banana leaf and returned to the oven. A Dutch Burgher legacy: the name comes from lomprijst, 'packet rice'.
s: Make a stock with the three meats, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon; set the meats and stock aside separately.
Fry the rice in ghee with the whole spices, then cook it in the strained stock, never in water.
Dice the meats and simmer them in curry and coconut milk until the sauce is short.
Fry the aubergine in slices and candy it with tamarind, sugar and chillies: this is brinjal moju.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame to soften them, fill with rice and the accompaniments, fold into parcels and bake for 25 minutes at 180°C.

dal-bhat-tarkari.d: Rice, lentils and seasonal vegetables served together on a tray, twice a day, for a lifetime. Himalayan porters made a saying of it: 'dal bhat power, twenty-four hour'.
s: Rinse the lentils and cook them for 30 minutes with the turmeric, until they collapse completely.
Prepare the jhaneko, the tempering: sizzle the fenugreek, cumin, garlic, ginger and dried chillies in scorching ghee.
Pour this fragrant butter into the dal — it spits violently — and cover at once for a minute to trap the aromas.
For the tarkari, fry the vegetables with the same spices and a little tomato, covered, for 20 minutes.
Serve the rice in the centre of the tray, the dal in a bowl, the tarkari alongside, with yogurt and a pickle.

panch-phoron-torkari.d: A vegetable stew with panch phoron, the Bengali blend of five whole seeds that is never ground. Nigella, fennel, fenugreek, cumin and mustard: five flavours that reveal themselves one after another in hot oil.
s: Heat the mustard oil until it smokes then let it settle: raw it is acrid; smoked it turns sweet.
Drop in the whole panch phoron and the bay, and wait for the mustard seeds to pop — not before, not after.
Add the grated ginger and split chillies, then the vegetables in large pieces, firmest first.
Dust with turmeric, salt, add a pinch of sugar, and cover: the vegetables cook in their own water, with none added.
Give them 25 minutes over low heat, shaking the pan, and cover with coriander off the heat.

shivit-oshi.d: Deep green noodles, coloured by dill juice kneaded into the dough, under a stew of vegetables and meat. They are found only in Khiva and the villages around it: elsewhere in Uzbekistan nobody knows them.
s: Blend the dill with a glass of water and press it through a cloth: it is this green juice, and nothing else, that colours the dough.
Knead the flour, eggs, salt and dill juice for 15 minutes; rest for an hour.
Roll very thin, fold and cut 2 mm noodles, then flour them generously.
Sear the diced meat, add onion, carrot, pepper, tomato, garlic and cumin, cover with water and simmer for 40 minutes with the potatoes.
Cook the noodles for 3 minutes, arrange them in a nest and crown with the stew. Serve the yogurt alongside.

kuurdak.d: A fry-up of mutton and offal with onions and potatoes, cooked in a cast-iron kazan. It was the first dish made after slaughtering an animal, with the cuts that would not keep.
s: Render the diced mutton fat in the kazan until only scratchings remain, and lift them out.
Sear the meat in large cubes in that fat over high heat, without stirring too soon: it must brown.
Add the trimmed offal, then the sliced onions — a great many, as much as there is meat — and let them melt for 20 minutes.
Add the cumin, cracked pepper and bay, cover and simmer for 40 minutes in nothing but the released juices.
Add the potatoes in large pieces for the last 25 minutes, and serve with flatbread and coriander.

chelo-kabab-barg.d: Slices of fillet marinated in onion and saffron, grilled on flat skewers, served with rice crisped at the bottom of the pan. That golden tahdig is fought over at the table more than the meat itself.
s: Grate the onions and press out their juice; mix it with infused saffron, yogurt and lemon, and marinate the meat for 12 hours.
Rinse the rice seven times then soak it for 2 hours in salted water: this is what gives long separate grains.
Par-boil it for 6 minutes in plenty of water, drain, then mound it in a buttered pan with saffron.
Cover with a cloth and a lid and cook for 45 minutes over very low heat: a golden crust forms at the bottom.
Thread the meat onto flat skewers and grill for 3 minutes a side over fierce embers. Serve with the rice, the tahdig, grilled tomato and sumac.

maqluba.d: A dish of rice, aubergine and chicken built in layers then turned out in one piece onto a tray. Maqluba means 'upside down': the moment of inversion is done in silence, and applauded if it holds.
s: Poach the chicken for 40 minutes with onion, bay, cardamom and allspice; keep the broth, which will cook the rice.
Fry the aubergine slices and cauliflower florets until golden, then drain them.
Soak the rice for 30 minutes, drain it and mix it with the ground spices.
Line the base of a pot with aubergine in a rosette, then the boned chicken, the cauliflower, and finally the rice, well packed.
Pour in hot broth to two centimetres above the rice, cover and cook for 40 minutes. Rest for 15 minutes before inverting in one decisive movement.

kibbeh-nayyeh.d: Raw lamb pounded in a stone mortar with fine bulgur and spices, served as a smooth carpet under a thread of oil. It is made on the day of slaughter, and eaten within the hour: that is the rule.
s: Choose a leg of lamb slaughtered the same day, trim it of all fat and sinew, and keep it ice cold until the last moment.
Rinse the fine bulgur and squeeze it: it should be damp but not sodden.
Pound the onion and spices in a mortar into a paste, then add the meat in small amounts.
Pound at length, working in the bulgur and a few spoonfuls of iced water, until the mass is perfectly smooth.
Spread it thinly on a tray, draw furrows with your fingers, pour over olive oil and serve at once with mint, spring onions and bread.

ash-e-reshteh.d: A thick soup of pulses, herbs and noodles, finished with kashk — a dried fermented whey. Made for Nowruz, the Persian new year: the noodles stand for the threads of fate being untangled.
s: Soak the chickpeas and beans overnight, then cook them for 1 hour with the turmeric and one onion.
Add the lentils and continue for 25 minutes.
Chop all the herbs very finely — they should make an enormous volume, nearly two packed litres — and add them to the soup.
Break the noodles and drop them into the broth for 10 minutes; stir, as they catch easily.
Prepare two garnishes: onions fried to deep brown, and dried mint fried in oil with garlic. Serve with kashk swirled over.

khachapuri-megrelien.d: A round cheese bread, filled and also topped with sulguni, unlike the boat-shaped Adjarian version. Samegrelo doubles the dose: cheese inside and on top, and nobody apologises for it.
s: Dissolve the yeast and sugar in the warm milk, then knead with the flour, yogurt, one egg, melted butter and salt.
Prove for 1½ hours: the dough should be very supple, almost sticky.
Grate the sulguni and work two thirds of it by hand until it turns elastic.
Roll the dough into a disc, pile the cheese in the centre, gather the edges to the middle and turn the ball over. Flatten it gently with a rolling pin.
Glaze with egg, cover with the remaining cheese and bake for 20 minutes at 240°C. Butter it generously as it comes out.

rfissa.d: Chicken with fenugreek and ras el hanout served over hand-torn msemen pancakes. It is traditionally made for a new mother on the third day: the fenugreek is said to restore her strength.
s: Soak the fenugreek overnight: without this it stays hard and bitter.
Fry the sliced onions in the oil and smen until they melt, then add the spices and saffron.
Add the whole chicken, the lentils, the drained fenugreek and the tied bunch of herbs; cover with water.
Simmer for 1¼ hours, then lift out the chicken and reduce the sauce until it coats.
Tear the msemen by hand into wide shreds, lay them in the dish, ladle broth over so they swell, and crown with the chicken and lentils.

tanjia-marrakchia.d: Veal shank sealed in an earthenware jar and entrusted to the hammam stoker, who buries it in the ashes of the water furnace for five hours. It is the dish of the medina's bachelors: nobody cooks it at home.
s: Choose a well-marbled shank, cut into large pieces with the bone: the collagen makes the whole texture.
Crush the whole garlic, mix it with the cumin, ras el hanout, infused saffron and quartered preserved lemon.
Put everything into a narrow-necked jar with the smen, the oil and half a glass of water — no more.
Close the neck with tied greaseproof paper, pierced with a single needle hole.
Bury the jar in hot ash or cook it for 5 hours at 140°C. It is tipped onto a dish without ever being stirred.

chakhchoukha.d: Rougag flatbreads torn into small pieces and drenched in a lamb and chickpea sauce with chilli. The tearing is done by several people, by hand, the day before: women's work and an occasion to gather.
s: Knead fine semolina with warm water and salt, rest it, then roll very thin flatbreads cooked dry on an earthenware griddle.
Stack them, let them cool, then tear them by hand into pieces the size of a fingernail.
Fry the lamb and onion in the oil, add the tomato paste, paprika, harissa and caraway.
Add water, the soaked chickpeas and the cinnamon, and simmer for 1¼ hours.
Steam the torn bread for 10 minutes, moisten with a ladle of sauce, toss, and lay the meat over the top.

mloukhia-tunisienne.d: An almost black sauce of pounded jute leaves, cooked for five hours until the oil rises to the top. It is served at the Muslim new year so that the year will be green — that is, prosperous.
s: Slake the jute powder in cold water very gradually, whisking: tipped in at once it forms lumps that cannot be undone.
Heat the olive oil in a tall pot, throw in the garlic and bay, then pour in the green paste.
Cook uncovered for 2 hours over very low heat, stirring every twenty minutes with a wooden spoon.
Add the meat in large cubes, the spices and hot water, and continue for 3 hours.
The sauce is ready when it has blackened and the oil beads on the surface. It keeps a week and improves every day.

lablabi.d: A chickpea broth with garlic and cumin poured over stale bread crumbled in the bottom of the bowl, with a poached egg and harissa. The winter breakfast of Tunis labourers, served from five in the morning.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight with a pinch of bicarbonate, then cook them for 1¼ hours with half the garlic.
On no account throw away the cooking water: cloudy and fragrant, it is what makes the dish.
Pound the rest of the garlic with the cumin and salt, and slake it in a little broth.
Crumble the stale bread into each bowl, ladle scalding broth over it generously and let it drink.
Add the chickpeas, poached egg, a spoonful of harissa, olive oil, capers, olives, tuna and lemon. Each diner mixes.

bazeen.d: A dome of boiled barley dough set in the middle of the dish, ringed by a lamb sauce and crowned with hard-boiled eggs. It is eaten with the hand, pinching the dough and dipping it: never with a spoon.
s: Fry the lamb and onion, add the tomato paste and let it darken for two minutes: raw, it stays acidic.
Add the spices, the soaked chickpeas and water, and simmer for an hour with the potatoes.
Bring a litre of salted water to the boil and tip in the barley flour all at once, without stirring, leaving a well.
Cover and leave for 15 minutes, then work vigorously with a wooden stick until the dough is smooth and dense.
Shape a dome in the middle of the dish with wet hands, ring it with the sauce and set the hard-boiled eggs around.

mafe-thiof.d: A whole grouper stuffed with pounded herbs and baked under a mountain of lemony onions. Thiof is Senegal's emblematic fish, so prized that the word is a compliment: to call someone thiof is to call them handsome.
s: Pound the parsley, six garlic cloves, a chilli and salt into a green paste, the roff.
Score the fish diagonally on both sides and push the roff deep into each cut.
Marinate the sliced onions with lemon, mustard and bay for 2 hours, then soften them for 30 minutes in the oil.
Set the fish in a dish, cover it entirely with the onions and bake for 35 minutes at 190°C.
Never turn the fish: serve it in its dish, with white rice and the onion juices.

yassa-poulet.d: Chicken marinated in lime and grilled, then simmered in a mountain of melted onions. The proportion is disconcerting: as much onion as meat, and that is what makes the dish.
s: Marinate the chicken and sliced onions for 6 hours in lime juice, mustard, garlic and bay.
Drain and keep the marinade; grill the chicken pieces over charcoal until the skin is charred in places.
Melt the onions in the oil for 30 minutes, covered: they should turn golden and translucent without burning.
Pour in the marinade, add the chilli whole — unsplit, or the dish becomes inedible — and the olives.
Return the chicken, cover and simmer for 25 minutes. Serve over white rice.

to-au-gombo.d: A firm smooth paste of millet or maize, dipped in a slippery okra and soumbala sauce. It is swallowed unchewed, in balls shaped by hand: the stringy texture is precisely the point.
s: Bring two litres of water to the boil and slake a handful of millet flour in it to make a thin gruel.
Rain in the rest of the flour and work it with a wooden stick, pressing against the side, for 20 minutes.
The tô is ready when the paste comes away in one mass; mould it into a dome in a wetted bowl.
For the sauce, fry the onion and tomato in palm oil, add the dried fish, soumbala and chilli.
Add the sliced okra and baobab leaf powder, and give it 15 minutes: the sauce should trail in threads behind the spoon.

poulet-dg.d: Chicken and fried plantain tossed with crisp vegetables. DG stands for directeur général: in the 1980s only bosses could afford a whole chicken, and the name stuck as a joke.
s: Marinate the jointed chicken for an hour in pounded garlic and ginger, white pepper and thyme.
Fry it until golden and cooked through, then drain.
Fry ripe plantains cut on the bias in the same oil: they should caramelise at the edges.
Fry the onion, tomato and chilli in a little clean oil, then add the vegetables cut into batons.
Toss over high heat for 5 minutes — the vegetables must stay crunchy — then fold in the chicken and plantain off the heat.

koki-beans.d: A pudding of hulled cowpeas beaten with palm oil, steamed in banana leaves. The beating is the secret: the batter must become so light that a spoonful floats on a glass of water.
s: Soak the cowpeas for 6 hours, then rub them hard between your hands to remove every skin.
Blend them with the onion and chilli into a thick paste, without adding too much water.
Warm the palm oil and trickle it into the paste while beating with a wooden spoon, for a full 15 minutes.
Test the lightness: a spoonful dropped on a glass of water should rise and float. If not, beat on.
Fold in the shredded spinach, fill the softened banana leaves, close into parcels and steam for 1¼ hours.

egusi-soup.d: A thick soup of ground melon seeds, which set into small golden lumps in the palm oil. It is not stirred for the first twenty minutes: that is what lets the lumps form.
s: Cook the beef, tripe and stockfish for 45 minutes with the onion; keep the broth.
Grind the egusi seeds and mix them with a little water into a thick paste.
Heat the palm oil until it clears, then drop in the paste in spoonfuls, without stirring.
Let the lumps set for 10 minutes, then pour the broth gently around them and simmer for 20 minutes untouched.
Add the crayfish powder, locust beans, chilli and spinach, and continue for 10 minutes. Serve with cassava fufu.

red-red.d: Cowpeas stewed in red palm oil with very ripe fried plantain. The name comes from the double redness: that of the palm oil and that of the tomato sauce, never one without the other.
s: Soak the cowpeas for 4 hours, then cook them for 45 minutes with the bay, unsalted: salted too early, they toughen.
Heat the palm oil until it clears, without letting it smoke.
Soften the onion, garlic and ginger in it, add the tomato paste and let it brown for two minutes.
Add the crushed tomato, ground dried shrimp and whole chilli, and reduce for 15 minutes.
Fold in the drained beans and stew for 20 minutes. Serve with very ripe plantain fried on the bias.

poulet-kedjenou.d: Chicken smothered in a sealed clay canari, without a drop of added water. Kedjenou comes from Baoulé and means 'to shake': the pot is never opened, only shaken to stop it catching.
s: Joint the chicken and combine it with crushed tomatoes, quartered onions, African aubergines and the aromatics.
Season, pour in the oil and pack everything into an earthenware pot.
Seal the lid with a band of flour-and-water dough, or failing that a double sheet of foil pinched tight.
Cook for 1½ hours over low heat or in a 160°C oven, shaking the pot every fifteen minutes, never opening it.
On opening, the vegetables will have given up all their juice: it is the only liquid in the dish. Serve with rice or attiéké.

thiakry.d: Steamed millet couscous pearls drowned in sweetened soured milk, served very cold. It is the Ramadan dessert of all Senegambia, and breakfast for the rest of the year.
s: Moisten the millet couscous with a little salted water and let it swell for 10 minutes, separating the grains by hand.
Steam it for 15 minutes, separate the grains again, then let it cool completely: warm, it would turn the milk.
Whisk the yogurt, soured milk, condensed milk, sugar and scraped vanilla.
Fold in the cold couscous, grated nutmeg, raisins and orange blossom water.
Chill for at least 3 hours: the pearls should drink the milk without collapsing.

kitfo.d: Raw beef chopped by knife and warmed in spiced niter kibbeh butter, served with fresh cheese and collard leaves. Among the Gurage it is eaten on Meskel, around a fire lit at dusk.
s: Choose a fillet slaughtered the same day, trim it completely and keep it cold until the last minute.
Chop it by knife, never in a mincer: the fibres must stay distinct to the bite.
Warm the niter kibbeh without letting it smoke — it should not cook the meat, only warm it.
Combine the meat, butter, mitmita and ground cardamom with your fingertips.
Serve at once with the fresh cheese, chilli-stewed collards and injera. You may ask for leb leb, barely warmed, or yebesele, cooked.

shiro-wat.d: A purée of roasted, spice-ground chickpeas simmered until it bubbles like lava. It is the dish of the Orthodox fast, free of animal products, eaten more than two hundred days a year.
s: Soften the very finely chopped onion dry, without fat, for 10 minutes: it gives up its water and concentrates.
Only then add the oil, the pounded garlic and ginger, and fry for 5 minutes.
Stir in the berbere off the heat, then the tomato, and cook for 5 minutes.
Slake the shiro powder in half a litre of cold water, lump-free, and trickle it in while whisking.
Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring often: the purée should make large lazy bubbles. Serve on injera with a green chilli.

tsebhi-birsen.d: A red lentil stew with berbere, cooked until the lentils collapse into a thick purée. It is Eritrea's commonest fasting dish, served on injera with a raw green chilli to bite into.
s: Soften the very finely chopped onion dry for 10 minutes, without fat: it gives up its water and concentrates.
Add the oil and the pounded garlic and ginger, and fry for 5 minutes.
Stir in the berbere off the heat, then the tomato paste and tomato, and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and a litre of hot water, and simmer uncovered for 45 minutes.
Stir often for the last half hour: the lentils must collapse completely. Serve on injera.

fah-fah.d: A lamb broth intensely green with herbs and chilli, served with flatbread to mop it up. Also called soup number five, Djiboutians hold it a remedy for fatigue and fever.
s: Blanch the lamb and bones for 10 minutes, discard the water and rinse: the broth must stay clear.
Return them to three litres of water with the onion, garlic and cumin, and simmer for 1 hour, skimming.
Add the vegetables in large pieces and continue for 25 minutes.
Blend the coriander, parsley and green chillies with a ladle of broth into a vivid green purée.
Stir it into the soup off the heat — cooked, it would brown — and serve with lime and flatbread.

suqaar.d: Cubes of beef fried with xawaash, the Somali blend of cumin, coriander and cardamom, with pepper and onion. It is served with a raw banana, split lengthways.
s: Cut the beef into 1.5 cm dice and marinate for 30 minutes in the xawaash, garlic and lemon.
Heat the oil until it just smokes, and sear the meat in small batches.
Lift it out as soon as it is coloured: it will finish cooking when it returns to the pan.
Fry the onion and pepper for 5 minutes, add the tomato and chilli, and let it reduce.
Return the meat, warm through for a minute, cover with coriander and serve with rice and a raw banana.

mukimo.d: A green mash of potato, maize, beans and pumpkin leaves, pounded with a stick. Among the Kikuyu it is brought to the bridegroom on the wedding day: its vivid colour is a wish for abundance.
s: Soak the beans overnight then cook them for 50 minutes; the maize needs as long as they do.
Boil the peeled potatoes for 25 minutes in salted water.
Blanch the pumpkin leaves and spinach for 5 minutes, squeeze them dry and chop them very finely.
Bring everything together while still hot and pound with a wooden stick: the mash should stay lumpy, the grains still recognisable.
Fold in the butter-softened onion and adjust the salt. Serve as a dome, with a meat stew alongside.

urojo.d: A tangy yellow soup of green mango, topped with fritters, potatoes and skewers. Sold in the evening on the Forodhani gardens, it is also called 'Zanzibar mix': each diner builds their own bowl.
s: Cook the diced potatoes in a litre of water with the turmeric, garlic, ginger and grated green mango.
Slake the chickpea flour in cold water and trickle it in while whisking: the soup should coat without being thick.
Add the tamarind and coconut milk, and simmer for 15 minutes.
Prepare the toppings: potato fritters, fried cassava, grilled beef skewers.
Each diner builds their bowl: scalding soup, toppings, chilli sauce, coriander chutney and lime.

matoke-luwombo.d: Chicken and a groundnut sauce sealed in a banana-leaf parcel and steamed for three hours. Created in 1887 by the chef of Kabaka Mwanga II, it was originally served only at the Buganda court.
s: Pass the banana leaves over a flame until they green and soften: otherwise they split when folded.
Fry the onion, tomato and pepper, add the curry powder, then the jointed chicken.
Slake the peanut butter in a little hot water and stir it in: the sauce should stay very thick.
Set everything on two crossed leaves, gather into a purse and tie with a strip of leaf rib.
Steam for 2½ hours above the plantains cooking in the same pot. The parcel is opened at the table.

muamba-de-galinha.d: Chicken with palm oil and palm-nut pulp, with okra and squash. Angola's national dish, a direct cousin of Congolese moambe, which Portugal carried as far as Brazil.
s: Marinate the chicken for 2 hours in pounded garlic, lemon, salt and pepper.
Colour it in the palm oil, then add the onion and tomato.
Slake the palm-nut pulp in a litre of hot water and pass it through a sieve to remove the fibres.
Simmer uncovered for 40 minutes, until the orange oil rises clearly to the surface.
Add the cubed squash and whole okra for 20 minutes, with the chilli. Serve with cassava funge.

chikanda.d: A dense cake of wild orchid tubers, groundnut and bicarbonate, whose texture recalls meat. Known as 'African polony', its popularity now threatens the orchids of the high plateaus.
s: Dry the tubers then grind them to a fine flour in a mortar or mill.
Roast the groundnuts, rub off the skins and grind them in turn into an oily powder.
Bring a litre of water to the boil with the bicarbonate, salt, chilli and oil.
Rain in the tuber flour and groundnut powder, whisking constantly to avoid lumps.
Work with a wooden spoon for 30 minutes over low heat, until the paste leaves the bottom, then pour into a mould and let it set. Slice cold.

bunny-chow.d: A quarter loaf hollowed out and filled with curry, the crumb serving as both lid and spoon. Invented by Durban Indians under apartheid, to sell takeaway to those who could not enter a restaurant.
s: Fry the onion, cinnamon, star anise and curry leaves in the oil until the onion turns golden.
Add the pounded garlic and ginger, then the curry powder, and let it open up for 2 minutes.
Add the lamb and let it coat, then the grated tomato, and barely moisten.
Simmer covered for 1 hour, add the potatoes for 25 minutes: the sauce must be very thick, or the bread drowns.
Cut the loaf into four, hollow each quarter, fill with curry and set the removed crumb on top as a cap. Serve with a grated carrot salad.

potjiekos.d: A stew cooked in layers in a three-legged cast-iron pot set on embers and never stirred. The Voortrekkers carried it by wagon; the rule has not changed: whoever stirs ruins the potjie.
s: Render the bacon in the pot set over moderate embers, then sear the meat on all sides.
Add the onion and let it turn golden, pour in the wine and stock, and simmer covered for 1½ hours.
Arrange the vegetables in distinct layers, longest-cooking first: carrot, potato, squash, beans.
Salt only the surface and on no account stir: each tier must cook in the steam of the one below.
Give it another hour, then serve by digging in with a ladle from the edge, so the layers stay visible.

chakalaka.d: A relish of grated vegetables with curry and beans, born in the miners' hostels of the Witwatersrand. Every family swears its version is the right one, and no two use the same vegetables.
s: Fry the sliced onion in the oil until translucent.
Add the garlic, ginger, chilli and curry powder, and let it open up for a minute.
Add the peppers in strips, then the coarsely grated carrots — never finely, they would melt away.
Add the crushed tomato, cover and cook for 15 minutes: the carrots must stay firm.
Fold in the beans and cabbage at the end. Serve warm or cold, with pap or a braai.

ravitoto.d: Pounded cassava leaves, almost black, stewed with fatty pork and coconut milk. The pounding takes an hour in a wooden mortar: the raw leaves are toxic, and only this long cooking makes them safe.
s: Pound the cassava leaves at length in a wooden mortar, until you have a dark fibrous mass.
Blanch them for 15 minutes in plenty of water and squeeze them dry: this step is not optional.
Sear the pork in large lardons in its own fat, then add the onion, garlic and ginger.
Add the pressed leaves and a glass of water, cover and simmer for 1 hour over low heat.
Pour in the coconut milk for the last twenty minutes. Serve with white rice and a fiery sakay.

civet-de-zourite.d: An octopus civet with red wine, turmeric and kaffir lime, stewed until the flesh yields. Zourite comes from Malagasy orita; in Réunion it is beaten against a rock before cooking, and that is still done.
s: Beat the octopus, or freeze and thaw it: the fibres break and the flesh turns tender.
Cut it into lengths and stiffen it dry in the pot until it releases its water; throw that water away.
Add the oil, sliced onions, pounded garlic and ginger, and the turmeric.
Add the tomato, red wine, thyme, kaffir lime and whole chilli, and simmer covered for 1 hour.
Uncover for the last twenty minutes so the sauce coats. Serve with rice and red beans.

bobo-de-camarao.d: Prawns in a cassava cream with coconut milk and palm oil. The word bobó comes from Fon; the dish descends directly from West African ipeté, which reached Bahia with the slave trade.
s: Peel the prawns and make a stock with the shells; marinate them in lime and garlic.
Cook the cassava for 40 minutes in the stock, pull out the central fibre and blend it with the liquid into a smooth cream.
Make a refogado of onion, garlic, tomato and pepper in olive oil, 15 minutes.
Pour in the cassava cream and coconut milk, and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring.
Add the prawns and the palm oil for 4 minutes only: any longer and they turn rubbery. Coriander off the heat.

moqueca-capixaba.d: The moqueca of Espírito Santo, without coconut milk or palm oil, coloured only with annatto and cooked in a black clay pan. It has quarrelled forever with the richer, redder Bahian version.
s: Marinate the fish steaks for 30 minutes in lime, pounded garlic, salt and pepper.
Heat the clay pan gently — a thermal shock would crack it — and pour in the oil coloured with annatto.
Lay a bed of sliced onion, then the fish, then the tomato, never stirring.
Cover and cook for 20 minutes over medium heat: the fish gives up its juice, which becomes the broth.
Crown with coriander and spring onion off the heat. Serve with rice and pirão made from the broth thickened with cassava flour.

baiao-de-dois.d: Rice and cowpeas cooked together with dried beef and coalho cheese. The name comes from a dance for two: rice and bean, they say, dance in the same pot.
s: Soak the dried beef for 12 hours, changing the water three times, then cook it for 40 minutes and shred it.
Cook the cowpeas for 30 minutes with the bay, keeping the cooking liquid.
Fry the onion, garlic, sausage and shredded beef in the butter and oil.
Add the rice, let it turn pearly, then pour in the beans and their liquid: two parts liquid to one of rice.
Cover and cook for 18 minutes, then fold in the diced coalho cheese and the herbs off the heat.

barreado.d: Beef cooked twelve hours in a jar sealed with cassava-flour paste, until it falls into fibres. It was served at carnival to feed the men for three days without relighting the fire.
s: Cut the beef into large cubes and marinate for 4 hours with the onion, garlic, cumin, bay and cracked pepper.
Line the base of an earthenware jar with bacon, then pack in the meat and marinade without adding water.
Knead a paste of cassava flour and water, and seal the lid all the way round with it.
Cook for 10 to 12 hours over very low heat — the jar must never boil hard, only tremble.
Break the seal, shred the meat with a fork and serve with cassava flour, mashed banana and a slice of orange.

chupe-de-camarones.d: A soup of river prawns with milk, fresh cheese and ají panca, with a poached egg and corn. It is Friday's dish in Arequipa, and the heads traditionally go in, for flavour.
s: Peel the prawns and make a stock with the heads and shells for 20 minutes, then press it through a sieve.
Fry the onion, garlic and ají panca for 10 minutes: this base, the aderezo, must darken without burning.
Add the tomato, stock, rice, potatoes, corn and broad beans, and cook for 20 minutes.
Pour in the milk and let it steam without boiling, then add the diced fresh cheese and the huacatay.
Slide in the prawns and crack the eggs into the soup for the last three minutes only.

juane.d: A ball of turmeric rice and chicken wrapped in a bijao leaf and boiled. It is eaten on Saint John's day, 24 June: the ball is said to represent the Baptist's head on its platter.
s: Marinate the jointed chicken for 2 hours in garlic, cumin, turmeric and sacha culantro.
Colour it, then poach it for 25 minutes in the stock; keep the liquid.
Cook the rice three-quarters through in that yellow stock, drain it and let it cool.
Mix in four beaten eggs, then mould balls around a piece of chicken, half a hard-boiled egg and an olive.
Soften the leaves over a flame, wrap each ball in two crossed leaves, tie, and boil for 45 minutes.

rocoto-relleno.d: Rocoto peppers stuffed with minced beef, olives and hard-boiled egg, gratinated with cheese, alongside a potato gratin. The rocotos are blanched three times in sweetened water: without that, nobody could swallow them.
s: Cut the tops off the rocotos, remove the seeds and white ribs, which carry most of the heat.
Boil them three times for five minutes in sweetened, vinegared water, changing the water each time.
Fry the onion, garlic, ají panca and cumin, add the minced beef, then the peanuts, raisins and olives.
Stuff the peppers with this mixture and a slice of hard-boiled egg, cap them with cheese and their own lids.
Set them on a gratin of thinly sliced potatoes in milk, and bake for 35 minutes at 190°C.

locro-argentino.d: A stew of white hominy, squash and several meats, cooked for three hours and served with a chilli oil. It is eaten on 25 May and 9 July, the two patriotic dates: a national-holiday dish.
s: Soak the hominy and the beans overnight, separately.
Cook them for 1½ hours in four litres of water, without salt, until the grains begin to split.
Add the meats in large pieces and the cubed squash, and simmer for another 1½ hours.
Crush some of the squash against the side of the pot: it is what thickens the stew, never flour.
Make the salsa de freír: soften spring onion in the oil with paprika and chilli, off the heat. Each diner helps themselves.

humita-en-chala.d: A paste of freshly grated corn, onion and cheese, cooked in the husks of the cob itself. Far older than the conquest, it is made across the former Inca empire under different names.
s: Husk the cobs keeping the leaves whole: they will form the parcels. Blanch them for 2 minutes.
Grate the raw kernels on a coarse grater — never in a blender, which makes the paste watery.
Soften the onion and pepper in the oil with the paprika, without colouring them.
Combine the grated corn, vegetables, milk, basil and diced cheese; salt, add a pinch of sugar.
Cross two leaves, spoon on two tablespoons, fold into a parcel, tie with a strip of husk and steam for 40 minutes.

carbonada-criolla.d: A beef stew with dried and fresh fruit, served in a hollowed pumpkin that has baked in the oven with it. The sweet-savoury balance comes from Andalusia, but the pumpkin as vessel is a New World idea.
s: Cut a lid from the pumpkin, hollow it out and butter the inside; bake it for 25 minutes at 180°C.
Sear the cubed beef, lift it out, then soften the onion and pepper in the same fat.
Add the tomato, stock, bay and the meat, and simmer for 50 minutes.
Add the potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn in lengths and dried fruit for 25 minutes.
Pour the stew into the hot pumpkin, replace the lid and return it to the oven for 20 minutes. Serve scraping flesh from the walls.

curanto.d: Shellfish, meats and potato cakes cooked in a pit lined with scorching stones and covered with nalca leaves. It is as much a party as a dish: it takes twenty people and half a day.
s: Dig a pit a metre deep, line it with stones and light a fire on top until they glow red: allow two hours.
Rake out the embers, cover the stones with nalca leaves and lay the shellfish first, as they release the juice.
Add the meats, then the milcaos and chapaleles — cakes of grated potato and flour — then the peas.
Cover with leaves, a wet cloth and earth, letting not the least wisp of smoke escape.
Cook for 2½ hours without opening. The curanto is uncovered in one movement, and the shellfish juice is drunk first.

charquican.d: A thick mash of squash, potato and dried meat, crowned with a fried egg. The name mixes Quechua charqui, dried meat, and Mapudungun can, stew: two languages in one dish.
s: Soak the dried meat for 4 hours, drain it and chop it finely by knife.
Fry the onion and garlic in the oil, add the paprika, cumin and oregano off the heat.
Add the meat, then the squash and potatoes in large cubes, and add water only halfway up.
Cook covered for 35 minutes, then mash roughly with a fork against the side: neither smooth purée nor whole pieces.
Add corn, peas and green beans for 10 minutes, and serve each plate crowned with a fried egg.

lechona-tolimense.d: A whole pig emptied, stuffed with yellow peas, rice and its own meat, then baked ten hours in a wood oven. The skin must ring like glass: the only criterion Tolimenses recognise.
s: Soak the yellow peas overnight, then half-cook them: they will finish swelling inside the pig.
Bone the pig keeping the skin whole, and dice the meat, frying it with onion, garlic and cumin.
Mix meat, peas, raw rice and annatto; season very generously, the stuffing should taste saltier than seems reasonable.
Fill the skin without stretching it, sew it up with a trussing needle and prick the rind all over.
Rub with coarse salt and sour orange juice, and cook for 10 hours at 140°C, then 30 minutes at 220°C to blister the skin.

sancocho-valluno.d: A hen, green plantain and cassava soup, cooked over a wood fire on the riverbank. On Sundays Cali families go down to the river with the pot: the ritual matters as much as the recipe.
s: Cook the hen for 1 hour in four litres of water with the garlic, cumin and spring onion.
Break the green plantains by hand into irregular pieces: cut with a knife they blacken the broth.
Add them with the corn in lengths and cook for 25 minutes.
Add the cassava and potatoes for 25 minutes; the cassava should split into fibres.
Cover with coriander off the heat and serve with white rice, avocado and a wedge of lime.

pandebono.d: Small yeastless rolls of cassava starch and fresh cheese, crisp outside and elastic within. The name is said to come from an Italian baker crying 'pan de bono', good bread, in the streets of Cali.
s: Grate the fresh cheese very finely: it, not the flour, gives the dough its structure.
Mix it with the cassava starch, precooked maize flour, sugar and salt.
Add the eggs and butter, and knead by hand into a smooth supple dough, without adding water.
Shape rings or balls, tucking a cube of guava paste inside if you like.
Bake for 18 minutes at 220°C: they should puff and colour. They are eaten warm, never cold.

pabellon-criollo.d: Shredded beef, black beans, white rice and fried plantain, laid out in four separate quarters. It is often read as the country's three peoples: the white of the rice, the black of the beans, the brown of the meat.
s: Cook the flank steak for 1½ hours in water with the onion and bay, then let it cool in its broth.
Shred it by hand along the grain — never with a knife, the strands must stay long.
Fry the onion, pepper, garlic and tomato, add the cumin and the meat, and let it stew for 25 minutes with a little broth.
Cook the soaked black beans for 1 hour with a sofrito, finishing with a pinch of sugar: that contrast makes the dish.
Fry very ripe plantains on the bias and plate the four elements side by side, unmixed.

hallaca.d: Annatto-coloured corn dough filled with a stew of three meats, olives and capers, folded in banana leaf. They are made fifty or a hundred at a time in December, the family working a production line.
s: The day before, make the guiso: dice the three meats small, fry them with onion, pepper and garlic, add wine and simmer for 1 hour. Let it rest overnight.
Heat the oil with the annatto until it turns bright orange, and strain it.
Knead the precooked maize flour with the guiso broth and the coloured oil, into a supple dough that does not stick.
Pass the banana leaves over a flame, spread a flattened ball of dough, fill with guiso, olives, capers and raisins.
Fold into a rectangle, wrap in a second leaf, tie crosswise and boil for 45 minutes. They keep a week.

majadito.p: Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia
majadito.d: A rice of the Bolivian lowlands cooked with dried charque beef, coloured with annatto, served with a fried egg and plantain. It is wanted batido, soft, or seco, grain by grain — two camps that will never agree.
s: Soak the charque for 8 hours, then boil it for 30 minutes and shred it, pounding it lightly in a mortar.
Fry it in the oil until the fibres crisp, then set half aside for serving.
Fry the onion, pepper, garlic, tomato, cumin and annatto for 10 minutes.
Add the rice, let it turn pearly, then add three parts water to one of rice if you want it batido.
Cook covered for 25 minutes. Serve with fried plantain, a fried egg and the reserved crisp meat.

fanesca.d: A soup of twelve grains and salt cod, made just one week a year, at Easter. The twelve grains are the apostles and the cod is Christ: the dish is a catechism.
s: Soak the cod for 24 hours, changing the water four times, then poach it in the milk; keep that fragrant milk.
Cook each pulse separately: they do not share a cooking time, and together some would collapse.
Make a refrito of onion, garlic, cumin and annatto, the base of the whole soup.
Add the mashed pumpkin and courgette, then the cod milk, the cream and the peanut purée.
Bring all the grains together, simmer for 30 minutes without boiling, add the flaked cod and the cheese. Serve with hard-boiled egg, fried plantain and empanadas.

seco-de-chivo.d: A kid stew simmered in beer and naranjilla juice, served with rice and plantain. Seco means 'dry', though it is saucy: the word means a dish without separate broth, not without liquid.
s: Marinate the kid for 6 hours in the beer, pounded garlic, cumin and naranjilla juice.
Drain it, pat it dry and sear it over high heat in oil coloured with annatto.
Make a refrito of onion, tomato and pepper, then return the meat with all its marinade.
Simmer covered for 2 hours, adding a little water if the sauce catches.
Blend the coriander with a little sauce and stir it in at the end, with the panela. Serve with rice, fried plantain and avocado.

vori-vori.d: A hen soup with dumplings of maize flour and cheese, rolled by hand one at a time. The name comes from Guaraní vorý vorý, 'ball ball': the doubling says there are many.
s: Fry the onion, pepper and tomato, add the jointed hen and let it colour.
Add three litres of water, the bay and the turmeric, and simmer for 1 hour.
Mix the maize flour and grated cheese, then add a ladle of hot broth, a spoonful at a time.
Roll small balls the size of a walnut between lightly oiled palms.
Drop them gently into the simmering soup and give them 15 minutes without stirring: they rise when they are done.

chaja.d: A cake of sponge, whipped cream, peaches and crumbled meringue, created in 1927 in Paysandú. The pastry cook Orlando Castellano named it after a marsh bird whose ruffled plumage it resembles.
s: Whisk four whole eggs with 150 g of sugar over a warm bain-marie to the ribbon, then fold in the sifted flour.
Bake the sponge for 20 minutes at 180°C and let it cool before cutting it into three discs.
Whip the remaining whites with 250 g of sugar into a firm meringue, pipe it in strips and dry it for 90 minutes at 100°C.
Whip the very cold cream with the vanilla, without over-beating: it should stay soft.
Build the cake alternating sponge soaked in peach syrup, cream, dulce de leche and peaches, and cover it entirely in crushed meringue.

chupin-de-pescado.d: A stew of river fish — surubí or dorado from the Paraná — layered with potatoes and peppers. Fishermen cooked it on the bank in a single pot, layering and never stirring.
s: Cut the fish into thick steaks on the bone: the bone is what gives the broth body.
Line the pot with oil, then a layer of onion, pepper and sliced tomato.
Add a layer of potatoes, then the fish, then the vegetables again, salting each tier.
Pour in the white wine and just enough water to come level, add the bay and paprika.
Cover and cook for 40 minutes without ever stirring: only shake the pot. Parsley off the heat.

caldo-de-piedra.d: A fish soup cooked in seconds by a white-hot river stone plunged into a gourd. Among the Chinantec only men prepare it, and the gesture is as old as the village.
s: Heat smooth river stones in a wood fire for two hours, until they glow red.
Cut the fish into large pieces and peel the prawns; on no account cook them in advance.
Divide between gourds the raw fish, prawns, tomato, onion, garlic, chilli and herbs.
Pour in cold salted water to cover, then lower in a scorching stone with wooden tongs.
The water erupts into a boil and cooks everything in thirty seconds. Lift out the stone and serve at once with lime.

tlayuda.d: A large dried tortilla, grilled until it cracks, spread with black bean lard and covered in quesillo. It is folded in two over the coals: eaten flat it is a tlayuda; folded, a late-night clayuda.
s: Cook the black beans with epazote, then mash them and reduce them in the lard into a thick black paste, the asiento.
Grill the cecina and chorizo over the coals and cut them into pieces.
Lay the large tortilla on the grill and spread it with asiento as it heats.
Add the shredded quesillo and let it melt: the tortilla should crisp without burning, about 4 minutes.
Crown with finely shredded cabbage, meat, tomato, avocado and a pasilla chilli salsa. Fold in two and eat by hand.

papadzules.d: Tortillas rolled around hard-boiled egg, cloaked in a green pumpkin-seed sauce with its separated pepita oil. The Maya name is said to mean 'food of the lords'; the dish predates the conquest.
s: Toast the pumpkin seeds dry without letting them brown, then grind them very finely.
Infuse the epazote in half a litre of hot salted water, and strain.
Work the seed powder with this warm water, kneading by hand: the green oil separates and rises. Spoon it off.
Make a tomato sauce with the onion, garlic and whole habanero, and pass it through a sieve.
Dip each tortilla in the seed paste, roll it around chopped hard-boiled egg, cloak with tomato sauce and drizzle over the reserved green oil.

chiles-en-nogada.d: A poblano chilli stuffed with meat and fruit, cloaked in a fresh walnut cream and scattered with pomegranate. Green, white, red: the colours of the flag. It is served only in August and September, when the walnut is milky.
s: Char the poblanos over a flame until the skin blisters, close them in a bag for 10 minutes, then peel and empty them through a slit.
Make the picadillo: fry onion and garlic, add the meats, the tomato, then the diced fruit, raisins, almonds and cinnamon. Cook down for 30 minutes.
Peel the fresh walnuts one by one, removing the thin bitter skin: it is slow, and it is essential.
Blend them with the fresh cheese, cream and sherry, without sugar: the nogada must stay a frank white.
Stuff the chillies, cloak them in cold nogada and scatter pomegranate seeds and parsley. Never reheat.

birria-de-res.d: A beef stew with guajillo chillies and cinnamon, whose red broth is used to dip the tacos. Birria once meant 'worthless thing': the colonists scorned goat, and Mexicans made a masterpiece of it.
s: Toast the chillies dry for 30 seconds a side — no more, or they turn bitter — and soak them for 30 minutes.
Blend them with the tomato, garlic, spices and vinegar into a smooth sauce, and pass it through a sieve.
Rub it over the meat and marinate for 6 hours.
Cook for 3 hours covered, with water halfway up and the bay, until the meat falls apart.
Shred the meat and skim the broth, keeping the red oil from the top: it is what the filled tortillas are fried in before being dipped in the consommé.

machaca-con-huevo.d: Sun-dried beef pounded until fluffy, fried with eggs and a pico de gallo. Machacar means 'to pound': in the northern desert the dried meat was beaten with a stone to tenderise it.
s: Soak the dried beef in warm water for 15 minutes, squeeze it dry, then pound it in a mortar until it falls into strands.
Toast it dry in a very hot pan to rehydrate it and concentrate its flavour.
Add the oil, onion, garlic and serrano chilli, and soften for 4 minutes.
Add the crushed tomato and let it evaporate completely: moisture would make the eggs runny.
Pour in the beaten eggs and scramble over low heat, barely setting them. Serve in flour tortillas.

kak-ik.d: A vivid red Q'eqchi' turkey soup with cobanero chilli and annatto. The name comes from kak, red, and ik, chilli; a Maya ceremonial dish declared Guatemalan national heritage.
s: Cook the jointed turkey for 1 hour in three litres of water with the onion and garlic; keep the broth.
Char the chillies, tomatoes and tomatillos dry on a griddle, until they blacken in patches.
Blend them with the annatto and a ladle of broth, then pass through a fine sieve.
Cook this purée for 20 minutes over low heat, stirring, then stir it into the broth.
Return the turkey, add the coriander and mint ten minutes before the end, and serve with tamalitos or rice.

sopa-de-caracol.d: A Garifuna conch soup with coconut milk, cassava and green plantain. It travelled the world in 1991 on a Banda Blanca song, and many know the chorus without knowing the dish.
s: Beat the conch with a mallet to tenderise it, then cut it into strips and rub it with lime.
Fry the onion, garlic and annatto in the oil, and add the cumin.
Add a litre of water with the cassava, the green plantain broken by hand and the carrot.
Cook for 30 minutes, then pour in the coconut milk and let it steam without boiling.
Add the conch for 8 minutes only: overcooked it turns to rubber. Coriander and lime off the heat.

olla-de-carne.d: A Costa Rican boiled dinner with seven different roots, cooked for three hours on Sundays. The broth is drunk first from a cup, before the meat and vegetables come to the table.
s: Cook the shank on the bone for 2 hours in four litres of water, with the onion and garlic, skimming regularly.
The collagen from the bone is essential: without it the broth stays thin and flat.
Add the roots in order of firmness — cassava, yautía, sweet potato — at twenty-minute intervals.
Finish with the squash, chayote, corn and plantain, which need 20 minutes.
Serve the broth in a cup first, then meat and vegetables in a deep plate, with rice and lime.

tamal-en-cazuela.d: The Cuban tamal freed from its husk: fresh corn and pork cooked together in a pot, like polenta. It was invented out of frank laziness, and nobody in Havana apologises for it.
s: Marinate the diced pork for 2 hours in sour orange, garlic, cumin and oregano.
Render the bacon, sear the pork, then lift it out and make the sofrito: onion, pepper, garlic, tomato, 20 minutes.
Grate the fresh corn and blend it with the maize flour and a litre of water; sieve to remove the fibres.
Pour this cream into the sofrito and cook for 45 minutes over low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon.
Return the pork for the last 20 minutes. The cazuela is ready when the spoon stands up in the middle.

arroz-con-gandules.d: Puerto Rico's national rice, with pigeon peas and sofrito, prized for its caramelised bottom crust, the pegao. Serving rice with no pegao is taken as an admission of clumsiness: it is scraped up and fought over.
s: Render the salt pork and smoked ham in a cast-iron caldero, until they crisp.
Add the sofrito and annatto, and fry for 5 minutes: the fat should turn orange.
Add the tomato sauce, olives, capers and spices, then the drained pigeon peas.
Pour in the rice and water to one centimetre above it, and never stir after that moment.
Let it evaporate uncovered, then cover for 20 minutes over very low heat. Raise the heat for 2 minutes at the end to form the pegao.

soup-joumou.d: A pumpkin and beef soup drunk every 1 January. Under the colony it was forbidden to the enslaved; independence in 1804 made it the symbol of freedom regained, and UNESCO listed it in 2021.
s: Wash the meat with lime, as custom requires, then marinate it for 4 hours in epis.
Cook it for 1 hour with the thyme, cloves and whole chilli; keep the broth.
Boil the pumpkin in pieces until it collapses, then blend it with its water into a smooth cream.
Combine the purée and the broth, add the vegetables in order of firmness and give them 30 minutes.
Add the vermicelli for the last eight minutes. The soup should coat the spoon without being thick.

sancocho-dominicano.d: A thick soup of seven meats and seven root vegetables, served on great occasions. Each meat goes in at its own moment; a cook who adds them all at once is shown the door.
s: Marinate each meat separately in sour orange, garlic and oregano for 2 hours.
Sear them one after another in the pot, starting with the goat and beef, which take longest.
Add five litres of water and simmer for 1 hour before adding pork, chicken and sausage.
Add the roots in order of firmness: yam, yautía, cassava, then plantain and squash.
Crush a little squash and plantain against the side to thicken the soup. Serve with white rice and avocado.

pelau.p: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
pelau.d: Chicken caramelised in burnt sugar, then cooked with rice, pigeon peas and coconut milk. The sugar must blacken and smoke before the meat goes in: the gesture that defines the whole dish.
s: Marinate the chicken for 4 hours in green seasoning, the Trinidadian herb and garlic paste.
Heat the oil and brown sugar in a heavy pot, without stirring, until the caramel smokes and blackens.
Drop the chicken in at once and stir to coat: it should take on a mahogany colour.
Add onion, carrot, squash, pigeon peas, thyme and ketchup, then the rinsed rice.
Pour in the coconut milk and water to one centimetre above the rice, set the whole chilli on top, cover and cook for 25 minutes.

hangi.d: Meat and vegetables cooked in an earth oven on white-hot volcanic stones, under wet sacking. In Rotorua some families use geothermal steam directly: there the ground cooks the meal by itself.
s: Dig a pit a metre square and sixty centimetres deep, and stack volcanic stones on a hardwood fire in it.
Let them heat for three hours: the stones must be grey with heat and no longer black.
Rake out the wood, level the stones, and cover them with green leaves or wet cloths to prevent scorching.
Stack the baskets: meat at the bottom, roots in the middle, greens on top. Throw on a bucket of water to raise the steam.
Cover with wet sacking then earth, letting no steam escape, and leave for 3 hours. The hāngī is unearthed in silence.

boil-up.d: A broth of smoked pork bones, wild pūhā and kūmara, with dumplings called doughboys. It is the everyday Māori dish, made when the pot must feed everyone without warning.
s: Blanch the smoked bones for 10 minutes and throw away that first, very salty water.
Return them to three litres of clean water with the onion and simmer for 1 hour.
Wash the pūhā several times and rub it between your hands until the milky sap runs: this is what removes the bitterness.
Add the roots in large pieces and cook for 25 minutes.
Make the doughboys from flour, baking powder, butter and milk, drop them on the broth, cover and let them swell for 15 minutes. Add the pūhā last.

damper-au-feu.d: An unleavened bread baked under ash, invented by bush drovers who had neither oven nor yeast. It is broken by hand and eaten with golden syrup, never cut with a knife.
s: Build a hardwood fire and let it fall to thick embers: you need hot ash, not flame.
Mix the flour, baking powder and salt, then rub in the cold butter with your fingertips.
Pour in the milk all at once and bring the dough together in a few movements only: overworked, it bakes hard as a stone.
Shape a flattened round, cut a cross in the top and flour it generously.
Bury it under hot ash for 40 minutes, or bake for 35 minutes at 200°C. The loaf sounds hollow when it is done.

vakalolo.d: A cake of grated cassava cooked in leaves, coated with a caramel of coconut milk and cane sugar. It is shared at the lovo, the Fijian earth oven, and the first portion goes to the village elders.
s: Grate the peeled cassava finely and squeeze out some of the juice: too wet, the cake will not set.
Mix it with half the coconut cream, a third of the sugar and a pinch of salt.
Spread the paste 3 cm thick on banana leaves softened over a flame, and fold into a flat parcel.
Cook for 50 minutes by steaming or in the lovo, until the paste turns translucent.
Make a caramel with the remaining sugar, pour in the rest of the coconut cream off the heat and coat the warm cake with it.

panipopo.d: Yeasted buns baked in a coconut milk sauce that caramelises around them. Pani comes from English 'bun', popo means coconut: the name alone tells the history of the Pacific.
s: Dissolve the yeast and a spoonful of sugar in the warm milk, and let it froth for ten minutes.
Knead with the flour, melted butter, egg, 50 g of sugar and the salt for 10 minutes, then prove for 1 hour.
Shape 60 g balls and set them close together in a buttered dish, without quite touching.
Let them rise for 40 minutes, then pour round the coconut milk whisked with the remaining sugar and the cornstarch.
Bake for 30 minutes at 190°C: the buns swell as they drink the sauce, which caramelises underneath.

ota-ika.d: The Tongan cousin of kokoda, drier and more peppery, where the fish steeps only a few minutes. In Tonga it is made on Sunday after church, on the beach, with fish caught the day before.
s: Cut very fresh tuna into even cubes and keep it on ice until the last moment.
Salt it and pour over the lime juice: leave only ten minutes, the flesh must stay red at the centre.
Drain without pressing and discard the juice.
Add the coconut cream, thinly sliced red onion, tomato, cucumber and chilli.
Season generously with pepper and serve at once, before the salt draws water from the vegetables.

saksak.p: Rabaul, New Britain, Papua New Guinea
saksak.d: A pudding of sago starch and banana cooked in coconut cream, translucent and elastic. Sago comes from the heart of a felled palm: one tree feeds a family for months.
s: Slake the sago starch in cold water and let it settle, then pour off the clear water on top.
Mash the very ripe bananas with a fork and combine them with the sago paste.
Heat the coconut cream with the sugar and a pinch of salt, without letting it boil.
Pour in the mixture, stirring constantly: the paste turns translucent and starts to stretch within minutes.
Turn it out onto banana leaves, roll into a log, tie it and let it firm for an hour before slicing.

simboro.d: Rolls of grated cassava wrapped in island cabbage leaves and poached in coconut milk. It is the everyday laplap: quicker, without an earth oven, but still grated on stone.
s: Grate the peeled cassava very finely and squeeze out some of its juice, without drying it out.
Salt the paste and shape finger-sized rolls between wet palms.
Wrap each in two or three island cabbage leaves, pulled tight, and tie with a strip of leaf.
Pack them closely in a pot and cover with coconut milk let down with a little water.
Poach for 50 minutes over low heat without boiling, then finish with coconut cream and spring onion.

ika-mata-rarotonga.d: Raw tuna with coconut milk and lime, and very little else: spring onion, cucumber and salt. Restraint is the rule in the Cooks — you are meant to taste the fish, not the garnish.
s: Cut the tuna into 1.5 cm dice, discarding sinewy parts.
Toss it with salt and lime juice and leave 15 minutes, no longer.
Drain thoroughly: the fish should stay pink at the centre.
Add the fresh coconut milk, sliced spring onion, diced cucumber and tomato.
Serve immediately, in very cold bowls or half coconut shells.

poe-banane.d: A dense pudding of mashed banana and cassava starch, baked and drowned in fresh coconut milk. It was once cooked underground in the ahimaʻa; the modern oven shortened it without betraying it.
s: Choose very ripe, almost black bananas: all the sweetness of the dish comes from them.
Mash them with a fork, never in a blender, to keep some texture.
Mix them with the cassava starch, sugar, scraped vanilla and lime zest.
Pour into a buttered dish 4 cm deep and bake for 50 minutes at 180°C: the top should brown and the centre stay wobbly.
Let it cool, cut into squares and serve drowned in fresh coconut milk, never heated.

ali-nazik.d: A purée of smoked aubergine with yogurt and garlic, crowned with knife-chopped lamb. Legend says Sultan Selim, served in Gaziantep, asked whose gentle hand had made it: 'eli nazik'.
s: Char the whole aubergines directly over a flame until the skin is black and the flesh collapses.
Let them steam in a bag, peel them and drain them for 20 minutes: the bitter water must go.
Mash the flesh with a fork with the yogurt and pounded garlic, and keep it warm over a bain-marie — never direct heat.
Chop the lamb and fat by knife, sear them over high heat without stirring, add the tomato paste and tomato.
Spread the purée in the dish, hollow a well, spoon in the meat and pour over butter melted with Aleppo pepper.

perde-pilav.d: A pilaf of chicken, almonds and currants sealed in a golden dome of pastry. It was served to newlyweds: the curtain of dough stands for the home, the almonds for children to come.
s: Poach the chicken for 40 minutes; bone it, dice it and keep the stock.
Fry the blanched almonds and pistachios in butter, add the rinsed rice, then the stock, currants and spices. Cook for 15 minutes and let it cool.
Knead the flour, butter, eggs, yogurt and baking powder into a supple dough; rest it for 30 minutes.
Butter a deep mould and line it with dough rolled to 5 mm, leaving the edges hanging.
Fill with the pilaf, well packed, fold the dough over, glaze with egg and bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. Turn it out hot, in one movement.

manti-kayseri.d: Minuscule lamb dumplings served under garlic yogurt and chilli butter. In Kayseri they say a good daughter-in-law fits forty on one spoon: the size is an examination.
s: Knead the flour, eggs, water and salt for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it for an hour.
Chop the lamb with the onion and parsley, and season generously.
Roll the dough until you can see the grain of the table through it, then cut 2 cm squares.
Place a speck of filling the size of a rice grain on each, and pinch the four corners together at the centre.
Poach for 8 minutes in salted water, plate under garlic yogurt and pour over butter melted with chilli and dried mint.

tepsi-baytinijan.d: A gratin of fried aubergine, meatballs and tomato, layered in a tray. Tepsi means the tray itself: in Baghdad it was sent to the neighbourhood oven, since homes had none.
s: Cut the aubergines into thick rounds, salt them and let them drain for 30 minutes; pat them thoroughly dry.
Fry them until golden, then the potatoes and peppers in the same oil.
Mix the minced meat, grated onion, parsley and baharat, and shape small flat patties, which you sear.
Layer in a tray: aubergine, patties, potato, pepper, sliced tomato.
Pour over the tomato paste slaked in a glass of water and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C. Serve with white rice.

kibbeh-bil-sanieh.d: Two layers of pounded bulgur and lamb, hiding a filling of meat, onion and pine nuts. Diamonds are scored before baking: decorative, but above all it lets you cut portions without breaking the crust.
s: Rinse the fine bulgur and squeeze it; it should be damp, never sodden.
Pound the trimmed leg with a third of the onion and the spices, then work in the bulgur, adding iced water little by little until the paste is smooth.
Make the filling: softened onion, minced lamb, toasted pine nuts, pomegranate molasses, cinnamon.
Spread half the paste 1 cm thick in a buttered tray, cover with the filling, then the second half, smoothing with a wet hand.
Score diamonds with a blade, pour over melted butter and bake for 40 minutes at 200°C. Serve with minted yogurt.

maftoul.d: A Palestinian couscous hand-rolled into pearls far larger than in the Maghreb, served with chicken and chickpeas. Rolling maftoul is village knowledge: it is done by several people, on a large tray.
s: Moisten the fine bulgur with salted water and roll it on a tray, dusting with flour, in circular movements.
Continue until the pearls are the size of a peppercorn, then sift to remove loose flour.
Poach the chicken for 50 minutes with the whole spices and onion; keep the broth.
Steam the maftoul for 25 minutes above the broth, fluffing it twice with a fork.
Soften the sliced onions in olive oil, fold them into the maftoul with the chickpeas, and set the chicken on top.

galayet-bandora.d: Tomatoes seared in olive oil with garlic and green chilli, reduced until jammy. It is the September harvest dish: when tomatoes are abundant, they are scorched rather than stewed.
s: Choose very ripe tomatoes and cut them into large wedges, without peeling or seeding them.
Heat the olive oil until it shimmers, and drop in the crushed whole garlic and split green chillies.
Add the tomatoes all at once and let them sear untouched for 5 minutes: they should blacken in places.
Crush them roughly with a spoon and reduce uncovered for 20 minutes.
Season, add the Aleppo pepper and mint off the heat. It is eaten from the pan, dipping bread.

sayadieh.d: Brown rice cooked in a broth of fish and caramelised onions, topped with fried steaks and a tahini sauce. The colour comes from no spice: only from onions taken to a deep brown.
s: Salt the fish steaks and let them stand for 30 minutes, then pat dry and fry them; set aside.
Fry the sliced onions in the same oil for 30 minutes, to a deep brown: this step, and nothing else, gives the colour.
Take out a third for serving, and blend the rest with a litre of hot water; strain this brown broth.
Cook the rice in it with the cumin, cinnamon and bay, 18 minutes covered.
Whisk the tahini with lemon, garlic and a little water until it whitens. Plate rice, fish, fried onions, almonds and pine nuts, sauce alongside.

zurbian.d: A lamb rice with yogurt, saffron and potato, cooked in layers and scented with agarwood. It is smoked at the end: a coal set in a small dish in the heart of the rice, under the lid.
s: Marinate the lamb for 4 hours in the yogurt, garlic, ginger and hawaij.
Fry the sliced onions to a deep brown and set half aside.
Cook the lamb and its marinade for 1 hour with the whole spices, then add the potatoes.
Par-boil the rice for 6 minutes in plenty of salted water and drain it half cooked.
Layer meat, rice, fried onion, saffron and ghee; cover for 30 minutes over low heat, then smoke with a coal for 5 minutes.

qoozi-bahreini.d: A whole lamb set on a mountain of rice with dried fruit, cooked four hours at low temperature. It is served at the centre of the table for weddings, and taken apart by hand, without a knife.
s: Rub the lamb with baharat, salt and melted ghee, and leave it 6 hours in the cold.
Seal it in a covered dish with a little water and cook for 3½ hours at 150°C: the steam does all the work.
Strain the released juices and use them to cook the soaked rice, with the pierced dried limes and whole spices.
Fry the almonds, pine nuts and raisins separately in ghee, and candy the carrots cut into fine julienne.
Uncover the lamb and give it 25 minutes at 220°C to colour. Set it on the rice, covered with the nuts and saffron in rose water.

mashuai.d: A whole kingfish grilled over coals, served on black-lime rice. The fish is rubbed only with salt and turmeric: in Muscat a good fish is held to need nothing else.
s: Gut and scale the fish, and score it three times on each side down to the bone.
Rub it with turmeric, coarse salt and pounded garlic, working into the cuts, and leave it 1 hour.
Grill it over moderate coals for 20 minutes a side, basting with lemon ghee.
Cook the rice with the pierced dried limes, cardamom and fried onion, in barely salted water.
Serve the whole fish on the rice, with lemon and coriander. It is opened at the table, by hand.

balaleet.d: Sweet vermicelli with saffron and cardamom, covered with a thin savoury omelette. The simultaneous sweet and salty disconcerts visitors; in the Emirates it has always been the Eid breakfast.
s: Break the vermicelli by hand into 4 cm lengths and colour them in the ghee, stirring constantly.
They should turn hazelnut, not brown: ten seconds too long and they turn bitter.
Pour in boiling water to cover, barely salt it, and cook for 6 minutes.
Add the sugar, infused saffron, cardamom and rose water, and let it evaporate completely, uncovered.
Make a very thin, barely set omelette, seasoned, and lay it whole over the vermicelli. Pistachios on top.

khoresh-fesenjan.d: A dark brown stew of ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses, sweet-sour and very old. It appears on Assyrian tablets; in Sari it is served with duck rather than chicken.
s: Grind the walnuts very finely, almost to a paste, then dry-toast them for 10 minutes over low heat, stirring constantly.
Fry the onions golden, add the turmeric, then the chicken, and let it colour.
Add the walnuts and a litre of hot water, and simmer uncovered for 1½ hours, stirring often.
The walnut oil must rise and the stew darken to almost black-brown: it is the only test of doneness.
Add the pomegranate molasses, sugar and saffron, and give it another 30 minutes. Serve over saffron rice with pomegranate seeds.

dolma-azerbaidjan.d: Three stuffed vegetables served together — tomato, pepper and aubergine — called the three sisters. Azerbaijani dolma is UNESCO-listed; the mint and fennel in the filling set it apart from its neighbours.
s: Cut the tops off the three vegetables and hollow them carefully, keeping the lids: the walls must stay thick enough to hold.
Salt the inside of the aubergines and let them drain for 20 minutes, then rinse them.
Mix the minced lamb, raw rice, very finely chopped onion, chopped herbs and ground fennel.
Fill without packing — the rice swells — and replace each vegetable's lid.
Pack them tightly in a pot, add a glass of water and the butter, cover and cook for 50 minutes over low heat. Serve with garlic yogurt.

harissa-armenienne.d: A porridge of hulled wheat and chicken beaten until silky, unsalted until the very end. Tradition links it to the siege of Musa Dagh: villagers are said to have pooled the last of their wheat and poultry.
s: Soak the hulled wheat overnight in cold water.
Poach the chicken for 1 hour in four litres of water, bone it and return the meat to the broth.
Add the drained wheat and cook for 4 hours over very low heat, stirring every half hour so nothing catches.
Beat with a whisk or pestle for the last hour, until wheat and meat become a single cream.
Salt only at the very end — salted too early, harissa never binds. Serve under a pool of cumin-browned butter.

khinkali.d: Large meat dumplings whose broth is drunk first, biting into the side. You hold the khinkali by its dough tail, which is never eaten: guests count the tails left on the plate.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it for an hour under a cloth.
Mix the minced meats, grated onion, garlic, coriander and spices with 200 ml of iced water: the filling must be frankly liquid, as it becomes the broth.
Roll 12 cm discs, thicker at the centre than at the edges.
Place a large spoonful of filling and pleat the edge round, counting at least nineteen folds, then pinch the tail.
Poach for 12 minutes in barely simmering salted water. Pepper generously, bite the side, drink the juice, then eat — leaving the tail.

chakapuli.d: Milk-fed lamb stewed in white wine with sour green plums and a mountain of tarragon. A strictly seasonal spring dish: without green tkemali and fresh tarragon, it is not made.
s: Cut the lamb into large pieces on the bone and lay it in a pot, with no fat and no prior browning.
Cover with a thick layer of sliced spring onions and the whole green plums.
Pour in the white wine — it should not cover the meat — put on the lid and cook for 40 minutes over low heat.
Only then add the picked tarragon in very large quantity, with coriander, parsley, garlic and chilli.
Continue for 20 minutes covered: the herbs should wilt without blackening. Serve in the pot, with bread.

beshbarmak-kazakh.d: Boiled horse and lamb served on wide squares of pasta and moistened with onions in broth. The name means 'five fingers': it is eaten by hand, and the eldest distributes the pieces by rank.
s: Simmer the meats for 2½ hours in a large pot, skimming relentlessly.
Knead the flour, eggs, a little broth and salt into a firm dough; rest it for 40 minutes.
Roll it very thin and cut 8 cm diamonds.
Poach them for 5 minutes in the skimmed broth — never in plain water, they would lose all their flavour.
Wilt the onion rings in a ladle of scalding broth. Plate the pasta, sliced meat and onions, and serve the broth separately, in bowls.

oshi-palav-tadjik.d: Tajik palov, with yellow and red carrots mixed, cooked in a kazan and served on a single platter. UNESCO-listed in 2016: it accompanies every birth and every wedding in the country.
s: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it in warm salted water.
Render the mutton fat in the kazan, remove the scratchings, and sear the meat over high heat.
Add the onion, then the yellow and red carrots in thick batons, never grated.
Cover with water, add chickpeas, quince, garlic heads and cumin, and let the zirvak simmer for 40 minutes.
Spread the rice on top without stirring, add boiling water to two fingers, let it evaporate then cover for 25 minutes. Invert onto the platter to serve.

dograma.d: Flatbread, meat and onion crumbled by hand into a scalding lamb broth. Everything must be torn by finger, never cut: the knife is banned, and the blade is said to spoil the taste.
s: Cook the lamb and fat for 2 hours in three litres of water with the bay, skimming.
Lift out the meat, let it cool, then shred it entirely by hand.
Crumble the churek bread between your fingers, into irregular pieces the size of a fingernail.
Slice the onion very finely, salt it and crush it by hand to soften it.
Combine bread, meat, onion and tomato in a large bowl, pour the scalding broth over and serve at once, before the bread collapses.

ashak.d: Dumplings of wild garlic chives under garlic yogurt and a meat sauce with split peas. The gandana chive grows only in Afghanistan; exiles substitute leek, and always apologise for it.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt for 12 minutes into a firm dough and rest it for an hour.
Slice the leek and spring onions very finely, salt them and let them drain for 20 minutes, then squeeze them hard: every drop must go.
Roll the dough very thin, cut 8 cm discs, fill them and seal into half-moons, pleating the edge.
Make a sauce with the onion, minced beef, soaked split peas, tomato paste and ground coriander, 40 minutes.
Poach the ashak for 6 minutes, set them on the garlic yogurt, spoon over the sauce and dust with dried mint.

sajji-baloutche.d: A whole chicken staked on a wooden skewer around an open fire, salted only, without spices. The Baloch judge doneness by sound: the skin must crack when struck with the back of a knife.
s: Score the chicken deeply and rub it with coarse salt, lemon and green papaya paste, which tenderises the fibres.
Leave it 4 hours: any longer and the papaya breaks the flesh down.
Stuff it with half-cooked rice, sew the opening shut and stake it on a green wooden skewer.
Plant the skewer at an angle forty centimetres from a wood fire and turn it every ten minutes, for 1½ hours.
Strike the skin: if it sounds hollow and splits, it is ready. Dust with chaat masala and serve with bread and raw onion.

buuz-mongol-oulan.d: Flat mutton pasties fried in fat, eaten by the dozen during Naadam. They are counted: a man who eats fewer than ten over the three days of festivities is thought unserious.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt into a firm dough and rest it for 40 minutes.
Chop the mutton and its fat by knife, mix with very finely chopped onion, garlic, caraway and a little water: the filling must stay moist.
Roll 12 cm discs, place a spoonful of filling, fold over and seal the edge with a flat pleat.
Flatten each pasty with the palm: this is what distinguishes them from steamed buuz.
Fry them 4 minutes a side in mutton fat at 170°C, until they blister and turn golden.
